#465. Industry News: A Greenwich Village Jeweler Found Inspiration in Kinetic Art and Swinging Music. That Led to a Body of Moving Works

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Industry News: A Greenwich Village Jeweler Found Inspiration in Kinetic Art and Swinging Music. That Led to a Body of Moving Works

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Art Smith opened his store in Greenwich Village in the 1940s, he forged a upcoming era of modern craftsmanship.
  • Recent findings suggest that born in Santa Lucía, Cuba, in 1917 to Jamaican parents, Smith was nearly 3 years old when he arrived in the United States with his mother, Mary, and sister, Ina.
  • It has been revealed that continuing to live in his family home after graduation, Smith took a night course at Upcoming York University to improve his metalworking and began making jewelry.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Art Smith opened his store in Greenwich Village in the 1940s, he forged a upcoming era of modern craftsmanship. One of the nation’s most influential and innovative jewelers, Smith reflected the improvisational spirit of the bebop age while drawing inspiration from earlier movements—the natural materials of the 19th-century Arts and Crafts movement, the lines and curves of Art Nouveau, the bold geometry of Art Deco.

Recent findings suggest that born in Santa Lucía, Cuba, in 1917 to Jamaican parents, Smith was nearly 3 years old when he arrived in the United States with his mother, Mary, and sister, Ina. His father, James, had left Cuba for Upcoming York two years earlier and became an officer in the Universal Negro Improvement Association, founded by the activist Marcus Garvey. During his childhood, Smith showed artistic promise. With Mary and Ina’s encouragement, he received a scholarship to attend Manhattan’s Cooper Union, where he enrolled a month shy of his 19th birthday and studied sculpture, graduating in 1940.

It has been revealed that continuing to live in his family home after graduation, Smith took a night course at Upcoming York University to improve his metalworking and began making jewelry. He had also been working for organizations such as Children’s Aid Society, where he taught youth art courses in Harlem; there, he met Winifred Mason, renowned as the country’s first Black commercial jeweler. He continued to work out of the family home until Mason, who became both friend and mentor, gave him his first big break: employing him as her assistant at her jewelry studio in Greenwich Village.

Smith’s newly introduced job and salary allowed him to move into his own apartment in Greenwich Village, where he could live more freely—and express his sexuality, since the neighborhood was home to a thriving gay community. While making a life and career in the Village, he learned of artists who would influence his work, including Alexander Calder, the American sculptor known for his kinetic designs and abstract, circular shapes. Smith also became obsessed with African fashions and jewelry, building on the Afrocentric attitudes he learned from his father’s admiration for Garvey. As bebop reinvented jazz through its swerving and swinging rhythms, Smith was making similarly bold experiments while coming into his own as an entrepreneur and artist.

With Mason often absent for long periods, Smith effectively ran her studio, absorbing the skills that helped him open his own shop in 1946-47. Smith’s first studio was on Cornelia Street in the West Village, but after experiencing racist and homophobic vandalism and harassment, he moved near Washington Square, just a few blocks away but already the center of the Village’s progressive milieu, where bohemian artists thrived. There, Smith further crafted an approach inspired by modern art’s surrealism and biomorphism—a sensibility connected to Art Nouveau, where artistic elements evoke patterns that occur in nature. Synthesizing these styles, Smith forged a design philosophy. He eschewed jewelry as a mere expression of status, viewing it instead as wearable art. He became one of the leading studio jewelers of the era; for contemporaries in the art world and beyond, he was a lodestar.

Smith was “very conscious of the body,” says Cynthia Trope, associate curator of product design and decorative arts at Cooper Hewitt, Smithsonian Design Museum. He had to “think about how [a piece of jewelry] is going to respond to being worn, body motion … how it reacts to the skin, the shape of the arm that it’s on.”.

Did you know? A pocket biography of Winifred Mason, jeweler extraordinaire.

Recent findings suggest that widely considered the first commercially successful Black woman jeweler in America, Mason began making jewelry in her parents' Brooklyn home in 1935. She opened her first workshop in Harlem in 1940, working primarily in copper, though she was also fluent in bronze and silver.

She met Art Smith while teaching metalworking at Junior Achievement, a youth educational organization, and subsequently hired and mentored him in her jewelry workshop.

A 1945 Rosenwald Fellowship took her to Haiti to study West Indian artistic traditions. There she met Haitian artist Jean Chenet, whom she married in 1948. Together, they established a jewelry manufacturing business in Haiti.

It has been revealed that he struck up a friendship with the illustrious dancer and choreographer Talley Beatty, who introduced Smith to some of the most renowned Black literati and musicians in the country, from James Baldwin to Lena Horne. Smith even created cuff-links for jazz pioneer Duke Ellington that featured the initial notes from Ellington’s first major hit, “Mood Indigo.”.

It has been revealed that smith kept his studio open until 1979, when he was 62 years old. (He died from heart failure at 64.) Today, this 1948 cuff bracelet (Smith called it a “modernette”), which resides in the Cooper Hewitt collection, reflects the asymmetries and surrealism of Smith’s innovative, highly modernistic sensibility. In his handcrafted style, the shape is abstractly circular with four hammered brass bands across the circumference—and, as he would say, it remains incomplete unless worn.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine.

Kovie Biakolo is a writer, journalist, editor, and multiculturalism scholar specializing in culture and identity.

#464. Chihuahuas Seem to Carry a Tiny Bit of Coyote DNA—but That's Probably Not Why They Have Fearless Personalities

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (782 w)

Chihuahuas Seem to Carry a Tiny Bit of Coyote DNA—but That's Probably Not Why They Have Fearless Personalities

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thousands of years ago, the ancestors of Chihuahuas mated with wild coyotes.
  • Recent findings suggest that A study published in July in the journal Nature Communications has found a sliver of coyote DNA buried in the Chihuahua genome, their complete set of genetic material.
  • Scientists made this discovery by accident.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thousands of years ago, the ancestors of Chihuahuas mated with wild coyotes. Today, traces of that ancient interbreeding live on in the DNA of the popular pint-size dogs—but they likely aren’t responsible for the creatures’ fearless personalities.

Recent findings suggest that A study published in July in the journal Nature Communications has found a sliver of coyote DNA buried in the Chihuahua genome, their complete set of genetic material. Researchers don’t know exactly when coyote DNA entered the tiny pooch’s gene pool, but their findings suggest the genetic link arose long ago, before Europeans arrived in the Americas.

Scientists made this discovery by accident. They were testing a upcoming high-resolution, genomic ancestry software algorithm and decided to include the DNA of three Chihuahuas, plus numerous other canid breeds and species.

“The genetic calling cards found in the Chihuahua are unmistakably coyote,” study co-author Alexander Ioannidis, a geneticist at Stanford University, tells the Latest York Times’ Franz Lidz.

Researchers weren’t necessarily surprised by this result. Past evidence has suggested that dogs and coyotes interbred in the Americas before the arrival of Europeans. However, this is the first time scientists have found genetic traces of that interbreeding in modern dogs, Adam Boyko, a canine geneticist at Cornell University who was not involved with the new work, tells the Times.

Industry observers note that chihuahuas are believed to have descended from the Techichi, a now-extinct, mute breed kept by the Toltec civilization in what is now Mexico as early as the 9th century C.E. About 4 percent of the Chihuahua genome comes from the Techichi. Within that 4 percent, an even smaller fraction comes from the coyote.

According to recent reports, in total, researchers estimate that coyote DNA makes up roughly 0.1 percent of the entire Chihuahua genome. Unfortunately for anyone hoping to pin the pooch’s significant personality on its wild ancestry, this tiny amount of coyote DNA probably hasn’t influenced the breed’s temperament, the scientists say.

The team also found identical segments of coyote DNA in the Chinese crested, a close evolutionary relative of the Chihuahua. This suggests the genetic material entered the dogs’ family tree long ago, through interbreeding between coyotes and an ancient breed—possibly the barkless Techichi—that eventually gave rise to both modern breeds. But researchers say they need to conduct additional genomic research to confirm this idea.

Quick fact: World’s first known dog.

In March, researchers reported that dogs lived alongside humans in western Eurasia around 14,000 to 16,000 years ago, pushing back the earliest genetic evidence of a domesticated canine by about 5,000 years.

How and why did ancient dogs interbreed with coyotes? It’s possible these trysts occurred naturally, because many members of the canid family are closely related enough to mate and produce pups. Coyotes and wolves, for example, have been known to interbreed in eastern North America, producing hybrid offspring called “coywolves.” Additionally, a dog-fox hybrid was recently discovered in Brazil.

However, these pairings may not have happened entirely by chance. Historical records suggest ancient humans may have deliberately bred coyotes with domesticated dogs in the Americas before Europeans got there, per the Times.

In a recent development, the scientists also investigated the genome of the Xoloitzcuintli, also known as the Mexican hairless dog. They found that roughly 4 percent of the breed’s DNA comes from indigenous dogs that lived in the Americas before European colonization—meaning the Xoloitzcuintli, like the Chihuahua, is one of the last living links to the now-extinct companion animals kept by ancient Mesoamerican cultures.

Based on the Xoloitzcuintli data, researchers estimate that indigenous dogs in the Americas were interbreeding with European dogs around 1700 C.E.—a finding that “aligns with evidence suggesting that Europeans and Indigenous [human] populations mixed around the same time in early Mexico,” writes Jacqueline Boyd, an animal scientist at Nottingham Trent University in England who was not involved with the study, for the Conversation.

Unfortunately, colonists’ dogs eventually devastated indigenous pup populations. “People in Europe and the Americas were genetically distinct, and so were their dogs,” stated Greger Larson, an evolutionary genomicist at the University of Oxford in England, in a statement in 2018. “And just as Indigenous people in the Americas were displaced by European colonists, the same is true of their dogs.”.

Industry observers note that disease and persecution likely contributed to the disappearance of certain native dog breeds, like the Techichi. Today, most American canines descend from animals that traveled across the Atlantic Ocean.

#462. See Stunning Images of the Universe Captured by Europe's Euclid Space Telescope, Which Is Building the Biggest 3D Map of the Cosmos

See Stunning Images of the Universe Captured by Europe's Euclid Space Telescope, Which Is Building the Biggest 3D Map of the Cosmos

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that after roughly 13 months of scientific observations, the Euclid space telescope—built by the European Space Agency (ESA)—has released its first significant batch of data.
  • According to recent reports, the contents of the 1.7-million-gigabyte data drop, unveiled on November 12, are astounding.
  • In a recent development, euclid launched in July 2023 to journey to a spot nearly one million miles from Earth called Lagrange Point 2, joining NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that after roughly 13 months of scientific observations, the Euclid space telescope—built by the European Space Agency (ESA)—has released its first significant batch of data. The observations cover an area of the sky roughly equal to 9,500 full moons as viewed from Earth, and that’s just a tiny portion of what the observatory will capture as it builds the largest-ever 3D map of the cosmos.

According to recent reports, the contents of the 1.7-million-gigabyte data drop, unveiled on November 12, are astounding. They include more than 900 million galaxies; more than 60 million potential quasars, the bright cores of faraway galaxies; and about 15,000 candidates of an elusive phenomenon called strong gravitational lensing, which can help shed light on a cosmic mystery: the dark universe.

In a recent development, euclid launched in July 2023 to journey to a spot nearly one million miles from Earth called Lagrange Point 2, joining NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. ESA’s instrument aims to investigate two mysterious, invisible things: dark matter, which acts as cosmic glue, and dark energy, thought to be behind the universe’s accelerating expansion. Scientists suspect that together, they make up 95 percent of the universe, but neither can be measured directly. That’s why scientists are excited about the thousands of strong gravitational lensing candidates in this batch of data.

Did you know? Another Lagrange Point 2 buddy.

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is right now en route to the second Lagrange point, where it will search for exoplanets and help unravel the mysteries of dark matter and dark energy.

According to recent reports, gravitational lensing occurs when light from a distant galaxy gets distorted by a galaxy between it and the light detector—in this case, Euclid. The way the light gets warped around the obstacle allows researchers to indirectly investigate the dark universe.

In a recent development, “How strongly the light is bent tells us how much matter a galaxy contains, including invisible components like dark matter. With thousands of lenses, we can study how dark ​matter is spread through galaxies and understand how galaxies form and evolve over cosmic time,” Natalie Lines, an astrophysicist at the University of Portsmouth in England and Euclid team member, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham.

The 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates in Euclid’s recent batch of data, officially called Data Release 1-Foundation, collectively represent the largest catalog of this phenomenon. It’s even bigger than all previous databases combined, according to a statement.

It has been revealed that euclid can also see different wavelengths, or spectra, within the light from a galaxy—similar to how a prism splits white light into a rainbow—which can reveal its distance, origin and composition. With these measurements, scientists can start building a 3D map of the universe and its cosmic web of galaxy clusters. And it really is just a start; Data Release 1-Foundation includes only around 14 percent of the entire portion of the sky that Euclid will observe.

That small percentage includes spectra from more than 160 million sources as well as gorgeous images—puzzle pieces of large sky mosaics. And Euclid is special because it’s collecting data on a huge portion of the sky in incredible detail.

While there are bigger sky surveys at lower resolution, as well as smaller, pinpointed observations at high resolution, Euclid remarkably achieves both metrics, Andy Taylor, an astrophysicist at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland and Euclid team member, tells the Guardian’s Nicola Davis.

“The technological leap that’s Euclid is that we can keep that high resolution, but now we can basically map huge volumes of the sky, huge volumes of the universe,” Taylor explains.

And more observations will be released soon, with the full Data Release 1 expected to drop in mid-2027.

“So much discovery is yet to come,” states Valeria Pettorino, ESA’s Euclid project scientist, in the statement.

#460. Latest Update: Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1703 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Latest Update: Before public bathrooms, women were kept on a ‘urinary leash.’ Then department stores changed everything.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week?
  • It has been revealed that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty.
  • For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your fresh favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

It has been revealed that today’s episode features the three hosts of Vanity Veritas, a delightful podcast about the history of beauty. VV’s co-host Kristina dove into the history of public toilets—and the longstanding lack thereof, at least for women.

For most of modern human history, a woman’s range of motion in the world was limited by how long she could hold her pee. Historians call this the “urinary leash.”.

You might be wondering how this could possibly be a gendered problem, given the universality of the need to urinate. There was almost certainly a time when humans of all types could duck behind trees (or not) and relieve themselves with pretty similar levels of comfort and ease. But by the time Ancient Romans were using public latrines in the 2nd century BC, women of good standing weren’t supposed to go anywhere near them.

So when “monkey closets”—the first public flush toilets—debuted at London’s Great Exhibition in 1851, women didn’t benefit much. Some men thought women would be (or maybe should be) too embarrassed to enter a public restroom, so they were often excluded. And sometimes, if bathrooms were installed for women, they were sabotaged by men who took offense. By the time municipal toilets started popping up, they were often isolated and unsupervised, which meant even women willing to break the taboo had to worry about safety concerns. A woman on the go might come across a genteel lounge reserved for ladies, but they were designed for swooning in and kept decidedly toilet-free.

Ergo the “urinary leash”: you could only travel as far as your bladder allowed. That’s about two to five hours, if you don’t want to put your health at risk. Keep in mind that this was before cars, so a trip across the city would easily take up a good chunk of that time.

Sources indicate that the options when you were away from home were pretty grim. You could take a wide-stance squat over a grate, if you were desperate. On the one hand, bloomer crotches were split down the middle to allow for easy evacuation. On the other hand, a woman would have four to eight layers of skirts to try to protect from backsplash. Wealthy ladies might use a fancy porcelain urinal called a “bourdaloue.” (Fun fact: Many antique dealers now sell these as gravy boats.).

In a recent development, the solution? Department stores. Obviously the actual solution was just providing women with decent public bathrooms, but no one bothered to do so until the owner of Marshall Field’s in Chicago realized that safe, clean toilets would draw women to the store—and allow them to shop for longer. Their luxurious facilities opened in 1907, and not a moment too soon. They featured extra-wide stalls (for bustles, naturally) and a staffed nursery.

Industry observers note that harry Selfridge, who rose up in the ranks at Marshall Field’s before striking out on his own, later took the idea to London when he opened his eponymous department store there. But he actually upped the ante and added hot running water, telephones, writing desks, and more. (Editor’s note: Please bring back department store coworking spaces.) Marshall Field’s and Selfridge’s weren’t doing this for the sake of women’s lib; a safe place to pee meant women could spend more time out of the house, which meant spending more money. But these spaces did set a precedent that helped activists push for women’s restrooms in more places, and they also made it easier for suffragists to hang out and strategize. In 2023, Selfridge’s celebrated its place in the history of peeing in public with Exhibition, an artwork by Gray Wielebinski reflecting on the rich cultural significance of communal bathrooms—and the threats they still face today.

In a recent development, these days, access to public bathrooms is nowhere near as widespread as it should be. That’s especially true for trans people, who have been subjected to a wave of state laws attempting to restrict which restrooms they can use. As the history of public toilets—and the dreaded urinary leash—should remind us, a bathroom isn’t “just a bathroom,” and restrictions on their use have a chilling effect on autonomy.

For more on the massive cultural impact of department stores, check out Vanity Veritas.

Sources indicate that because this week’s episode featured three special guests, I decided to keep my fact short. Cockney rhyming slang—a code that came out of East London in the 19th century—is not a subject I have a lot to say about, but it is something I want to make sure you know exists. Contrary to popular belief, there’s no strong evidence that this cheeky and cryptic lexicon arose to facilitate criminal acts. But whatever fueled its creation, it’s persisted in various subcultures to this day. The system works like this: pick a phrase that rhymes with the word you’re actually referring to, then drop the part that actually rhymes. Tricky? Yes. Whimsical? Very.

If you’ve ever wondered why that fart sound you make with your lips is called a “raspberry,” you have Cockney Rhyming Slang to thank. Fart rhymes with raspberry tart, which then gets shortened to raspberry. Things get stranger when you move into double and triple rhyme territory. “Bottle and glass” meant arse, so “bottle” did too. Then “bottle” got rhymed with Aristotle, which got shortened to “Aris,” which got rhymed with plaster of Paris. Congratulations, “plaster” now means butt.

You can check out a full dictionary of Cockney rhyming slang—with folks weighing in to confirm words or mark them as made-up “Mockney”.

It has been revealed that opera diva Maria Callas famously shed her weight with the help of a tapeworm, just like loads of Victorian women did. Right? Well, not quite. In fact, the truth is probably even more disgusting.

Actual opera singer (and Rachel’s sister!) Chelsea Feltman did a deep dive on Callas for Vanity Veritas a while back, so she dove into the nitty gritty of the tapeworm myth for this week’s Weirdest Thing.

Maria Callas really did drop a troubling amount of weight over the course of 18 months in the 1950s, and she really did have a beef tapeworm. But according to a 2022 review in Parasitologia, the idea that the tapeworm was her go-to weightloss hack is actually backwards. She most likely caught the tapeworm as the result of the high-protein, rare-meat diet she favored for weight loss. Sources disagree on whether Callas ever infected herself on purpose, but the fact remains that this parasite was not a diet hack: Even a five-meter beef tapeworm wouldn’t cause much weight loss, though it could definitely leave you vitamin-deficient. Some tapeworms can even form cysts in your brain.

The idea of popping worm pills popped up in December 1912, when the Washington Post reported that a society woman in Peoria had paid for two suspicious capsules that her husband then analyzed. Inside, he said, he found tapeworm parts. The woman, the vendor, and the government agent were never named, which strongly suggests this story was probably at least kinda made up. The next day, the surgeon general said he’d never seen such a pill, and the Hygienic Laboratory’s director called it the wildest story he’d heard in a while. The legend kept growing anyway, with a bigger price tag in an Ohio paper in 1914 and a comic-strip “diet doctor” with wriggling capsules in 1927. It may even trace back to an 1899 Indiana medicine-show man arrested for giving patients artificial tapeworms to “pass” as proof his cure worked. Mostly, this seems to be a cultural meme that served to mock vain, silly women.

Unfortunately, this hasn’t stopped real people from trying to take advantage of this fake historical trend. In 2013, Iowa’s state medical director warned about a patient who’d swallowed a tapeworm they bought online.

(If you’re looking for the picture of the cheese-baited tapeworm-catching device, here you go.).

In the early 20th century, about 100 American women died of cervical cancer every day. The only diagnostic test was a biopsy, and by the time women experienced symptoms it was usually too late for anyone to help them. The test that changed it all came from a Greek immigrant who never set out to find it.

George Papanicolaou moved to Upcoming York in 1913 and drifted through odd jobs, including playing violin in a restaurant and a stint as a famously bad carpet salesman. He finally landed a lab gig under Charles Stockard, a prominent eugenicist who wanted to understand human reproduction as a means of better controlling it (ugh). There, Papanicolaou found he could swab live guinea pigs for cervical cells instead of doing invasive biopsies. He wondered whether the method would work on humans.

His wife Mary became (human) guinea pig number one. For 21 years, she gave a sample almost every day—roughly 7,600 pap smears—while also staining slides, recruiting friends, and later training the technicians who read results. George introduced her to people as “my wife and victim.”.

In 1925 George spotted cancer cells in a hospital sample. He took that historic discovery to a 1928 conference sponsored by eugenicists, where he presented blurry slides to doctors who preferred the biopsy method over his smear concept. Things… didn’t go well.

It took Stockard’s death, a fresh boss for George, a collaboration testing more than 3,000 women, and artist Hashime Murayama’s vivid cell illustrations to turn the test into a medical landmark. By the late 1950s, women were lining up around the block for pap smears, and US cervical cancer deaths fell by about 70 percent.

#459. Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1463 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Livescience

Voyager 1's light-day milestone: See the photos behind the discoveries

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1463 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Livescience

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.
  • The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.
  • In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Early Wednesday (Nov. 18), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit a new space exploration milestone: The probe, which launched in 1977, became the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth.

The milestone is largely symbolic, but it comes with practical consequences: While Voyager 1 cruises through interstellar space at roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from our planet, it now takes a full 24 hours for radio signals moving at the speed of light to get from Voyager 1 to Earth, and vice versa.

In a recent development, the growing space between Voyager and Earth makes it increasingly hard to troubleshoot problems on the nearly 50-year-old probe. But with Voyager 1 still collecting data with two of its science instruments, which are expected to stay powered up into the 2030s, NASA scientists say one thing is certain: The spacecraft isn't done surprising us.

"What Voyager has taught me is to expect the unexpected," Linda Spilker, who joined the Voyager team in 1977 and is the mission's current project scientist, told Live Science in an interview. "So many times the ideas and theories we had, Voyager was able to prove them wrong.".

Here, we look back at some of Voyager 1's most groundbreaking discoveries, told through its incredible photos.

NASA's Voyager 1 probe launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 launch vehicle from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

NASA's Voyager 2 probe launched before Voyager 1, on Aug. 20, 1977. Voyager 1 took off a few weeks later, on Sept. 5. (The two spacecraft took slightly different routes through the solar system, allowing Voyager 1 to reach interstellar space first after a gravity boost from Jupiter and Saturn.).

Spilker, who joined NASA right out of college, attended the historic Voyager 2 launch and recalls "that feeling of watching the rocket lift up off the launchpad, feeling the roar of those rocket engines and knowing this was a mission going to visit places I'd always been curious about.".

A few weeks after launching, Voyager 1 took this photo of a crescent Earth and moon from 7.25 million miles (11.66 million km) from Earth.

On its way to the outer solar system, Voyager 1 snapped this image of a crescent Earth and its moon, captured in the same frame for the first time ever.

Voyager 1 photographed Jupiter from January to April 1979, reaching a minimum distance of 174,000 miles (280,000 km) in March 1979, according to NASA. As the spacecraft zoomed closer to the giant planet, it snapped an image every 96 seconds, creating this incredible time-lapse animation of the planet's turbulent atmosphere.

A time-lapse animation of Voyager 1 approaching Jupiter over the course of one Earth month.

The close-up view showed that Jupiter is a far more dynamic world than previously thought. But Voyager also made key discoveries about the planet's many moons.

Industry observers note that while passing by the Jovian moon Io, Voyager 1 witnessed an explosion: the first volcanic eruption ever seen beyond Earth. This proved that there were other geologically active worlds in our solar system, opening up entirely new avenues of inquiry and exploration.

A blue eruption on Jupiter's moon Io, the first volcanic eruption seen on another world.

"Going in, we thought that the moons would look a lot like our own moon: ancient dead worlds," Spilker stated. "And yet we found out they were very different worlds — like Io with active volcanoes. It was just an incredible change in our thinking.".

By viewing these eruptions, scientists saw parts of Io's surface being changed in real time. "As we got closer [to Io], scientists kept saying the surface is getting younger and younger, because they didn't see any substantial craters, no medium sized craters, no little craters — until finally parts of its surface are just minutes old," Spilker noted.

A mosaic view of Callisto taken from Voyager 1 photos at a distance of about 250,000 miles (400,000 km).

Industry observers note that some of Voyager's close-up observations also confirmed old theories. For example, Voyager 1's flyby of the moon Callisto in March 1979 revealed vast fields of well-preserved impact craters, proving that Callisto was geologically dead.

Jupiter and its thin ring of dust backlit by the sun in a Voyager 1 image.

A final surprise at Jupiter came when Voyager 1 swooped around the planet's nightside, seeing the gas giant backlit by the sun. This view revealed a thin ring system around the planet, made partly of the dust particles Io spewed into space.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 reached Saturn in November 1980 and made its closest approach to the planet on Nov. 12 of that year. Four days later, the spacecraft took this image of the planet's nightside, showing a broad shadow cast onto the surrounding rings.

Sources indicate that "That is one of my favorite pictures: an outbound image, taken by Voyager looking at [Saturn] in a way you could never see from the Earth," Spilker mentioned, noting that we can only ever see Saturn's sunlit side from our planet. "The rings just look so beautiful shining there, and you can actually see the shadow of Saturn on the rings themselves. It's a really, really special picture.".

In addition to discovering a previously unknown ring, Voyager 1 spotted five fresh moons around Saturn and took close-up photos of several other known satellites.

Voyager 1's closeup view of Titan revealed a dense, hazy atmosphere.

The mission required Voyager to swing by the moon Titan in order to bend the probe's trajectory, sending it away from the solar system's planetary plane and toward a rendezvous with interstellar space. Before that, Voyager 1 revealed Titan's atmosphere to be so hazy that it completely obscured the moon's surface. This highlighted that Titan's clogged atmosphere was far denser than those of Earth and Mars.

By 1990, Voyager 1 was so far from the planetary plane that our solar system's planets looked like little more than specks of light. But before turning off its camera for good, Voyager 1 looked back at our cosmic neighborhood and took some of the most iconic space photos of all time.

In a series of 64 images taken from roughly 40 times Earth's distance from the sun, Voyager snapped its solar system "family portrait," a mosaic of images capturing six planets together for the first time. The portrait included views of Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Frames from Voyager 1's family portrait showing Venus, Earth, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

The image of Earth from this collection is famously known as the "Pale Blue Dot.".

It has been revealed that "We took the pictures of the planets in color, and that one is especially one of my favorites," Spilker said. "There's Earth captured in a sunbeam. A tiny world less than a pixel in size representing all the life that we know in our solar system — just a very special image reminding us just how special and precious our planet is.".

Earth appears as a pale blue dot in this iconic Voyager 1 image.

In a recent development, voyager 1 turned off its camera immediately after taking these images, concluding its role as the greatest tourist in the history of our solar system. In 2012, Voyager 1 passed beyond the heliopause — the boundary where the sun's radiation gives way to the interstellar medium — becoming the first interstellar spacecraft in history.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018 and is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035. In the meantime, several science instruments remain active on both probes, allowing them to measure the strange and mysterious environment between stars.

Even way out there, the probes are still detecting whispers of the sun's power.

Recent findings suggest that "We are still seeing effects from the sun that come out, hit the heliopause, and send shocks and pressure fronts out into the interstellar medium," Spilker stated. "I wonder where we will finally reach the point where the sun doesn't influence what we're seeing, and we're in the pristine interstellar medium — and I hope that happens while Voyager 1 is still operating.".

Sources indicate that brandon is the space / physics editor at Live Science. He holds a bachelor's degree in creative writing from the University of Arizona, with minors in journalism and media arts. His interests include black holes, asteroids and comets, and the search for extraterrestrial life.

  • “We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, notes in a statement to Casey Weldon and Kristen Swilley of Axios.
  • The incident, which occurred earlier this month, was an accident, the zoo states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it was an almost impossible series of events. At the Cincinnati Zoo, a child tossed a knit cap into the air, where a ceiling fan caught it and sent it flying to the side. The hat sailed through a one-foot opening above 12-foot-high viewing windows in Fiona the hippo’s enclosure. The animal ingested the item.

“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” Michelle Curley, a spokesperson for the zoo, notes in a statement to Casey Weldon and Kristen Swilley of Axios.

The incident, which occurred earlier this month, was an accident, the zoo states. Now, the veterinary and hippo care teams are monitoring Fiona around the clock and working to help her pass the object. They’ve given her fluids and an enema, as well as medications to reduce nausea and act like laxatives.

Sources indicate that “We know from consulting with specialists … that surgery isn’t an option for full-grown hippos,” Mike Wenninger, director of animal health at the Cincinnati Zoo, noted in a video upgrade on Tuesday. “Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass this on her own.”.

On Monday, the team wrote that they are “cautiously optimistic” on Facebook. “We know how much Fiona means to so many of you.”.

Recent findings suggest that fiona became widely beloved in 2017 after she was born six weeks prematurely, weighing just 29 pounds, instead of the average 55 to 120 pounds. In multiple tube feedings each day, caretakers gave her a custom milk formula, and they used an IV catheter to deliver fluids. The public followed eagerly along as she took her shaky first steps and recovered, and Fiona gained a base of lifelong fans. She even inspired a book and a line of beer.

According to recent reports, fiona, currently 9 years old, has a younger brother named Fritz who was born at the Cincinnati Zoo in August 2022. His birth inspired an ice cream flavor.

According to recent reports, A few days after ingesting the hat, Fiona’s appetite started to decrease. This week, her care team ran diagnostics again and repeated fluid therapy to promote her hydration. They borrowed a nine-foot scope from the Columbus Zoo to conduct a colonoscopy, but they couldn’t reach the hat in her digestive tract. An ultrasound suggested the hippo’s small intestine is bunching, as if she is passing something through it.

According to recent reports, “At this point, what we can do is supportive care,” Wenninger said in the video. “We’re trying to give her all of her favorite foods and try to get her to keep passing things through.”.

Ron Magill, goodwill ambassador and conservation liaison for the Zoo Miami Foundation, tells CNN’s Chris Boyette that it is not uncommon for zoo animals to consume items that have been accidentally dropped into their enclosures.

The major concern for Fiona is “primarily that it doesn’t cause an obstruction in her digestive tract, which could lead to impaction and damage leading to serious infection and sepsis,” Magill tells CNN.

According to recent reports, fiona will remain off exhibit while her care team continues to monitor her. As the public awaits more updates from the zoo, many are hoping that the resilient hippo recovers.

“Fiona’s a trooper,” Curley tells Axios.

Carlyn Kranking is Smithsonian magazine's associate web editor for science.

#457. Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (712 w)

Mathematicians make a breakthrough in 174-year-old problem

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (712 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers.
  • In a recent development, the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward.
  • According to recent reports, it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While mathematicians technically solved a nearly 175-year-old theorem known as the Four-Color Problem in 1976, the problem continues to vex researchers. For some in the field, their fascination with the perniciously complex concept runs so deep, that they liken their obsession to a lingering disease. But after a decade of analysis, an international team of mathematicians has made the first major breakthrough in the ongoing Four-Color Problem saga in 30 years. At this year’s Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS) conference, investigators laid out the optimal, most efficient algorithm that solves the Four-Color Problem.

In a recent development, the underlying conceit to the Four-Color Problem is deceptively straightforward. In 1852, 19th century English mathematician Francis Guthrie posited that you only need a quartet of hues to fill every border-enclosed region on a map. Think all territories, regions, states, and nations filled in with only four colors. The first proof was introduced in 1879, and seemed solid for 11 years. That is, until Guthrie’s colleagues found an error in the calculations.

According to recent reports, it took more than 85 years until a full proof arrived—a particularly notable moment, since it was also the first major theorem proven by a computer program. However, many in the mathematical community took matter with the digital discovery after having difficulty verifying it themselves.

Recent findings suggest that A more accessible proof arrived in 1997, but even then, the algorithmic system became painfully slow as sample maps grew larger. A handful of mathematicians around the world have pondered latest approaches to the problem ever since—including University of Copenhagen computer scientist Mikkel Thorup, who likens his interest to a “four-color disease.”.

Industry observers note that “I would guess that at least 1,000 mathematicians have caught the four-color disease, spending months trying to make it work but never quite succeeding,” Thorup stated in a university profile. “It is the disease people have suffered from since 1852.”.

According to recent reports, it took years, but Thorup and his colleagues made progress after uncovering a novel detail regarding map-like surfaces known as planar graphs. The researchers realized these graphs feature many more reducible arrangements than experts previously assumed. This provided them a much more discreet set of starting points.

“Think of reducible configurations as handles you can grab hold on to start four-coloring,” added study co-author and Technical University of Denmark (DTU) mathematician Carsten Thomassen. “We show that graphs do not contain just one handle, but an astonishing number of them. Nobody knew that before.”.

Instead of one or two handles in a graph, the team could now identify many more handles throughout any given map. This allowed them to simultaneously begin filling regions with four colors, which exponentially quickened the overall process. Thomassen said this boosted their algorithm from quadratic time (where calculation speed increases proportionally to the square of an input size) to linear time.

In a recent development, “This means that if a map contains ten times as many regions, the computation only becomes about ten times slower. With the previous algorithm, it would have become about 100 times slower,” he added.

Industry observers note that but does this really change anything beyond theoretical mathematics? According to researchers, the answer is a resounding “yes.”.

“The remarkable thing is that because there are so many handles, the idea can also be applied to other kinds of surfaces besides a flat map,” remarked Thorup. “For example, surfaces with holes, such as a swim ring or a piece of…cheese.”.

Sources indicate that okay, so the implications may be somewhat subtle for most people’s day-to-day lives. That doesn’t change the fact that mathematicians finally worked through symptoms of their disease for the first time in 30 years. As to why Thorup and his colleagues spent a decade on a theorem whose major immediate implications are “cheese,” he had a relatively succinct explanation.

In a recent development, “Because mathematicians are slightly crazy. Most of what mathematicians work on consists of very nerdy questions,” he remarked. “We become obsessed with this type of problem because it challenges the human intellect. And if we find the answer, we’ll probably also find answers to other mathematical puzzles.”.

  • But this week, just hours before the first bids were set to be submitted, Kahlo’s painting was pulled from the sale amid questions of its provenance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since it was announced last month that a celebrated Frida Kahlo painting would be put up for auction at Christie’s highly anticipated 20th Century Evening Sale, excitement and intrigue had steadily built.

It has been revealed that experts estimated that Kahlo’s 1952 Congreso de los pueblos por la paz (Congress of the Peoples for Peace), would fetch between $2.5 million and $3.5 million, a 52 percent increase from its most recent sale just six years ago. The piece shared the pre-auction spotlight with other high-profile works, including a Wassily Kandinsky masterpiece, a Gustav Klimt canvas and a long-lost Georgia O’Keeffe landscape that was recently rediscovered in a Manhattan closet.

But this week, just hours before the first bids were set to be submitted, Kahlo’s painting was pulled from the sale amid questions of its provenance. The interceding effort was led by a group called Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection), which seeks to protect Mexico’s cherished cultural artifacts from illegally leaving the country.

Industry observers note that in a statement issued this week, the group claims that the painting was included in a 1957 inventory that Kahlo’s husband, the famed painter Diego Rivera, created for the Casa Azul Trust, which left thousands of the pair’s artworks, artifacts and personal items to the Mexican people. The group goes on to allege that the work “left the Casa Azul for strange reasons and came into the hands of a New York gallery owner, and after several transfers and an auction it ended up in private hands that are now offering it, through Christie’s, for between $2 million and $3.5 million,” El País’ Beatriz Guillén reports.

The Casa Azul is the blue-colored house in Mexico City where Kahlo was born and spent most of her life, until her death in 1954. It was inaugurated as a museum in 1958.

A representative from the Frida Kahlo Museum told ARTnews’ Tessa Solomon: “In accordance with established protocols, the auction house Christie’s has been informed that the work is part of an ongoing investigation being conducted by the competent Mexican authorities … An investigation file exists that gathers information on several works, including Congreso de los pueblos por la paz.”.

This investigation was rolled out after Hilda Trujillo, who served as the director of the Frida Kahlo Museum from 2009 to 2020, published a tell-all blog post last year alleging that her own internal investigations clearly showed that multiple Kahlo artworks had gone missing from the collection in the years before she began her role.

“The documents I was able to read from this report showed that pieces originally catalogued in 1957 now belonged to private collections,” Trujillo wrote in April 2025. “How and when did these artworks leave the Casa Azul?”.

She added: “Pieces from the original collection are in private funds and I consider that, as a Mexican society, we are owed an explanation in this regard.”.

Among the specific pieces Trujillo lists as wrongfully missing is the 1952 painting Congreso de los pueblos por la paz. By 1988, she wrote, records indicated it was in private hands, where it has remained ever since.

According to recent reports, gabriela Mosqueda, a Mexican curator, tells the New York Times’ Victoria Burnett that the Mexican government, which has been called upon to better protect its cultural items, “did nothing” in the aftermath of Trujillo’s accusations. “I have little hope that the government will put its house in order,” she adds.

Industry observers note that kahlo created the painting to commemorate the 1952 Congress of the Peoples for Peace, held in Vienna, Austria. It features a white dove perching on a fruited tree, which separates night from day.

“The finest representatives of art and science from every country on Earth proclaimed before Congress their determination to preserve peace intact, knowing that this defense is the best defense of themselves and their creative potential,” the magazine Tiempo wrote in a 1953 editorial, according to El País.

In a recent development, kahlo’s painting is not the only high-profile painting in recent weeks to have its sale disputed. Earlier this month, a French court annulled the $1.6 million sale of a Camille Pissarro landscape after allegations that it had been looted by Nazis during World War II. And this week, the contested auction of a $180 million Van Gogh painting—alleged to have been originally sold under Nazi pressure in the 1930s—was allowed to move ahead after a settlement with its rightful heirs was reached.

Nesting season has officially begun for the seabirds visiting Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge near Hawaii. The first egg of the season was laid by a black-footed albatross (Phoebastria nigripes) or kaʻupu in Hawaiian. Field biologist and photographer Dan Rapp captured video of this exciting first, which Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge shared on social media.

Black-footed albatrosses are typically the first to lay eggs beginning in November. The Laysan albatross (Phoebastria immutabilis) or mōlī in Hawaiian, will lay their eggs in late November through December. Every fall, this remote group of islands about 1,250 miles from Honolulu temporarily becomes the world’s largest albatross colony. Albatrosses are a group of large migratory seabird species, and includes the wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans), which has the largest wingspan of any living bird species.

According to recent reports, one special albatross couple has already been spotted—George and Geraldine. The duo is together for the 10th straight year. George was first spotted exactly one month ago on October 18, and the couple was reunited by October 22. The pair are short-tailed albatrosses (Phoebastria albatrus) or makalena in Hawaiian. Short-tailed albatrosses can live up to 50 years and are monogamous—clearly.

Sources indicate that wisdom, a particularly famous bird in these parts, has not been spotted just yet. The over 70-year-old Laysan albatross is the oldest known banded wild bird in the world. She was first identified and banded in 1956 by wildlife biologist Chandler Robbins after she laid a single egg. Biologists estimate that she has produced 50 to 60 eggs and as many as 30 of her chicks have fledged in her lifetime. In 2024, Wisdom became the world’s oldest known wild bird to successfully lay an egg at the estimated age of 74. In March, she became a grandmother again.

Viewers can take in the sights and sounds of the albatross colony via live cameras and follow Friends of Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge for updates.

Viewers can expect to see the birds return to the islands, perform various courtship dances, begin to nest, lay their eggs, and eventually watch albatross chicks in all their fluffy glory.

#452. Tech Report: From Penicillin to the Polio Vaccine, a Fresh Exhibition Reveals How Far We’ve Come With Lifesaving Medical Innovations—and How Much Further We Have to Go

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1433 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Tech Report: From Penicillin to the Polio Vaccine, a Fresh Exhibition Reveals How Far We’ve Come With Lifesaving Medical Innovations—and How Much Further We Have to Go

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A pair of clogs with cracked soles and worn leather tell more than just the story of the New York City nurse who wore them.
  • In a recent development, lindsay’s shoes have not been polished or restored.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We did no treatment to them, because the cracks and the losses were part of the story,” claims Dawn Wallace, an object conservator at the museum.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A pair of clogs with cracked soles and worn leather tell more than just the story of the New York City nurse who wore them. Now on display at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, the shoes belonged to Sandra Lindsay as she cared for patients at a Queens hospital during the Covid-19 pandemic. In December 2020, Lindsay made history: She became the first person in the United States to receive the authorized Covid-19 vaccine outside of clinical trials. The shoes, along with the nurse’s ID badge, vaccination record card, scrubs and socks, are now in the Smithsonian’s collection.

In a recent development, lindsay’s shoes have not been polished or restored. And that’s the point.

Recent findings suggest that “We did no treatment to them, because the cracks and the losses were part of the story,” claims Dawn Wallace, an object conservator at the museum. The shoes embody the struggle of health care workers who, like Lindsay, stood on the front lines of a global health crisis.

That story unfolds across “First Do No Harm,” a upcoming exhibition at the museum that explores the complex legacy of American medicine. Artifacts, historical context and personal narratives prompt visitors to ask what medicine can do and for whom.

Sources indicate that the exhibition spans centuries, from early medical tools to contemporary devices, chronicling the field’s incredible progress. On view is a syringe that virologist Jonas Salk used when testing his revolutionary polio vaccine in the 1950s, as well as a medallion containing a preserved sample of penicillin mold from bacteriologist Alexander Fleming. He, along with colleagues, received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1945 “for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect in various infectious diseases.”.

Sources indicate that and technological advancements abound in the exhibition: A 1960s prototype CT scanner developed by physicist Allan M. Cormack garnered him and a colleague a Nobel Prize in 1979 for their work in the field; the first total artificial heart, created by surgeon Domingo Liotta, was implanted by Denton Cooley on April 4, 1969, in Houston. This device supported the patient, Haskell Karp, for about 64 hours before he received a human heart transplant.

According to recent reports, but threaded throughout the exhibition is another narrative—one of disparity. The same breakthroughs that have transformed lives have often bypassed those living on the margins.

“We’ve had such remarkable technological advances that truly save lives every day,” indicates museum director Anthea Hartig, who oversaw curation of the exhibition. “But then some people have had unlimited access and some people have very limited access.”.

Tuberculosis, for instance, continues to disproportionately impact racial and ethnic minorities even though medical innovations have fought back against the disease for generations. (A sputum flask designed for tuberculosis prevention from the late 19th or early 20th century is also among the items included in the exhibition.) In 2023, 90.1 percent of tuberculosis cases in the U.S. occurred among individuals who identified as racial and ethnic minorities.

Recent findings suggest that more recently, the Covid-19 vaccine rollout, also represented in the show by a vial that contained one of the first doses, revealed the disparities in public health outcomes. Research from 2022 indicated that health care facilities in counties with higher Black populations were less likely to administer Covid-19 vaccines in May 2021, and a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) report from March 2022 found that vaccination coverage with an initial dose was lower in rural counties (58.5 percent) compared with urban counties (75.4 percent).

In rural communities, medical advancements can often feel far removed, says Alan Morgan, CEO of the National Rural Health Association. He points to the specific challenges faced by these populations: “Rural is a unique health care delivery environment. It’s not just a smaller version of urban,” Morgan says. “Rural communities often have the fewest health care options, despite having populations that are older, sicker and poorer, making their health needs more urgent than many urban areas.”.

According to recent reports, natural disasters cause environmental and public health devastation, and exacerbate these health disparities. In the exhibition is a homemade mosquito net and women’s health kit made to help survivors of Hurricane Maria, which struck Puerto Rico and other Caribbean islands in 2017.

One exhibition object speaks directly to how the nation has sought to address health disparities: a copy of the 1985 “Report of the Secretary’s Task Force on Black & Minority Health.”.

“In the Reagan presidency, the Health and Human Services Secretary Margaret Heckler, she was like, ‘Look, the overwhelming evidence is that Black Americans are much less healthy than white Americans,’” Hartig says. “She put together a whole commission and a whole study. And in 1985, this report comes out, which for the first time was when the federal government acknowledged the discrepancies in health care.”.

According to recent reports, another section tells the stories of the HIV/AIDS crisis in America, including awareness buttons, information pamphlets and the belongings of the Reverend Steve Pieters, a gay man who spoke forthrightly about living with AIDS in the 1980s. Hartig, referencing the museum’s display of Pieters’ medication bottles, claims that collectively they show “what he had to do to try, after he was positive for HIV, to stave off death.”.

Pieters survived the 1980s, and he died in 2023 at age 70 of sepsis.

The museum also looked at the idea of “harm” beyond the human world and linked human health to the health of the planet. In one interactive display, museumgoers are invited to figure out the best ways to help save honeybees, an indicator species.

“When any one thing happens in ecology, it has an effect on humans and non-humans, and vice versa,” says Katherine Ott, a curator in the museum’s Division of Medicine and Science. The very systems that preserve life are also reshaping the environment in ways we’re only beginning to understand. Progress in one realm can sometimes lead to harm in another. For example, as the use of medical plastics has increased, so has the amount of medical waste. Some of that waste winds up in Earth’s oceans, where it damages the environment.

It has been revealed that each year, the U.S. health care sector generates 6.5 million tons of waste, with plastics making up about 28 percent of that total, according to a 2025 study published in Recycling.

“First Do No Harm” has been a long time coming, and Ott remembers the early conversations about it. “Our museum hadn’t done a major exhibition on health and medicine in nearly 30 years,” she states. With thousands of medical artifacts in its collection, the museum had the resources—and the responsibility—to tell a fuller, more nuanced story. That story, Ott says, is one of contradictions.

“Medicine is a paradox,” she indicates. “There’s more than one truth about everything.”.

The exhibition at times asks visitors to sit with discomfort—one section uncovers the history of eugenics, and a particularly disturbing pair of images juxtapose a boy cured of smallpox and a boy suffering from smallpox.

“The topics are pretty difficult for a lot of people,” Ott states.

Recent findings suggest that it also encourages visitors to consider how medical advances have changed their own lives and their family’s lives. After all, health is both personal and public.

Microbiologist Maurice Hilleman is credited with saving many lives through his creation of vaccines. Part of his public health achievements came about because of a close personal tie he had: In 1963, his 5-year-old daughter, Jeryl Lynn, was showing symptoms of the mumps. So, Hilleman collected a sample of the virus from her throat, brought it to his lab and got to work. That sample, Britta Hallberg writes for the CDC Foundation, “would become the foundation for the development of the mumps vaccine.”.

Hilleman was ultimately able to create a vaccine for the mumps, Hartig says, “because his daughter got it.” A canister that preserved the Jeryl Lynn viral seed stock is on display in “First Do No Harm.”.

The mumps vaccine, officially licensed in 1967, eventually “became a crucial component of the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, one of the most widely used and effective vaccines in the world,” Hallberg writes.

MMR vaccines still utilize the “Jeryl Lynn strain” of the virus to this day.

“First Do No Harm” is ongoing, on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History for about three years.

Ella Jeffries is an editorial intern with Smithsonian magazine.

Kayla Randall is Smithsonian magazine's digital editor, museums.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

South Korea will use emergency alert system to warn about exam cheaters

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters.
  • Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone.
  • In a recent development, the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday morning, millions of phones across South Korea will belt out a loud, buzzing alert normally intended to warn residents about earthquakes or other disasters. This time, the alert is targeting a much different kind of public threat: sneaky standardized test cheaters.

Officials plan to send the notifications ahead of Suneung, the country’s notoriously gruelling, eight-hour-long college entrance exam, in an attempt to flush out any of the roughly 550,000 test-takers who may have smuggled in a banned smartphone. Proctors will also inspect all pairs of glasses for hidden cameras, and students wearing clothes with buttons will have to cover them with stickers.

In a recent development, the aggressive, last-minute measures come just days after a student in a national tax accountant exam admitted he used a miniature camera and a generative AI tool to achieve a near-perfect score. That surprise revelation sent educators and officials scrambling to come up with solutions to instill confidence in the upcoming test.

Recent findings suggest that korea’s measures come as educators around the world are struggling to keep up with a growing arsenal of AI-enabled tools that make cheating easier than ever. But while AI is the focus today, students have been tinkering with new tech and other creative ways to skirt the rules for as long as tests have carried weight.

Industry observers note that the sudden rule changes in South Korea come days after a 34-year-old man named Han Won-seok posted a video on his lawyer’s YouTube channel admitting he used AI to cheat on the country’s national tax exam. According to the Associated Press, Han scored 397.5 out of 400 points on the first stage of the multiple-choice test, a suspicious result that made him the subject of several media interviews. Other test-takers saw those results and accused him of trickery.

Days after denying those allegations, Han reversed course. In the video, he admitted to using a miniature camera to photograph the exam questions, which were then fed to an AI tool. He then viewed the AI-generated answers on his smartphone. Now, Han says he is cooperating with investigators and is warning others against following his lead.

“I cheated on the tax accountant exam. I sincerely apologize for causing damage to a lot of people,” the student stated in the video, according to CNN. “If there is someone thinking of cheating like I did, I’m going to tell the investigators everything, so I hope you don’t think that you won’t get caught.”.

In the days since the videos, officials have rushed to put in place upcoming anti-cheating safeguards. South Korean Prime Minister Han Sung-sook reportedly held a meeting on Monday with the country’s top education officials, where they agreed to officially add smart glasses to the list of prohibited items in testing rooms. Some lawmakers had reportedly even called on officials to postpone the Suneung exam until they could come up with more rigorous anti-cheating safeguards, though the country’s Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin quickly shot that idea down, arguing delays would cause “even a larger disruption.” And while Han never mentioned he specifically used smart glasses to cheat, worries about that tech in particular aren’t hypothetical. Earlier this year, two other South Korean students taking an exam to assess English skills were also caught using camera-equipped glasses.

Concerns about AI-enabled cheating aren’t limited to South Korea either. Last week, England’s Office for Students, an independent higher education regulator, released a statement warning that AI tools are making it “close to impossible” to assess university classwork. In China, major tech companies disabled features on their AI apps during last year’s national college entrance exam (the gaokao), to keep students from using them to cheat. Educators in the United States and elsewhere are also increasingly requiring students to take exams in person and defend papers orally due to the pervasiveness of AI-generated submissions. Sales of Blue Books have soared as a result.

Sources indicate that while fancy AI tools and camera-equipped smart glasses may be newly introduced concerns, creative cheating isn’t. In fact, evidence of sneaky test-takers dates back centuries. One example is this replica of a linen vest from China’s Qing dynasty (1644–1911). The impressive garment has 62 essays, more than 40,000 characters in all, hidden inside. Students wearing the vest would sneak peeks during the country’s grueling imperial exams, which played an crucial role in determining government employment and social status. An even older Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644) jacket was covered with some 50,000 characters from classical texts likely served a similar purpose.

Industry observers note that creative cheating has of course persisted into the modern era. In 2015, police in India’s Bihar state detained more than 1,000 people after relatives of test-takers were photographed scaling the walls of an exam center to pass cheat sheets to students through a window opening. A college student in the U.S. made headlines in 2011, after he was arrested for allegedly using fake IDs to stand in for at least six high school students during SAT exams. In China, a team of exam proctors equipped with  surveillance drones regularly seizes a variety of wearables and other devices students use to try and cheat. Among the seized items were a hidden camera placed inside a pen and glasses with cameras connected to a tiny receiver embedded in a coin.

One has to wonder if all that time and effort spent devising intricate cheating methods could have been used to study instead.

Industry News: Perovskite solar manufacturing could generate $7.92 billion in domestic value addition over 15 years in India

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Perovskite solar technology could generate approximately INR 74,000 crore ($7.92 billion) in domestic value addition in India over the next 15 years, creating opportunities for Indian companies to develop proprietary materials, manufacturing processes and intellectual property (IP), according to a fresh study by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA) and P3C Technology and Solution.
  • Industry observers note that the study, titled “Perovskite Solar: India’s Atmanirbharta Opportunity in Next Generation PV,” highlights the potential of perovskite technology to reduce import dependence, cut manufacturing costs and foster domestic innovation.
  • According to recent reports, india has expanded its domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity and is developing ingot and wafer production facilities under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Perovskite solar technology could generate approximately INR 74,000 crore ($7.92 billion) in domestic value addition in India over the next 15 years, creating opportunities for Indian companies to develop proprietary materials, manufacturing processes and intellectual property (IP), according to a fresh study by the Indian Solar Manufacturers Association (ISMA) and P3C Technology and Solution.

Industry observers note that the study, titled “Perovskite Solar: India’s Atmanirbharta Opportunity in Next Generation PV,” highlights the potential of perovskite technology to reduce import dependence, cut manufacturing costs and foster domestic innovation. It outlines how the technology could help India move beyond conventional crystalline silicon manufacturing and establish a foothold in advanced solar technologies.

According to recent reports, india has expanded its domestic solar cell manufacturing capacity and is developing ingot and wafer production facilities under the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme. However, the country remains heavily dependent on imported polysilicon, wafers and manufacturing equipment.

It has been revealed that according to the study, perovskite technology could help address these gaps in India’s solar manufacturing supply chain. Unlike conventional crystalline silicon technology, perovskite solar cell manufacturing can bypass the polysilicon, ingot and wafer production stages, where India’s import dependence is particularly high. This could offer an alternative route to expanding domestic manufacturing while reducing reliance on imported upstream components.

The study also points to potential cost advantages, estimating that capital expenditure for perovskite manufacturing facilities could be 70% to 80% lower than for conventional crystalline silicon production lines.

Recent findings suggest that it further suggests that lower temperature-related performance losses could increase the capacity utilization factor (CUF) from around 20% to 25% and reduce the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) by 30% to 40%. However, these projections remain subject to validation through long-term field performance data.

According to recent reports, the study estimates that capex for perovskite solar manufacturing could range from INR 22 ($0.24) to INR 28 per watt, compared with INR 38 to INR 42 per watt for crystalline silicon. It also projects higher energy yields for perovskite modules, with annual generation estimated at 2.19 million units per MW, compared with 1.75 million units per MW for crystalline silicon.

Industry observers note that the capacity utilization factor (CUF) could increase from around 20% to 25%, while the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) could fall from INR 2.4–2.7/kWh for crystalline silicon to INR 1.5–1.9/kWh for perovskite, representing a reduction of approximately 30% to 40%. However, the study estimates annual degradation of 0.5% to 1% for perovskite modules, compared with around 0.5% for crystalline silicon.

The study recommends a phased approach to technology adoption, starting with single-junction perovskite solar cells, followed by silicon-perovskite tandem cells based on India’s existing tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) manufacturing infrastructure. This approach could allow domestic manufacturers to leverage existing investments while gradually building capabilities in advanced PV technologies.

According to recent reports, to support the transition, the study calls for policy and regulatory measures, including a provisional two-tier classification under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), with clearly defined stability milestones. It also recommends dedicated research and development (R&D) and pilot project funding through the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) and the Anusandhan National Research Foundation (ANRF), alongside independent techno-economic assessments of commercial viability.

“India’s solar manufacturers have made significant investments in backward integration across cells, wafers and ingots. Perovskite is a promising next step that builds on this foundation. ISMA looks forward to working with the Government and industry on an enabling pathway for next-generation solar technologies,” mentioned Amit Manohar, secretary general of ISMA.

“P3C is developing its own absorber chemistry, assembly line and intellectual property in India. Our modules are undergoing reliability testing at NISE, and our priority is to build the field data that makes this technology bankable. We are glad to work with ISMA to take this conversation to manufacturers and policymakers,” said Sooraj Kumar, co-founder and CEO of P3C Technology and Solutions.

The study concludes that establishing a domestic perovskite manufacturing ecosystem will require sustained investment in research, technology validation, industry participation and policy support. Such efforts could help India expand its role beyond solar manufacturing and deployment to the development and ownership of next-generation PV technologies.
