#448. Medieval Readers Saw Floods, Plagues and Comets as Omens of Doom—So They Created a Mysterious Manuscript of Apocalyptic Artworks to Peruse at Will

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (822 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Medieval Readers Saw Floods, Plagues and Comets as Omens of Doom—So They Created a Mysterious Manuscript of Apocalyptic Artworks to Peruse at Will

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena.
  • In a recent development, that’s the central question of The Book of Miracles, an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century.
  • Industry observers note that now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in the Bible, God’s will often emerges through natural phenomena. The great flood cleanses the earth of human corruption, while the rainbow symbolizes the divine covenant “between God and every living creature.” For millennia, worshippers familiar with these stories have wondered: What meaning can be found in the movements of storms, seas and stars?

In a recent development, that’s the central question of The Book of Miracles, an illustrated manuscript dating to the mid-16th century. Featuring 167 imaginative paintings, the text begins with episodes from the Old Testament and ends with apocalyptic visions from the Book of Revelation. Between them is a catalog of earthquakes, comet sightings, locust plagues, volcanic eruptions and other events spanning antiquity through the manuscript’s creation.

Industry observers note that now, The Book of Miracles is heading to the auction block, where it’s expected to fetch between roughly $920,000 and $1.3 million. Bidders can vie for the volume during Christie’s Valuable Books and Manuscripts sale on December 10.

“The artists of The Book of Miracles have reinterpreted historical and contemporary sources with apocalyptic panache,” per the lot listing. Illustrations of earthquakes, floods and other natural disasters that occurred in Europe are “among the most energetic, imaginative and colorful illustrations in the manuscript.”.

Industry observers note that the text was rediscovered in the library of a Bavarian castle about two decades ago. It’s since changed hands several times. After acquiring the manuscript, London art dealer James Faber helped date it to the 16th century. The publisher Taschen released a facsimile edition in 2013.

It has been revealed that because The Book of Miracles depicts about a dozen events near Augsburg, a city in modern-day Germany, scholars think it may have been created there. Christie’s attributes the manuscript to two painters, Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, and their workshops. Nobody knows who commissioned the manuscript—or what exactly that individual had in mind. “Its existence was hitherto unknown, and silence wraps its discovery,” the Upcoming York Review of Books’ Marina Warner wrote in 2014. “This Book of Miracles is a gorgeous unheralded surprise: a foundling of unknown parents, a virgin birth.”.

The manuscript is divided into three parts. The Old Testament section features famous biblical scenes, including Moses parting the Red Sea and Jonah and the whale, while the Book of Revelation section depicts St. John’s apocalyptic visions. The middle section records historical events across the centuries, such as the eruption of Mount Vesuvius.

Quick facts: Mount Vesuvius’ eruption.

Industry observers note that each image is accompanied by a caption in German. For example, the text below the Vesuvius illustration describes how the volcano “burst open at its summit or peak and threw up such a fire that cities and villages and all the trees burned up.” The latest event depicted in the manuscript is a 1552 hailstorm over the Dutch city of Dordrecht, so terrifying that “the people thought the Day of Judgment was coming.”.

It has been revealed that some of the images from the middle section are fantastical—at least at first glance. One illustration depicts “wondrous dragons” crossing Bavaria’s skies in 1533; scholars think they may represent the northern lights. The five suns that “many trustworthy persons” saw over Leipzig in 1551 were likely an illusion known as a parhelion.

In a recent development, “Beyond their extraordinary beauty, these images offer us a glimpse into how people in the 16th century made sense of a world that could often seem mysterious and unpredictable,” Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, tells the Art Newspaper’s Maev Kennedy. “Today, we might understand a comet, an eclipse or an earthquake through science, but in the Renaissance, these phenomena could be interpreted as signs of something greater, even as warnings of what was to come.”.

According to the lot listing, the manuscript was influenced by illustrated broadsheets, or news bulletins that frequently covered strange celestial happenings. For readers who saw extreme weather as harbingers of horrors to come, “all of these events are portentous,” Donadoni tells the Guardian’s Donna Ferguson. Perusing The Book of Miracles may have been “a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”.

Recent findings suggest that nearly 500 years have passed since the manuscript’s creation, but humanity’s fascination with doom has endured. “One can easily imagine more recent catastrophes getting the Book of Miracles treatment, from people clinging to their rooftops in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina in 2005 to scenes of almost biblical devastation following the tsunami generated by the Tohoku earthquake in 2011,” Collectors Weekly’s Ben Marks wrote in 2014. “That may be the real message of Book of Miracles, that the veneer of civilization we place our faith in daily is actually rather fragile and thin.”.

Ellen Wexler is a staff writer and special projects editor, digital, for Smithsonian magazine.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Industry observers note that last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”.

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”.

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

According to recent reports, fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.

A Gene Variant Inherited From Neanderthals Might Affect Modern Humans' Brain Size and Provide Protection Against Schizophrenia

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tens of thousands of years ago, Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in billions of humans alive today carrying traces of these extinct cousins in their DNA.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, new research suggests one of those inherited genetic variants is associated with a slightly shrunken brain region and lower risk of schizophrenia, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on November 16.
  • Sources indicate that “This is a very important variant,” says Davide Marnetto, a computational biologist at the University of Turin in Italy who wasn’t involved in the research, to Michael Marshall at Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tens of thousands of years ago, Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals, resulting in billions of humans alive today carrying traces of these extinct cousins in their DNA. The bits of Neanderthal ancestry can affect mood, metabolism, disease risk and other traits.

Recent findings suggest that now, new research suggests one of those inherited genetic variants is associated with a slightly shrunken brain region and lower risk of schizophrenia, according to a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences on November 16. The findings further highlight the enduring impacts of modern humans’ trysts with Neanderthals.

Sources indicate that “This is a very important variant,” says Davide Marnetto, a computational biologist at the University of Turin in Italy who wasn’t involved in the research, to Michael Marshall at Nature. “Its effect is really one of the most beautiful and strong that I’ve ever seen.”.

According to recent reports, neanderthals had larger skulls than modern humans, and they were more elongated front-to-back, hinting at a different brain tissue layout. Evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo, of the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, suspected the occipital lobe—which sits at the back of the brain and processes visual information—had something to do with that distinct shape.

It has been revealed that so, the research duo investigated gene variants known to affect occipital lobe size in people of European descent, whose DNA typically contains around 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal ancestry. Then, they looked at which variants were not present in people of sub-Saharan African descent, who have little to no Neanderthal DNA because their ancestors didn’t mingle with the extinct hominins, which evolved in Europe and Asia.

The work revealed a genetic variant that affects the DAAM1 gene, which is linked to brain development. This variant upstream of DAAM1 was seen in all five available genomes—complete sets of genetic instructions—from Neanderthals, the team found. Importantly, it wasn’t present in the two tested genomes from Denisovans, another extinct cousin that interbred with humans. The scientists estimate that about 20 percent of people of European descent carry at least one copy of the variant, reports Science’s Michael Price.

Pääbo received the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for figuring out how to extract and analyze DNA from 40,000-year-old-Neanderthal bones.

Using data from the U.K. Biobank, which contains genetic information from about half a million participants, the team examined how the Neanderthal gene variant affects people today. Analyses revealed that having one copy—inherited from one parent—is associated with a 0.85-cubic-centimeter reduction in occipital lobe volume, whereas inheriting it from both parents doubles the shrinkage. That seems a bit surprising since Neanderthals are thought to have had bigger brains than Homo sapiens.

Recent findings suggest that “It sounds paradoxical, but it probably is not unexpected,” since traits like brain size are influenced by hundreds, or even thousands, of genes, notes Joshua Akey, a geneticist at Princeton University who wasn’t involved in the work, to Nature. “Neanderthals could have an overall larger occipital lobe, but they still contain some variants that contribute smaller sizes and some that contribute larger sizes,” he explains, and Homo sapiens may have inherited a variant that contributes to a smaller size.

Having two copies of the Neanderthal variant was also associated with a nearly 10 percent reduction in schizophrenia risk, though the exact mechanism behind that effect is unclear. Future research in animals or brain organoids could provide more information, Zeberg tells Science, “but the honest answer is we don’t understand the exact mechanics at this point.”.

Still, the findings align with research by Karen Berman, a neuroscientist at the National Institute of Mental Health, and colleagues, who reported in 2021 that people with more Neanderthal ancestry have lower rates of schizophrenia. The new study helps scientists further “understand the repercussions of the echoes of this genetic material in our present genetic underpinnings,” she tells the outlet.

According to recent reports, additionally, Zeberg and Pääbo examined the variant’s potential associations with intelligence, bipolar disorder, depression, ADHD and autism spectrum disorder. They found no link between these traits and the fragment of Neanderthal DNA, and they note that their findings suggest that the size of a brain region shouldn’t be equated with cognitive abilities.

The researchers are now continuing to sift through data to better understand Neanderthals’ fingerprints on modern humans’ genetic makeup, and they hope to turn up additional exciting discoveries.

“You might hear from us again,” Zeberg tells Jackie Flynn Mogensen at Scientific American.

Sara Hashemi is a science writer and fact-checker currently based in Newly introduced York City. Her work has appeared in Sierra, The Body, Maisonneuve magazine and more.

M.C. Escher artwork ©The M.C. Escher Heritage. EscherSite collection.

Recent findings suggest that maurits Cornelis Escher didn’t plan on becoming the darling of mathematicians. Born in 1898 in the canal-lined city of Leeuwarden in the Netherlands, Escher struggled with mathematics as a student, once remarking that he “never got a pass mark.” He ended up studying decorative arts and printmaking, and he used his artwork to explore the strange rules of nature that he found operating around him.

It has been revealed that escher saw that nature can sometimes produce impossible-seeming images. All around him, he saw distorted reflections, odd perspectives, and superimposed worlds, like the surface of a pond where you can see images of both the fish below and the trees reflected from above.

In a recent development, in rendering these and other visions, his artwork took on unmistakably mathematical qualities. “By keenly confronting the enigmas that surround us, and by considering and analyzing the observations that I had made, I ended up in the domain of mathematics,” he wrote in his introduction to the book M.C. Escher: The Graphic Work.

According to recent reports, his journey among these enigmas is the subject of an exhibition entitled Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher at the National Museum of Mathematics (MoMath) in Latest York City.

Industry observers note that escher’s path toward math started with his love of tilings. After completing his arts education in 1922, Escher visited Granada, Spain, and was taken with the tile patterns that decorated the Alhambra. Inspired, he began to systematically study how to fill a sheet of paper with repeating shapes without leaving any gaps.

Years later, Escher’s half-brother, a geologist named Berend, sent him a paper by a mathematician named George Pólya. The paper categorized all the ways to cover a flat space with tiles, broken down into 17 groups, each with different symmetries. Escher had intuited a mathematical question, and here he had a mathematical answer.

Industry observers note that escher carefully traced the paper’s diagrams and studied them meticulously. Over time, he developed his own system for tessellating space, finding ways to cover a print with irregular shapes that resembled fish, birds, bats, lizards, and so on.

“He had worked out a whole theory that he called his layman’s theory, so he knew which edges had to match which edges,” mentioned Doris Schattschneider, a mathematician and leading authority on Escher, and a curator of the exhibition.

Carolina MacGillavry, a Dutch crystallographer, took notice of Escher’s mastery of color symmetry — the rule ensuring that adjacent shapes in a tessellation are always different colors — and published a book in 1965 analyzing his drawings.

Industry observers note that “[MacGillavry] realized that [Escher] knew more than all the crystallographers about color symmetry,” Schattschneider said. “It was something he discovered very intuitively.”.

In 1954, his work was exhibited at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Amsterdam. There, he was introduced to the geometer Harold Scott MacDonald (H.S.M.) Coxeter. The two exchanged letters until Escher’s death in 1972, and these exchanges inspired some of his most mathematically complex work.

As Escher’s relationship with math grew, his artworks became more mathematically intricate, even inspiring the research of later mathematicians. But living his double life wasn’t always easy. “I’m starting to speak a language which is understood by very few people. It makes me feel increasingly lonely,” he wrote in a letter to his son in 1959.

The following images show the winding road that Escher took through art and mathematics. Mathematics and the Art of M.C. Escher at MoMath runs through February 8, 2027.

Escher created Relativity (top), named for Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity, after musing about a world where gravity points in three different directions at once. When the physicist Roger Penrose saw this piece, he was inspired to create a real shape that could replicate this paradoxical geometry, which became known as the Penrose tribar (bottom). Recent findings suggest that inspired in turn by Penrose’s tribar, Escher began creating worlds that used its impossible geometry. He was not in the business of optical illusions, as the writer Bruno Ernst points out in his book The Magic Mirror of M.C. Escher. Rather, Escher was demonstrating that drawing is deceptive. When representing three dimensions with just two, the artist can manipulate the rules of projection to deceive you into seeing, in this case, a perpetual motion machine, where the water flows in a strange loop that goes both downward and upward.

Starting from a boy looking at a print of a town, the image magnifies into the world of the print as the viewer’s gaze travels clockwise. Zooming in, we see that the town portrayed in the print contains the gallery in which the boy is found again, looking at the print.

Circle Limit IV, July 1960, woodcut, 16 3/8 in diameter.

It has been revealed that in 1958, H.S.M. Coxeter sent Escher a paper of his on tessellations of curved spaces. Escher wrote back saying that one of its diagrams “gave me quite a shock.” The figure demonstrated a circle filled with rounded triangles that get smaller as they approach the edge, ad infinitum. It’s a representation of two-dimensional hyperbolic space (bottom), a negatively curved space where parallel lines diverge. The arcs in the disk represent straight paths through hyperbolic space. Escher studied this figure, tracing its arcs and determining the pattern of the circles that were implicit in it. Using what he had learned, Escher created his Circle Limit series. In Circle Limit IV (top), the figures take the form of angels and bats, symbols of good and evil, of which infinitely many fit in the piece.

Escher wrote to Coxeter that “not one single component ever reaches the edge. … And yet this round world cannot exist without the emptiness around it … because it is out there in the ‘nothingness’ that the scaffolding lies, determining with geometric precision the centres of the circular arcs which form the skeleton.

Just within the last week, several innovative upcoming headphones and earbuds have been confirmed, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

Industry observers note that first up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the newly introduced Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

According to recent reports, the 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously confirmed $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Industry observers note that being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

Industry observers note that as for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

Industry observers note that the overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

It has been revealed that to ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

#441. They’re Not on the Payroll, but Bodega Cats Are Some of Fresh York City’s Most Beloved Employees

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1705 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

They’re Not on the Payroll, but Bodega Cats Are Some of Fresh York City’s Most Beloved Employees

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it was July 17, 2025, and New York City bodega owner Hamood Suliman walked into work on a full night’s sleep.
  • It has been revealed that but there she was: a small black ball of fur with a distinctive white stripe down her nose and paws to match.
  • As it turned out, Cleo, as she came to be known, was part of a litter from a cat that lived at a nearby bodega.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it was July 17, 2025, and New York City bodega owner Hamood Suliman walked into work on a full night’s sleep. It was one of the first times he wasn’t unlocking the corner store himself since he opened it in Brooklyn’s South Williamsburg neighborhood just a month prior, but he wasn’t expecting anything amiss.

He certainly wasn’t expecting a cat.

It has been revealed that but there she was: a small black ball of fur with a distinctive white stripe down her nose and paws to match. At first, Suliman was skeptical of the sleeping feline curled up on his counter. “I was like, ‘Is this cat sick?’” he remembers.

As it turned out, Cleo, as she came to be known, was part of a litter from a cat that lived at a nearby bodega. With no space for a whole brood, the bodega’s owners released the kittens into the neighborhood—and this one had made her way to Suliman’s market. She had no home to return to, so Suliman decided he would keep her.

In a recent development, “That’s when my life changed. Cleo has literally brightened up the store, brightened up my life,” he indicates. “She’s been so much fun. It’s beyond imagination.”.

Sources indicate that it’s been over a year since Cleo first wandered into Suliman’s bodega, and she’s woven herself into the fabric of both the store and the surrounding community. “She’s become literally a beacon of the neighborhood,” he states. They even threw her a “Churus and Churros”-themed birthday party, a play on the name of one of her favorite treat brands, this past July, on the anniversary of the day Suliman found her on his counter.

Sources indicate that in Newly introduced York City, Cleo’s story is hardly out of the ordinary. The city is home to thousands of bodegas, many of which feature a furry feline greeting customers at the door and catching rodents in the basement and alleyways. They work around the clock alongside their owners to help fuel the city that never sleeps.

Recent findings suggest that bodega Cats of Newly introduced York, a new book from two of the city’s avowed feline aficionados, author Dan Rimada and photographer Gulce Kilkis, captures snapshots from the lives of these working cats. Over the course of two years, the pair traveled to all five boroughs, visiting nearly 250 bodegas and capturing the tales of around 120 cats. Sixty of those stories—including Cleo’s—appear in the final product.

“There are actually fun anecdotes and little quirks that all these cats have,” Rimada says. “These cats are not here forever. We wanted to document the cats that existed during our lifetime and write down their stories.”.

Industry observers note that the book traces its origins to the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic when Rimada was passing by a bodega in Fort Greene. Distancing guidelines kept him from interacting much with the staff—but the cat pacing around the shop was fair game. He stopped to pet the resident feline, an idea already forming. When he got home, he opened Instagram: @newyorkbodegacats was born.

Recent findings suggest that rimada kept up with the account, and over time, it evolved from a social media spotlight of his neighborhood bodega cats to a full-fledged website chronicling their stories. In 2024, he reached out to Kilkis, an animal photographer whose shots he’d seen online. “I basically told her, ‘I want to start snapping more high-quality photos. I want to take the blog and make it into an official archive where we have more detailed stories and higher quality photographs,’” he recalls. Not long after, a publisher contacted them, interested in turning the archive into print.

Equipped with a color-coded excel spreadsheet, Yelp reviews and a Reddit forum where people posted their favorite bodega cats, the pair hit the streets. Over time, they developed a strategy: Once they were fairly certain they had found a shop with a cat, they would visit. There, they split up. Gulce scoured the store hoping to catch the cat in its natural environment while Rimada introduced the project to the bodega’s owner—and hopefully got an interview.

“They’re filling Grubhub orders and talking to their customers,” Rimada says, “and then I’m next to them, holding up my iPhone, trying to get this recording on tape so that I could transcribe it when I get home.”.

But enough owners were willing to talk, and Rimada and Kilkis captured the stories of more than 100 shop cats—stories that showed just how much love these bodega owners and their customers had for their feline employees. There was Layla, the black-and-tan-spotted cat who was such an effective rat catcher that her owner redid the store’s flooring to match her coat. And Jimmy, a chubby orange tabby whose unstoppable friendliness nets enough customers to generate his owner an extra $300 to $400 a day.

Sources indicate that one of Rimada’s favorite stories is of Zorro, a dark, fluffy cat who lives in an East Village deli. A health inspector had come to check out the store, and was walking out, satisfied. But before he could open the door, “Zorro reaches out and scratches the health inspector on his arm, from his elbow to wrist, and leaves a mark,” Rimada indicates. Instead of reprimanding the owner, the health inspector just shrugged and moved on. “It was a Fresh York moment.”.

Still, not every bodega owner was thrilled at the chance to show off their pet—some wouldn’t even fess up to having one in the first place.

According to recent reports, “There would be a literal cat bed, there would be open cat food on the floor,” Rimada says. But when he introduced the pair and their project, “They would look me and Gulce up and down … and just be like, ‘No, I have no cat. I have never heard of a cat. I’ve never seen a cat in my life. I don’t know what a cat is.’”.

Part of that hesitation may be because, under Newly introduced York City health codes, it is illegal to have any non-service animal inside retail food service operations, including bodegas. Rimada states this law puts bodega owners in a tricky position. Many of these working cats are former strays that simply wandered into the bodega and took up roost, and they provide valuable services, like rat-catching, that often would cost shopkeepers more than any potential health code violation fines.

In a recent development, did you know? Post-mousers general.

In the late 19th and early 20th centuries, the United States had a special budget just for cat food. The government had a rat problem in its post offices and turned to felines for help.

Industry observers note that newly introduced York City’s City Hall Post Office employed nearly 100 cats—using them to catch the rats nibbling away at packaging glue. To feed the whole feline workforce, the office received $5 a month, worth nearly $200 today.

“You have the cats that are prominently featured,” she states. “And then you also have the cats that are a little bit more hidden. They’re in the basement; sometimes, the only time you see them is when people are unloading merchandise into the basement of the store.”.

According to recent reports, fresh York City also has a feral cat problem: Some estimates place the total population of community cats, a designation comprising both stray and feral cats, as high as one million. The cats that survive kittenhood often only live around two years, though that life span increases with spaying or neutering. Bodegas may contribute to the problem, Copeland explains. Without proper tools or education, bodega owners may not spay or neuter their cats, leading to litters that make their way out into the streets.

Industry observers note that as Rimada visited all these bodegas, he noticed this problem—and wanted to help. In 2025, he debuted a petition to legalize bodega cats and establish uniform standard of care, providing regular veterinary care, vaccinations, spaying and neutering, as well as adequate food and water and a safe space to sleep away from food production.

It has been revealed that more than 14,000 people signed it, and lawmakers took note. Later that year, then-City Council Member Keith Powers put forward legislation to override the parts of the New York City health code that prohibit bodega cats. Powers now serves in the State Assembly, where there is a separate bill to establish statewide health and safety standards for cats living in retail food stores. For bodega cats to officially become a legal part of New York City life, both bills need to pass. Presently, the two are in committee review.

Rimada indicates this advocacy is his way of giving back to the cats he has spent the past six years chronicling. It’s also a form of care that, he says, is in line with what this project has taught him about the people—and pets—of Upcoming York City.

“Latest York has this reputation of being impatient and impersonal … and then you walk into a bodega and find this cat with a name and a routine and a neighborhood that keeps track of it,” Rimada claims. “There’s plenty of affection in the city, and it reveals up in these unexpected places.”.

In a recent development, rimada hopes his book will pique readers’ interest in the fuzzy felines. But he also hopes it will prompt people to consider what the animals mean to the communities that love them.

“Even something as seemingly insignificant as a cat that lives in a store, there’s actually a huge story there,” Rimada says. “It’s a story about the cat, about the neighborhood, about the person who cares for the cat, about the people who shop there just to see the cat.”.

A Modern Forensic Investigation Reveals the Cause of Death of a 2,000-Year-Old Body Found in a Bog in Northern Ireland

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, after more than 2,000 years, authorities Northern Ireland are making major discoveries in gruesome cold case.
  • Hosted at the Ulster Museum in Belfast, the proceeding synthesized findings from an international research consortium led by National Museums NI (NMNI).
  • Recent findings suggest that “Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare,” Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial at NMNI, tells the BBC’s Eve Rosato.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after more than 2,000 years, authorities Northern Ireland are making major discoveries in gruesome cold case. A public inquest-style inquiry has determined the cause of death of an young woman from the Iron Age, whose body was recovered in a peat bog in 2023. A coroner’s investigation concluded that she was deliberately beheaded from behind with a bladed weapon.

Hosted at the Ulster Museum in Belfast, the proceeding synthesized findings from an international research consortium led by National Museums NI (NMNI). Although not a formal legal inquest, the hearing applied contemporary investigative standards to examine the evidence behind a death more than 20 centuries ago.

Recent findings suggest that “Finds like this that are women are incredibly rare,” Hannah Crowdy, head of curatorial at NMNI, tells the BBC’s Eve Rosato. “She’s the first of her kind in Northern Ireland at all. This helps us piece together a part of history that is quite mysterious. To honor her, it’s notable to tell her story and bring that to the fore.”.

The remains were unearthed in October 2023, when peat workers from Bulrush Horticulture uncovered human bones in Ballymacombs More outside Bellaghy in County Londonderry.

Subsequent excavations recovered further skeletal remains and a woven artifact, though no skull was found. Researchers initially thought the body was male and dubbed the individual “Bellaghy Boy,” before forensic testing revealed the remains belonged to a young woman between 15 and 22 years old. She was subsequently renamed the Ballymacombs More Woman.

A post shared by Ulster Museum (@ulstermuseum).

Using micro-CT scanning, digital mapping, 3D imaging and targeted analyses of preserved bone, hair, skin, nails and the woven textile, researchers from nine institutions gathered clues about her diet, health and physical appearance.

Cut marks on the woman’s neck appear to indicate that she was “intentionally decapitated in the bog,” Niamh Baker, NMNI’s curator of archaeology, tells the BBC.

It has been revealed that the reason for this decapitation is unknown. “It may be that she falls into a pattern of ritual and sacrifice that took place across northwest Europe in the Iron Age period,” Baker explains, adding that comparable Iron Age male remains found in the Republic of Ireland have been linked to leadership positions.

It has been revealed that “Was she a female sovereign?” Baker asks. “Or it may be that it was related to an agricultural or weather issue at the time.”.

“The purpose of the exercise is not to impose modern legal conclusions upon the distant past, but to provide a framework through which the available evidence could be assessed and the story of a previously unknown young woman could be told,” Joe McCrisken, the coroner who chaired the investigation, said at the inquest, the Guardian’s Rory Carroll reports.

The Ballymacombs More Woman joins internationally famous bog bodies—including Denmark’s Tollund Man and Grauballe Man, as well as Ireland’s Clonycavan Man and Old Croghan Man—in offering rare insights into ancient societies.

Did you know? Bard of the bog bodies.

Bog discoveries inspired poems by the late Irish Nobel laureate Seamus Heaney, including “The Grauballe Man,” “The Tollund Man” and “The Tollund Man in Springtime.”.

Residents of Bellaghy have embraced the young woman as one of their own, naming her Áine after an Irish goddess.

“We feel that Áine is one of our own,” Séamus Mac an Fhirléighinn of the Bellaghy Historical Society tells the BBC. “This is her inquest, she needed her people, her family there with her to act on her behalf as advocates.”.

As the Ulster Museum prepares updates to its Early Peoples gallery, curators have decided not to display Ballymacombs More Woman’s physical remains, opting instead to evoke her life through mediums such as illustration and poetry, for example.

Recent findings suggest that “Ballymacombs More Woman was once a person, just like us,” Crowdy notes in a statement. “While the circumstances of her life and death belong to the past, her discovery raises questions that remain relevant to the future, not least the presence and care of human remains in museum collections today.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ireland-based heating systems supplier Pipelife has introduced a newly introduced indoor monobloc air-to-water heat pump designed specifically for residential apartment developments.

Dubbed Inova, the system uses propane (R290) as its refrigerant and is intended for installation entirely within an apartment, removing the need for external heat pump units on balconies, façades, or rooftops.

“For developers and specifiers working on residential apartment schemes, Inova removes the constraints that come with balcony or external wall placement — giving design teams real flexibility from the start,” the company remarked in a statement.

According to the manufacturer, the heat pump has a nominal heating capacity of 3.2 kW at a water temperature of 35 C, decreasing slightly to 3.14 kW at 55 C. Its seasonal coefficient of performance (SCOP) reaches 4.7 at 35 C and 3.49 at 55 C.

The unit can reportedly supply water temperatures of up to 75 C and is compatible with both underfloor heating and radiator systems. It also comes with a pre-plumbed 200-liter domestic hot water cylinder.

Sources indicate that the heat pump measures 724 mm × 595 mm × 495 mm and can be accommodated within an installation footprint of 800 mm × 800 mm. It operates on a 220 V to 240 V electrical supply and uses 450 grams of R290 refrigerant, according to the organization’s technical specifications.

Unlike conventional outdoor air-source heat pumps, the Inova draws in and expels air through ducts connected to the building exterior. Installers can use either 150 mm circular ducting or 220 mm × 90 mm rectangular ducts.

Pipelife said the heat pump can be positioned up to 10 meters from an external wall without performance losses, providing greater flexibility in apartment layouts and reducing constraints associated with outdoor unit placement.

The company also remarked that the system operates independently of the building’s ventilation system, enabling a decentralized heating configuration with one heat pump per apartment.

The Inova features app-based controls for remote monitoring and operation. According to Pipelife, it has been tested in accordance with the EN 14825 and EN 16147 Ecodesign standards and is designed to comply with Ireland’s Part L and Part F building regulations.

The manufacturer said the system is also suitable for modular construction projects, where heating equipment can be pre-installed off-site to simplify on-site assembly and commissioning.

Pipelife has not disclosed pricing or detailed commercial availability information for the new heat pump.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 100 MW solar project will be built in Dawa, southern Ghana, after securing an $88.6 million financing package.

The facility is being developed by locally-owned conglomerate LMI Holdings, through its subsidiaries Solar for Industries Ltd (SFI) and Enclave Power Manufacturer Ltd (EPCL), the latter of which is Ghana’s first and only licensed private electricity distributor, according to a news release.

The $88.6 million financing package comprises $60.6 million in debt alongside $28 million equity investment from LMI Holdings and is structured as a corporate facility with SFI and EPCL.

Recent findings suggest that the International Finance Corporation is providing a direct loan of $24.2 million while the Emerging Africa & Asia Infrastructure Fund (EAAIF) and global investment manager Ninety One have committed a combined $18.15 million in senior secured debt. The World Bank’s IDA is also participating in the co-financed debt package.

The 100 MW solar project represents the first phase of an intended 200 MW solar power plant.

Recent findings suggest that the first phase is expected to generate 129.5 GWh of electricity annually, with EPCL responsible for wheeling the power approximately 40 km across Ghana’s national grid to industrial customers in the Tema Free Zone and Dawa Industrial Zone. More than 95 industrial tenants are expected to receive electricity from the facility.

Nathalie Kouassi Akon, IFC Division Director for West Africa Gulf of Guinea, commented that the project “will help manufacturers lower electricity costs and reduce emissions strengthening their capacity to expand production, create jobs, and compete in regional and global markets”.

Ghana reached a cumulative installed PV capacity of 276.7 MW at the end of 2025, according to figures released by the country’s Ministry of Energy and Green Transition in its updated Renewable Energy Master Initiative (REMP) 2026–2030.

The REMP sets a target of 852 MW of fresh utility-scale PV, 214 MW of distributed solar, 5 MW of solar home systems and 1.97 GWh of battery storage by the end of the decade.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Austrian engine developer Frauscher Motors has developed a biomass-based combined heat and power (CHP) system that converts heat from a wood-pellet boiler into electricity using a compact Stirling generator.

The firm said it has been operating a demonstration system since the end of March 2026 to evaluate heat transfer, automatic cleaning and long-term operating stability.

Sources indicate that “We have demonstrated a maintenance-free operating time of 10,000 hours using natural gas as fuel. Long-term tests are ongoing with a view to extending this period,” the firm’s CEO, Josef Frauscher, told pv magazine.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the aims of the biomass research project is to determine the long-term durability of the heat exchanger, which is exposed to the flow of hot flue gas. Our goal is to achieve service lives comparable to those achieved when operating on natural gas,” he added. “Assuming 2,000 hours of operation per heating season and an average utilisation rate of 75% of the rated output, 1.5 MWh can be generated.”.

Industry observers note that at the center of the installation is Frauscher’s Gen70 Stirling generator, which converts externally supplied heat into mechanical energy and subsequently electricity. The 29 kg unit uses the organization’s patented Alphagamma Stirling engine configuration and operates without lubricating oil.

According to measurements conducted in January 2025, the Gen70T delivered 1,201 W of electrical output from approximately 4,256 W of supplied thermal power, corresponding to an electrical efficiency of 28.2%. The test also recorded approximately 2.92 kW of cooling heat output, which can be recovered for heating applications.

In a recent development, the generator produces approximately 800 W at a heater-head temperature of 500 C and reaches its highest reported efficiency at around 660 C. Frauscher specifies maintenance-free operation for up to 10,000 hours, after which the module can be refurbished by replacing piston rings and roller bearings.

In a recent development, the demonstration system uses a heat exchanger that captures both radiant heat from the glowing pellet bed and convective heat from the combustion gases. According to Frauscher, the configuration allows heat extraction to be adjusted across a wide range of boiler operating conditions.

An automatic cleaning mechanism, activated alongside the burner’s ash-discharge process, removes deposits from heat-transfer surfaces to maintain performance.

The generator starts automatically when sufficient heat flow is available and supplies a charging voltage of 48 V to 53 V DC for lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries.

Recent findings suggest that frauscher’s proposed system architecture includes a 5 kWh LFP battery and a 48 V DC to 230 V AC inverter rated at 3,000 VA. The electricity can be used to supply household loads or charge battery storage, enabling grid-connected, backup or stand-alone operation.

The technology is intended to complement existing residential PV systems by providing electricity during the heating season, when solar generation is typically lower and heating demand increases.

“In 48-volt systems, integration into PV installations takes place directly via the storage battery’s charging connection; in the case of high-voltage batteries, this is achieved via an inverter,” said Frauscher.

Frauscher is continuing to evaluate the durability of thermally stressed components and compliance with flue-gas emission requirements.

The manufacturer has not disclosed the installation cost, expected seasonal electricity generation or levelized cost of electricity. These parameters will be vital in determining the technology’s economic viability for residential applications.

“There is no other technology that converts thermal energy into electricity in such a simple and therefore cost-effective way,” Frauscher stated. “Consider, for example, complex steam-based processes or high-maintenance wood gasifiers coupled with internal combustion engines. No oil changes are required, and after 10,000 hours of operation, the only wear parts in the mechanical system that need to be replaced are the piston rings and roller bearings.”.

Based in St. Marienkirchen near Schärding, Austria, Frauscher Motors has been developing Stirling engine technology for more than two decades. Its generator portfolio covers electrical outputs from approximately 1.2 kW to 7.5 kW.

The company is targeting residential heating systems, off-grid applications and hybrid renewable energy installations, with the aim of providing an additional source of electricity alongside solar PV.

Hybrid monofacial-bifacial PV arrays boost power output under shading

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A research team in India has experimentally investigated the performance of a photovoltaic array combining monofacial and bifacial solar modules.
  • “To mitigate power increase and cost, a hybrid PV array arrangement incorporates a small number of bifacial modules within a traditional monofacial array,” the researchers remarked.
  • The researchers tested different configurations of a 3 × 3 PV array to determine how to increase power output while limiting costs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A research team in India has experimentally investigated the performance of a photovoltaic array combining monofacial and bifacial solar modules.

“To mitigate power increase and cost, a hybrid PV array arrangement incorporates a small number of bifacial modules within a traditional monofacial array,” the researchers remarked. “Employing a switching matrix-based reconfiguration approach, the most effective hybrid configuration was dynamically selected.”.

The researchers tested different configurations of a 3 × 3 PV array to determine how to increase power output while limiting costs.

In a recent development, they assembled a 3 × 3 PV array with nine modules electrically connected in a total-cross-tied configuration. They first measured the voltage, current, and power output of a reference array comprising nine 10 W monofacial modules. They then replaced three of the modules with 12 W bifacial modules to create a hybrid array.

Industry observers note that the team tested six configurations, placing the three bifacial modules in different positions: diagonally in the top-left, center, and bottom-right positions; across the top row; down the leftmost column; in the center and the two bottom corners; in the top-right and two bottom corners; and in the top-middle, top-right, and bottom-right positions. The remaining six positions in each configuration were occupied by monofacial modules.

The researchers conducted rooftop experiments at Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology in southern India under 12 irradiance conditions: no shading, uneven column shading, uneven row shading, diagonal shading, plus-shaped shading, center shading, corner shading, outer shading, short-and-wide shading, long-and-wide shading, left-corner shading, and random shading.

Sources indicate that they compared the electrical performance of each hybrid configuration with that of the all-monofacial reference array. They also investigated whether switching between different configurations could improve power output under changing shading conditions.

In the “double-hybrid” analysis, the researchers compared pairs of configurations, while the “triple-hybrid” analysis considered groups of three. For each shading pattern, they selected the configuration delivering the highest power output within each pair or group.

Recent findings suggest that “In the double-hybrid analysis, bifacial placements in the first column and grouped configurations ((2 × 2), (3 × 1), and (3 × 3)) consistently delivered superior performance, with power output ranging from 95 W under no-shading conditions to 26 W under severe shading, outperforming other configurations in nine shading scenarios,” the researchers stated. “Similarly, the triple-hybrid comparison showed that first-row and first-column placements, along with grouped configurations, achieved maximum power in a greater number of shading cases.”.

The researchers presented their findings in “An experimental investigation of photovoltaic array with mixed mono-facial and bi-facial modules,” published in Scientific Reports. The research team included scientists from India’s M. Kumarasamy College of Engineering, Kamaraj College of Engineering and Technology, Sri Vidya College of Engineering & Technology, Vardhaman College of Engineering, and Chitkara University.

#434. France unveils bidding terms for 500 MW technology-neutral renewables tender

France unveils bidding terms for 500 MW technology-neutral renewables tender

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that france’s energy regulator, the Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), has published its opinion on the draft specifications for the first round of the PPE3 Neutre technology-neutral renewable energy tender, which is expected to launch in January 2027.
  • Industry observers note that french renewable energy association SER has strongly criticized the limited capacity allocation.
  • The SER has called for dedicated PV tenders covering rooftop, ground-mounted, and hybrid solar-plus-storage installations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that france’s energy regulator, the Commission de régulation de l’énergie (CRE), has published its opinion on the draft specifications for the first round of the PPE3 Neutre technology-neutral renewable energy tender, which is expected to launch in January 2027. The tender will allocate just 500 MW of capacity across solar PV, onshore wind, and hydropower projects, while introducing an unweighted market reference price (M0) for the calculation of support payments.

Industry observers note that french renewable energy association SER has strongly criticized the limited capacity allocation. Its president, Jules Nyssen, expressed disappointment that the industry’s proposals had not been taken into account, highlighting the gap between the 500 MW available across three technologies and the 1.5 GW of solar capacity initially requested by the association.

The SER has called for dedicated PV tenders covering rooftop, ground-mounted, and hybrid solar-plus-storage installations.

The draft specifications set a maximum bid price of €100 ($109.6)/MWh. The weighting of the price criterion has also changed significantly compared with previous PPE2 Neutre tenders. Previously, price accounted for 70% of the evaluation score, with the remaining 30% allocated to carbon footprint and environmental criteria. Under the new framework, price will account for 95% of the score, intensifying competition among bidders and increasing downward pressure on awarded tariffs.

In a recent development, beyond the limited capacity allocation, the introduction of an unweighted M0 represents a significant change to the support mechanism. The fresh benchmark is intended to improve the comparability of bids across technologies and assess how developers account for the risk of electricity price cannibalization. The SER has argued that the mechanism should remain experimental until a more comprehensive review of renewable energy support schemes has been conducted.

Industry observers note that the CRE has also identified economic risks associated with the change. Aggregation contracts, which typically run for one to three years, are significantly shorter than the duration of contracts for difference under the premium-based support mechanism. This mismatch exposes producers to greater uncertainty over aggregation costs.

The introduction of an unweighted M0 could therefore lead to higher risk premiums, shorter contract durations, increased financing costs, and a reduction in the proportion of debt that projects can secure.

Pairing PV installations with battery energy storage systems could help mitigate these risks by allowing developers to shift electricity exports to periods of higher market prices.

To encourage hybrid projects, the CRE has recommended relaxing some of the eligibility requirements for the first tender round. In particular, developers would not be required to obtain administrative authorization for the storage component before submitting a bid. The regulator also proposed greater flexibility in the conditions for withdrawing storage from a project if the necessary permits cannot be secured or the storage component cannot be financed.

The CRE also welcomed the increase in the minimum eligibility threshold for PV projects from 500 kW to 1 MW.

However, the regulator noted that the lack of visibility over future tender volumes remains a significant constraint for developers. It noted this uncertainty should be considered when assessing the results of the first PPE3 Neutre tender round.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement on legislation aimed at streamlining permitting procedures for renewable energy projects and energy infrastructure across the EU.
  • “With tonight’s provisional agreement on the permitting directive, we have completed the first half of the European grids package.
  • “Successfully concluding the permitting directive follows months of interinstitutional negotiations, and this agreement represents one of the most significant legislative milestones in the EU’s energy agenda.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Council of the European Union and the European Parliament have reached a provisional agreement on legislation aimed at streamlining permitting procedures for renewable energy projects and energy infrastructure across the EU.

“With tonight’s provisional agreement on the permitting directive, we have completed the first half of the European grids package. We are delivering on the ambition in the ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap,” noted Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s minister for climate, energy and the environment.

“Successfully concluding the permitting directive follows months of interinstitutional negotiations, and this agreement represents one of the most significant legislative milestones in the EU’s energy agenda. I am proud of Ireland’s role in concluding this cornerstone file during our presidency,” he added.

The provisional agreement still requires endorsement by the Council and the European Parliament. Following legal review, both institutions will formally adopt the legislation. EU member states will then have 18 months to transpose the directive into national law.

According to recent reports, the proposed rules aim to remove administrative barriers, shorten permitting timelines and accelerate grid connections for renewable energy projects, energy storage facilities and electric vehicle charging stations. They also seek to simplify authorization procedures for new electricity and gas infrastructure.

“Member states will be able to prioritize the roll-out of renewable energy and electricity grids by presuming them to be of overriding public interest,” the Council remarked in a statement. “The provisional agreement aligns with the Council’s position, leaving to member states the discretion not to apply this principle in order to protect security and defence and cultural heritage interests.”.

The agreement builds on the European Grids Package unveiled by the European Commission in December 2025. The package includes measures to accelerate infrastructure planning, improve grid connection procedures and revise the Trans-European Networks for Energy (TEN-E) Regulation. In September, the European Parliament’s industry committee backed proposals to streamline cross-border energy infrastructure development, including changes to planning, permitting and investment procedures.

The latest agreement also comes amid mounting concerns over grid congestion and delays in connecting renewable energy projects across Europe. According to research published by Aurora Energy Research in January, more than 1 TW of renewable energy capacity was awaiting grid connection across the continent, with permitting procedures taking up to a decade in some markets. A subsequent analysis by Ember identified a gap of approximately 120 GW between planned renewable energy deployment and available grid capacity across most EU member states, highlighting the scale of the infrastructure constraints facing the sector.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is expanding its support for solar and battery energy storage projects in Bangladesh through a three-phase programme covering more than 1 GW of planned capacity.
  • The bank has agreed to provide transaction advisory services for five additional projects, building on its existing support for the 130 MW Sonagazi solar project in the Feni district of southeastern Bangladesh, which ADB says is due to tender next year.
  • ADB explains its expanded programme is expected to mobilise more than $1 billion in private sector investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) is expanding its support for solar and battery energy storage projects in Bangladesh through a three-phase programme covering more than 1 GW of planned capacity.

The bank has agreed to provide transaction advisory services for five additional projects, building on its existing support for the 130 MW Sonagazi solar project in the Feni district of southeastern Bangladesh, which ADB says is due to tender next year.

ADB explains its expanded programme is expected to mobilise more than $1 billion in private sector investment.

The agreement will see ADB work with investment authority Invest Bangladesh and the state-owned Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) to assess the suitability of government-owned land for the five additional projects. Details covering the planned capacity of each individual project are yet to be released.

The bank’s advisory services will cover project preparation, technical and financial assessments, market sounding, tender document preparation, and support for competitive bidding and contract awards.

“Bangladesh has an opportunity to build a more secure, sustainable, and investment-ready energy future,” said Qingfeng Zhang, ADB country director for Bangladesh.

He added that the expanded advisory mandate would help establish a scalable market for clean energy investment by strengthening project preparation, competitive procurement and the conditions needed to attract private capital.

Bangladesh has set a target of generating at least 20% of its electricity from renewable sources by 2030, increasing to 30% by 2040. The country at the moment has 1,871 MW of installed renewable energy capacity, including 1,492 MW of solar.

According to recent reports, in October, BPDB approved a 442 MW solar project with eight hours of battery storage, making it the country’s largest PV project under development. The government also recently established a $123 million fund for rooftop solar and other renewable energy projects.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Taiwan introduces bidding framework for storage deployment at existing PV plants

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (452 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) has introduced a regulatory framework designed to promote the integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) with existing solar photovoltaic installations.
  • The guidelines, issued on November 6, 2024, establish a competitive bidding and capacity allocation mechanism for eligible solar power facilities seeking to incorporate battery storage.
  • Sources indicate that under the fresh framework, existing grid-connected PV plants exceeding 1 MW in size may participate in the bidding process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA) has introduced a regulatory framework designed to promote the integration of battery energy storage systems (BESS) with existing solar photovoltaic installations. The initiative reflects Taiwan’s growing emphasis on grid stability, renewable energy optimization, and the development of a more flexible electricity system.

The guidelines, issued on November 6, 2024, establish a competitive bidding and capacity allocation mechanism for eligible solar power facilities seeking to incorporate battery storage.

Sources indicate that under the fresh framework, existing grid-connected PV plants exceeding 1 MW in size may participate in the bidding process. Eligible developers are required to install battery storage with a minimum energy capacity equivalent to 2.61 MWh for every MW of rated storage power.

The competitive bidding mechanism determines the battery capacity tariff offered to successful applicants, introducing market-based price competition. Projects receiving capacity allocation approval must generally complete battery installation and grid connection within 15 months.

The framework also requires successful participants to release grid connection capacity equivalent to 1.5 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to applicable conditions. This provision could help improve the utilization of Taiwan’s existing grid infrastructure and create opportunities for additional renewable energy integration.

The framework also includes provisions for a daily guaranteed billing quantity linked to 2.61 times the rated storage power capacity, subject to operational requirements and other conditions.

Electricity discharge will be coordinated according to national utility Taipower‘s scheduling and dispatch requirements. This approach is intended to shift part of Taiwan’s solar electricity output from midday periods toward times when stored energy can provide greater value to the electricity system.

Taiwan has been pursuing a broader expansion of renewable energy capacity alongside measures to improve market conditions.

Industry observers note that in January 2025, the Ministry of Economic Affairs revealed plans to accelerate solar and offshore wind deployment, targeting an additional 8.2 GW of combined capacity by the end of 2026. However, deployment has progressed more slowly than initially anticipated.

A December 2025 forecast by GlobalData projected that Taiwan’s cumulative solar capacity would reach 31.2 GW by 2035, with the 20 GW milestone now expected in 2029. The government has also maintained solar feed-in tariffs for 2026 at the levels established in the second half of 2025, aiming to sustain investment and deployment.

Energy storage is also gaining prominence. In October 2025, French battery manufacturer Saft announced plans to supply 356 MWh of battery storage for a project in Taichung, bringing its planned installed capacity on the island to 630 MWh by 2026.

The market has also seen earlier examples of storage integration with solar generation, including a 15 MW/15 MWh battery system connected to a 150 MW solar park in southern Taiwan.

Eagles are eating human-sized baboons in the Sahara desert

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home.
  • Newly introduced research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons.
  • Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, massive cats, and even eagles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an isolated  group of primates calls the rugged, sandstone Ennedi plateau in northern Chad, home. In this region in the middle of the Sahara Desert about the size of Switzerland, the olive baboons (Papio anubis) have lived a separate life away from other primate species. At 40 to 60 pounds, some olive baboons are about the size of our early hominin ancestors. But their size does not keep them safe from hungry Verreaux’s eagles (Aquila verreauxii).

Newly introduced research published today in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology details how these eagles appear to be preying upon these nearly human-sized baboons. The discovery is reshaping how scientists think about predator-prey interactions during human evolution.

Our ancestors were vulnerable to several predators, including crocodiles, massive cats, and even eagles. However, scientists believed that our species (Homo sapiens) and our hominin ancestors have been escaping these predators for roughly the past 2.5 million years. No primate over 28.6 pounds (13 kilograms) has been confirmed to be killed by raptors, so our body sizes appeared to be too heavy for even the large eagles with a 71- to 86-inch-long wingspan to pick up.

In this study, the team describes skulls and bones of adult male olive baboons that bear the signature marks of eagle predation. There were talon punctures to the skulls, and various scrapes and “rakes” on the shoulder bones.

“We saw the eagles while we were searching for the baboons, but we never imagined that they might be a threat to them,” Catherine Hobaiter, a study co-author and primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, remarked in a statement. “Then we found the first skull with a puncture mark, and then another, and another.”.

With these remains, the team was able to calculate how much the deceased baboons weighed. One individual was over 57.3 pounds (26 kilograms), well within the range of a hominin species.

“Having worked in this region for about three years, I had the opportunity to visit these gueltas (pockets of water that form within rock formations) and often observed Verreaux’s eagles. I had never imagined that these predators would target primates of this size until the research team stumbled upon evidence,” added Dr. Jean Didier Akpona from the African Parks Network. “This discovery leads us to explore further the mystery that surrounds the gueltas of the Sahara Desert.”.

Industry observers note that to defend against eagles, our primate ancestors would “mob” or charge the attacker to try to drive them away. The modern primates living in places with eagle predators often move in large groups mixed with other primate species. This also mirrors the evolutionary history of our early ancestors, who lived alongside other hominin species and other primates. While some conflict arose, plenty of cooperative advantages to sticking together also happened—like mobbing eagles.

The team hopes to learn more about the lives of the Ennedi baboons to see what other evolutionary secrets they may be holding.

“Baboons are some of the best studied monkeys in Africa, but our very first observations from Ennedi upended all sorts of notions about what these baboons should be doing—from their diet to their social lives, I can’t wait to see what new ‘rules’ they’ll break next!” Hobaiter concluded.

Voyager 1 is one light-day away from Earth, according to NASA estimate
