💡 Key Takeaways
  • After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe likely reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST this morning. Since it will take about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA will confirm that it reached the distance at a news conference on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

“The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he states. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 feet per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

But even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

In a recent development, even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

According to recent reports, “Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

According to recent reports, “Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

Voyager 1 launched on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In a recent development, in March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two new Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

Industry observers note that as part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

In a recent development, on February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

In a recent development, all good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are currently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical concerns, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

According to recent reports, “Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any newly introduced region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an key lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

“Do not be afraid to dream significant. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he notes. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI data centers are changing the duty cycle expected of battery energy storage.
  • The distinction begins with response time.
  • Industry observers note that EVE Energy structures its AIDC offering around these three layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI data centers are changing the duty cycle expected of battery energy storage. Alongside conventional requirements for backup capacity and renewable-energy integration, operators must manage rapid load changes associated with high-density computing. A single battery architecture is unlikely to meet every requirement efficiently.

The distinction begins with response time. At the source-grid interface, storage can support renewable integration, demand management, and frequency regulation. Within power-distribution systems, batteries must sustain high output during short interruptions. At server-rack level, even shorter fluctuations require millisecond-scale intervention.

Industry observers note that EVE Energy structures its AIDC offering around these three layers. For source-grid applications, its 20-foot, 5 MWh high-power storage system is designed for 1P operation and frequent cycling, with 93.6% system efficiency and an operating range of −40°C to 55°C. Its S5-1P system uses dedicated 315 Ah frequency-regulation cells with 395 Wh/L energy density. EVE reports no lithium plating under specified 1P charge-discharge and 1.22P frequency-regulation tests — demonstrating cell stability under demanding high-rate operation.

For longer-duration applications, the Mr.Giant 3.0 system integrates 6.9 MWh in a standard 20-foot container using 702 Ah cells. Published specifications include a 10,000-cycle system life at 70% state of health and a system temperature difference of no more than 5°C. Actual performance depends on operating conditions.

At the distribution layer, EVE’s 6C/10C backup cabinets target high-power, short-duration loads and compatibility with UPS and high-voltage DC architectures. The 10C configuration delivers a specified 660 kW over five minutes. At rack level, its battery backup unit uses 21700 LFP cylindrical cells, supports 15C–30C discharge rates, and specifies switchover within 2 milliseconds.

Industry observers note that coordinating cell behavior, battery management, power conversion, and operating strategies across these layers affects reliability and total cost of ownership. EVE combines cell development with BMS and system integration, offering operators a unified engineering interface.

The portfolio is being presented at the EVE Energy booth (N717 North Hall) at RE+ 2026, in Las Vegas, where the growing overlap between energy storage and digital infrastructure is becoming a practical design consideration for developers and system integrators.

Reconstructing Architecture Through Sound.

For years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

It has been revealed that for years, independent investigators could study Saydnaya Prison from the outside, including through satellite imagery, but had no access to its interior. Inside the military prison north of Damascus, much of what could be reconstructed depended on the memories of people who had been held there.

According to recent reports, in 2016, Forensic Architecture worked with Amnesty International to reconstruct the prison from the memories of five former detainees interviewed in Istanbul. Starting with a rough model based on satellite images and earlier written testimony, researchers developed the interior as survivors described cells, stairwells, and doors. The witnesses explored the rooms at eye level, corrected their proportions, and placed objects where they remembered them. Moving through the model sometimes brought back details they had never mentioned.

In a recent development, some dimensions came from physical memories of the building. One survivor remembered the size of a hatch in his cell door because guards had forced him to push his head through it. Another estimated the dimensions of a cell by counting its floor tiles.

Industry observers note that sound provided another way to reconstruct the interior. Detainees were frequently blindfolded or kept in darkness, and speaking was prohibited. They became attentive to footsteps, doors, and noises traveling through water pipes and ventilation ducts. Mapping the Divided Memories of a City.

What the Measured Drawing Leaves Out.

Architectural drawings preserve dimensions and spatial relationships, but the experience of a place is harder to document. A room can be measured through its walls, openings, and circulation, while its proportions may also be remembered through sound and movement. A city can be mapped as a continuous territory, even when political boundaries divide how its inhabitants experience it. A demolished building can survive in historical plans while its scale disappears from the ground. Each form of representation captures particular aspects of a place while leaving others undocumented.

#409. European solar module prices face additional pressure from surplus stock, cancelled projects

European solar module prices face additional pressure from surplus stock, cancelled projects

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1022 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the European solar industry is entering a newly introduced phase after several years of sharp price declines.
  • According to recent reports, “Over the past six months, we have continued to see pressure on module prices, particularly for TOPCon products,” Bart Wansink, CEO of Netherlands-based solar trading platform Search4Solar, told pv magazine.
  • Wansink noted actual transaction prices can vary considerably depending on order volumes, brands, technical specifications, availability and delivery terms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the European solar industry is entering a newly introduced phase after several years of sharp price declines. Manufacturers, distributors and installers are adapting to a market characterised by excess production capacity, intense price competition and changing purchasing behaviour.

According to recent reports, “Over the past six months, we have continued to see pressure on module prices, particularly for TOPCon products,” Bart Wansink, CEO of Netherlands-based solar trading platform Search4Solar, told pv magazine. “According to the September 2026 European PV Index published by sun.store, average transaction prices reached approximately €0.114 ($0.125)/W for bifacial TOPCon modules and €0.120/W for monofacial TOPCon modules, excluding VAT and delivery costs.”.

Wansink noted actual transaction prices can vary considerably depending on order volumes, brands, technical specifications, availability and delivery terms.

Industry observers note that “At Search4Solar, for example, we are offering selected solar modules at approximately €0.08/W, depending on purchase volumes and commercial conditions,” he noted. “This demonstrates how competitively modules can be priced when large volumes and efficient international distribution come together.”.

It has been revealed that however, Wansink stressed the importance of distinguishing large-volume transactions from standard distributor pricing. Prices negotiated for container-scale orders do not necessarily reflect those paid by installers purchasing smaller quantities for local delivery.

“Price differences between France, Germany, the Netherlands and Spain are often driven more by logistics, local inventories, order quantities and technical requirements than by fundamentally different manufacturing costs,” he stated.

Another factor influencing European module prices is the availability of equipment originally procured for solar projects that have been postponed, restructured or cancelled.

Wansink pointed to a transaction involving approximately 100 MW of Tier 1 solar modules that Search4Solar is distributing after the large-scale project for which they were originally intended failed to proceed as planned.

“Instead of remaining tied to one project, these modules can be redistributed to multiple customers across different European markets,” he said. “Solar equipment originally intended for one project can re-enter the market, sometimes at prices that are highly competitive compared with fresh factory orders.”.

Such transactions can offer purchasing opportunities but may also create additional price pressure for conventional distribution channels, according to Wansink.

He added that the ability to redistribute large quantities of modules is becoming increasingly key for manufacturers, project developers and investors seeking to manage surplus equipment.

China’s efforts to address excess manufacturing capacity are another notable factor shaping the global solar market.

Sources indicate that chinese manufacturers have faced sustained pricing pressure amid intense competition and persistent oversupply. On 1 April 2026, China eliminated value-added tax (VAT) export rebates for certain photovoltaic products, changing the cost structure for exporters.

According to recent reports, “This changes the economics of exporting certain solar products and can create additional pressure on manufacturers’ margins,” Wansink said. “However, we should distinguish between increasing production or export costs and the actual selling prices achieved in Europe.”.

He noted that higher export costs would not necessarily translate into higher module prices in Europe, particularly while significant manufacturing capacity and inventory remain available.

According to Wansink, Chinese manufacturers are increasingly focused on protecting their margins, although their ability to secure sustainable price increases will depend on market demand.

“We expect manufacturers to negotiate more carefully and become more selective about certain large-volume transactions,” he stated. “Nevertheless, existing European inventories and project-related surplus stock can continue to create downward price pressure, even when manufacturers are attempting to increase their selling prices.”.

Looking ahead to the next six to 12 months, Wansink expects European module prices to become more stable, with the possibility of moderate increases during 2027.

“However, we do not expect a dramatic or sustained price recovery without a more meaningful reduction in global manufacturing capacity or a stronger increase in demand,” he remarked.

Wansink identified several factors likely to determine the direction of European module prices, including manufacturing capacity adjustments in China, European inventory levels and the availability of surplus modules from delayed or cancelled projects.

“The market will be shaped by several key factors, including the gradual rationalisation of Chinese manufacturing capacity, which could help bring production and demand into better balance, and European inventory levels, which will continue to influence short-term pricing,” he said. “At the same time, modules released from cancelled or postponed projects may add further competitive pressure, while the pace of European installations, access to project financing and government policy will ultimately determine how quickly existing stock is absorbed.”.

He added that pricing trends could vary across module technologies, manufacturers and product formats.

“We do not believe there will necessarily be one uniform European module price trend,” he said.

Wansink expects inventory management, access to financing and international sales networks to play an increasingly notable role in determining the competitiveness of European solar distributors.

Recent findings suggest that “Holding the largest inventory is not necessarily a competitive advantage if prices are falling and financing costs are increasing,” he stated. “Instead, successful distributors will need strong customer networks, reliable logistics and the ability to identify demand before committing to large purchases.”.

Search4Solar is seeking to expand its role in European module distribution by strengthening relationships with manufacturers, distributors, engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors, and installers.

Recent findings suggest that “At Search4Solar, we are building an international renewable energy distribution platform connecting manufacturers, distributors, EPC contractors and installers,” Wansink stated. “Our ambition is to distribute increasingly large volumes of solar modules across Europe, with a long-term objective of reaching 1 GW of annual module sales.”.

The manufacturer is expanding its international sales network, targeting larger EPC companies and developing its digital purchasing capabilities.

Wansink believes distributors with strong international customer networks and efficient inventory turnover will be better positioned to compete in an increasingly price-sensitive market.

“The winners in European solar distribution will not necessarily be the companies holding the most stock,” he stated. “They will be the companies with the strongest international customer networks, the fastest stock rotation and the ability to distribute large volumes profitably.”.

“The market is moving from simply trading solar panels towards managing a European distribution network,” he concluded. “That is where we see the biggest opportunity for Search4Solar.”.

Breaking: The Country's Oldest Operating Lighthouse Predates the American Revolution and Still Shines on Newly introduced York Harbor After More Than 260 Years

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1400 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Until the 20th century, the only safe maritime route into New York Harbor zagged between shallow shoals.
  • Recent findings suggest that when the Revolutionary War began, 11 years later, rebel troops did their best to dismantle Sandy Hook’s lantern, to keep British ships from navigating into New York Harbor.
  • When the British finally withdrew from their last American strongholds, they blasted and burned to pieces the Boston Light, in 1776, and, in 1779, the Beavertail Light, in Rhode Island, two of the oldest beacons in the Colonies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Until the 20th century, the only safe maritime route into New York Harbor zagged between shallow shoals. At one particularly treacherous point, the shipping lane bent around the northern tip of the Sandy Hook peninsula, which the English politician Thomas Pownall described in 1755 as “a neck of low sandy hills covered with cedars and holly, ending in a low sandy point.” After a devastating series of shipwrecks in 1761, New York’s merchants petitioned the Colonial Assembly to build a navigational aid. Using £750 raised in a lottery, the Assembly purchased four acres of land near the tip of the Sandy Hook peninsula in New Jersey, about seven miles south of Coney Island across Lower New York Bay. On June 11, 1764, the fifth lighthouse in the Colonies was lit atop a stolid, tapered octagon of whitewashed rubblestone, 103 feet high.

Recent findings suggest that when the Revolutionary War began, 11 years later, rebel troops did their best to dismantle Sandy Hook’s lantern, to keep British ships from navigating into New York Harbor. Their efforts included an April 1776 escapade where, as the New-York Journal reported, a New Jersey troupe trapped a group of British soldiers in “the upper room of the lighthouse, where they were carousing,” by “taking away the lower part of the stairs.” But Sandy Hook soon fell under British control. Several other attacks by revolutionaries all failed to destroy the structure or wrest it from the royalists. The walls, more than six feet thick at the base, were simply too strong.

When the British finally withdrew from their last American strongholds, they blasted and burned to pieces the Boston Light, in 1776, and, in 1779, the Beavertail Light, in Rhode Island, two of the oldest beacons in the Colonies. By the end of the century, two other lighthouses that predated Sandy Hook—in Connecticut and Massachusetts—had succumbed to age, fire and battering seas.

Today, Sandy Hook is the oldest continuously operational lighthouse in the United States. It’s also a remarkably rich emblem for a pivotal moment in American statecraft. Before the 1789 Lighthouse Act, which made the country’s 12 surviving lighthouses national property, “the federal state was merely a state of mind,” writes Allen S. Miller, a longtime intelligence and risk-management analyst and civil servant, who is an expert in this history. Predating the act that formally created the Department of Treasury, and signed the same day as the act creating the Department of War, the Lighthouse Act turned those isolated beacons into a pointillist network of federal infrastructure, unifying a fledgling maritime economy and, in the process, helping invent a durable and coherent United States.

The Sandy Hook tower also served as a model for the first lighthouses that the U.S. built after independence, through the extraordinary surge in construction in the 19th century. In 1820, there were 55 lighthouses in the United States; by 1910, there were nearly 1,400. These beacons served a booming maritime shipping economy. Between just 1834 and 1860, the number of vessels entering New York Harbor from the Atlantic doubled—and because cargo ships were getting bigger and more efficient, the estimated collective weight of their cargo increased fourfold. But there were early signs that the light wouldn’t burn forever: As early as the Civil War, drifting sand deposits extended the coastline—and eroded the lighthouse’s commercial significance. Where in 1764 the lighthouse stood just 500 feet from the tip of the peninsula, by 1864, the distance had increased to 4,000 feet. Now it’s nearly a mile and a half.

According to recent reports, did you know? A lifesaving lighthouse keeper.

Sources indicate that one of the most famous lighthouse keepers in U.S. history was Kate Walker.

In a recent development, walker inherited the job after her husband died from pneumonia. His last words, it’s noted, were: “Mind the lights, Katie.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the U.S. Coast Guard, Walker “not only kept the light burning but by her own account may have saved as many as 50 people.”.

In a recent development, technological transformations in the 20th century, like radio, radar and the position-fixing system known as LORAN-C (plus earlier inventions like electric batteries and lanterns), gradually pushed lighthouse keepers, and eventually lighthouses themselves, into obsolescence. President Ronald Reagan’s 1983 authorization of GPS for commercial airlines opened the door to widespread civilian use of what had previously been a military technology. It was the end of lighthouses as essential navigational tools. Only about half of the 800 or so lighthouses right now standing on U.S. soil are still operational; many others are abandoned or in varying states of disrepair.

Industry observers note that despite their current marginalization in American commercial life, lighthouses were “instrumental in the development of the United States as an economic power and, subsequently, as a place for people to settle,” indicates Jeff Gales, executive director of the United States Lighthouse Society. For around 15 years after its completion in 1886, the Statue of Liberty operated as the first electric lighthouse in the United States, but before and after, it was the beacon of Sandy Hook—lit with oil until 1896, electricity until 1903, then kerosene until 1925, when electricity returned for good—that guided countless immigrants to shore. Even today, Sandy Hook, declared a National Historic Landmark on its 200th anniversary in 1964, continues to project its beam 19 miles out to sea.

In a recent development, lighthouses have always been more than just navigational tools. They represent fresh beginnings as well as the exhilarating edge of what we know, inspiring fear and comfort, melancholy and hope. “We’re inherently drawn to the end of things,” as Gales puts it, “to stand on the precipice and look outward.” Lighthouses illuminate the view and, eventually, when we’re ready, guide us home.

Sources indicate that in the winter of 1880, the keepers of St. Simons Lighthouse in Georgia got into an argument. It ended when one unloaded a shotgun into the other. Nearly 150 years later, some say the slain keeper still mans the light—his ghostly footfalls dutifully ascending the stairs, again and again.

Sources indicate that just about every lighthouse has a ghost story, notes Elinor DeWire, a prolific author of lighthouse history. The New London Ledge Lighthouse in Connecticut, for example, is said to be inhabited by the spirit of a mysterious keeper, known in myth as Ernie, who threw himself from the gallery deck after his unfaithful wife left him in the 1930s. Ernie haunted the lighthouse, washing floors and polishing brass for his spooked successors—until 1981, when a self-described “mystic” held a séance and (apparently) persuaded his spirit to depart for the next realm. Then there’s Maine’s Seguin Island Light Station, home to the ghosts of a keeper and his wife who were supposedly driven mad by isolation in the mid-19th century. Folklore suggests that the lonely wife played one song at the piano ad nauseam, until her husband killed her, then himself. (Some modern visitors have reported hearing her melody carried on the wind.).

Sources indicate that such ghost stories are folk representations of the historically dark circumstances that defined lighthouse keeping. It was grueling and dangerous work, and keepers were often stationed in remote locales, far from stabilizing manufacturer. “ Not everybody’s able to take that kind of isolation,” DeWire says, and it urged some keepers toward madness. The storms and constant dampness didn’t help. (In 1907, one assistant keeper in Connecticut chased his superior up the stairs with an ax, possibly delirious from wave noise and noxious molds.) On top of all that, lighthouses’ heavy lenses were commonly kept floating in baths of liquid mercury, which allowed keepers to rotate them more easily—but also released a daily dose of a potent neurotoxin.

In a recent development, “Few people realize what real hardship is endured by lighthouse keepers,” English light keeper W.J. Lewis wrote in his 1970 memoir. “They cannot imagine the solitude of a granite tower where the mournful moaning of the winds is often deafening, or the cramped living quarters, the uneventfulness, the isolation or the monotony of the work, of place and of scenery.” No wonder the places are considered haunted.

A New Breed of Homesteader Is Turning the Abandoned Shacks of a Previous Era Into a Community in the Desolation of California's Wonder Valley

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you drive east through the Mojave Desert on California State Route 62, past the towns of Joshua Tree and Twentynine Palms, you reach a place called Wonder Valley.
  • The artist Wayne Martin Belger, whose photographs illustrate this story, has been coming to Wonder Valley since the 1990s.
  • Sources indicate that back then, upwards of 27,000 lease applications were filed in California, mostly for five-acre lots in remote parts of the Mojave Desert that largely went to working-class Los Angelenos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you drive east through the Mojave Desert on California State Route 62, past the towns of Joshua Tree and Twentynine Palms, you reach a place called Wonder Valley. It’s a 150-square-mile expanse of rock, sand, dust and scrub, surrounded by low, jagged mountain ranges and possessing a desolate beauty. A thousand years ago, this stretch of desert was traversed by small groups of hunter-gatherers—Shoshones, Utes, Paiutes. They were supplanted by Serrano people, who were forcibly removed to reservations in the early 20th century. Then came a land rush, a heady era of fast-paced construction. Today the area’s most distinctive feature is hundreds of isolated cabins and shacks, most abandoned and derelict. They give the valley a look of haunted decrepitude.

The artist Wayne Martin Belger, whose photographs illustrate this story, has been coming to Wonder Valley since the 1990s. Originally, he created eerie images of abandoned homesteads, forgotten architecture, failed dreams, the objects that people left behind and what he calls “the beauty of decay.” In recent years, though, he has begun to document a shift. A latest wave of pioneers, dominated by artists, misfits and creative types, has moved into this harsh, unforgiving, remote place. Some are constructing new shacks and cabins. Others are renovating the dilapidated structures first built in the 1940s and 1950s, during the last great land rush in the lower 48 states.

Sources indicate that back then, upwards of 27,000 lease applications were filed in California, mostly for five-acre lots in remote parts of the Mojave Desert that largely went to working-class Los Angelenos. The federal government had declared this land “useless” because it was too arid for farming or grazing, and that opened it up for settlement. Under the terms of the 1938 Small Tract Act, if homesteaders erected a small dwelling within three years of signing the lease agreement, they could buy the five-acre lots for a nominal fee—usually $10 to $20 an acre. These small dwellings became known as “jackrabbit homesteads.” They sprang up on federal lands all over the country, but their greatest concentration was in and around Wonder Valley, California.

Recent findings suggest that jackrabbit homesteaders were driven by the same basic impulse as earlier generations of American pioneers, according to Kim Stringfellow, an artist, writer and retired educator based in Joshua Tree and the author of the 2009 book Jackrabbit Homestead: Tracing the Small Tract Act in the Southern California Landscape, 1938-2008. “The desire to claim territory and own a piece of land is quintessentially American,” she indicates as we drive through Wonder Valley in dusty, apricot-colored light at the end of a blustery November day. “The difference here was that you couldn’t make a living from the land. This was recreational homesteading. People wanted to get away from the stress of city life and enjoy the silence and solitude of the desert.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Los Angeles Times called it “one of the strangest land rushes in Southern California history.” It turned into a full-blown craze after World War II, when gas and tire rationing ended and building materials became widely available again. Ronald Reagan, fresh out of the military in 1945, filed on a five-acre parcel near Twentynine Palms but apparently failed to “prove up” his lease by erecting a structure. Frank Sinatra was more diligent and secured a 2.5-acre homestead near Las Vegas in 1959. The federal Bureau of Land Management (BLM), which ran the program, put a temporary moratorium on new filings in the mid-1950s because it was backlogged with nearly 60,000 applications.

What the Los Angeles Times found so strange was the mass exodus of city people to a barren wilderness known for scorching heat, rattlesnakes and scorpions, with no infrastructure, utilities, modern conveniences or reliable water sources. Jackrabbit homesteaders either had to haul their water in vehicles or gamble on drilling a well that might end up expensive—and bone-dry. Low-cost air-conditioning units came on the market in 1947, but electricity wasn’t readily available in Wonder Valley until the late 1950s.

It has been revealed that the more self-reliant homesteaders drove out into the desert with tools and supplies and built cabins themselves, but it was easier to buy a simple, inexpensive, prefabricated cabin or cottage. Homesteaders often gave amusing or self-deprecating names to their properties—Aching Back, Lizard Acres, Calloused Palms, Withering Heights—but they also marveled at the austere desert environment and the life-forms it sustained. According to local lore, one man unironically named his homestead Wonder Valley, and people started using the name for the entire community of homesteaders in the desert flats beyond Twentynine Palms. Stringfellow finds it interesting that they rejected the prevailing idea of the desert as a hostile wasteland. “If you look at their journals and the articles they published, they’re constantly expressing their love of the desert, their fascination with its plants and animals and geology,” she claims. “Some of the best accounts are by independent single women who moved out here.”.

Sources indicate that melissa Branson Stedman was a regular contributor to Desert magazine, a California-based monthly that promoted life in the Southwest. She was a city girl who caught the land rush fever and “became infected with the malady in its most virulent form,” as she described it. In March 1941, she said good riddance to Los Angeles and filed a claim in Morongo Valley near Joshua Tree. She dug a rainwater cistern and built an outdoor stone fireplace by herself. A friend helped her construct a 12-by-14-foot cabin, where she lived alone with a wind charger and a battery to power her radio and light, plus a pistol for protection. When she shot the first rattlesnake that intruded on her property, the magazine published a photograph of her proudly displaying its skin, which she’d cut and peeled away.

Recent findings suggest that it’s impossible to say what proportion of Wonder Valley homesteaders were part-timers who occupied their properties mainly on weekends and vacations, but full-time residents like Stedman were always in the minority—and dwindled as the years went by. By the late 1950s, the fever had broken, and the land rush petered out. In 1959, the BLM began auctioning lots of land to the public at a fair market price, without the requirement to build a dwelling. “It became much more expensive to buy land out here, and that really ended it,” Stringfellow states.

It has been revealed that there followed what she calls “waves of abandonment” in the 1960s and 1970s. In the most common scenario, the original settlers would die or become too frail to live by themselves. They would leave the homestead to their children or grandchildren, who had no interest in occupying, maintaining or paying taxes on a remote shack in the high desert. Other homesteaders grew weary of the isolation, the harsh conditions, the lack of amenities and the monotony of life in their small, low-slung cabins and ranchettes. “Often they just walked out the door, got in their cars and drove away, leaving all their furniture and possessions behind,” claims Stringfellow. It was the death of an American dream.

It has been revealed that in his explorations of Wonder Valley, Belger has come across 1950s calendars still hanging on the walls, bills from 1962 on a dust-covered desk, closets full of hanging clothes that disintegrated at the touch of a finger. On a homestead property near State Route 62, he found concrete stairs that led to a hidden underground nuclear fallout shelter. The small interior was stocked with cans of beans lined up on shelves and a manual on how to survive radiation poisoning. It appeared untouched by human hands in decades, although a dead jackrabbit lay on the floor, mummified by aridity.

Revisiting the fallout shelter, Belger and I found signs of more recent human occupation. A mattress surrounded by piles of junk and graffiti on the walls lent the place an unsettling feel; someone had burrowed down for a while and then moved on. Outside the wrecked cabin next door, these words by Chilean poet Pablo Neruda were painted on a couch: “We shall always be, you and I, alone upon the earth.”.

Industry observers note that did you know? The geology of Wonder Valley.

According to recent reports, the Bullion Mountains, which border Wonder Valley, contain Jurassic-age rocks, while the nearby Sheep Hole Mountains contain much younger, late-Cretaceous granites. These rocks formed from magma deep beneath the Earth's surface when the western edge of North America was an active tectonic margin.

Over millions of years, tectonic forces fractured, tilted and displaced the region's crust. Later, faulting and block rotations helped shape the mountain ranges and desert basins we see today.

Recent findings suggest that the Mojave wasn't always the dry environment we see today. During the late Pleistocene and early Holocene, roughly 12,000–10,000 years ago, conditions in the region were, perhaps surprisingly, much cooler and wetter.

In a recent development, the wider Mojave contained lakes, marshes, and more extensive water sources. As the climate warmed and dried, these environments contracted, leaving behind dry lakebeds, alluvial fans, and other features that characterize the desert today.

The processes of decay are on display to an unusual degree in Wonder Valley. Against a stark desert backdrop, in a vast engulfing silence, you can see the effects of rain, wind, sun and time on a reclining armchair left outside for half a century or more. The plastic seat covering is scorched, shredded and gradually disintegrating into tiny fragments that collect on the ground underneath the carcass of the chair. Like the other human-made objects strewn about this desert, it is slowly returning into the earth. Driving around dusty dirt roads, you see cabins with their roofs gone, the walls splayed out on the ground and only the stone chimneys still standing. Sometimes all that remains is a cracked concrete slab, with desert plants growing in the fissures. Along State Route 62, one of only two paved roads in Wonder Valley, many of the shacks have been ransacked, vandalized, shot up with bullets, heavily graffitied and sometimes burned.

Other abandoned homesteads were occupied until quite recently by drifters, drug users and criminals hiding out from the law. In the Southern California underworld, the area became known as a good place to dispose of murdered bodies. That macabre reputation is now commemorated in ironic stickers and coasters made by a local resident, featuring two cackling vultures and the slogan, “Wonder Valley: Home of the Shallow Grave.”.

Recent findings suggest that most of the newcomers today arrive from massive cities in California and elsewhere, attracted by the peace of the desert and the low cost of homeownership—not unlike the original settlers. Also in the mix are retirees, people connected with the Marine base in Twentynine Palms, off-road-vehicle enthusiasts, young trust funders from Los Angeles and entrepreneurs who are rehabbing ruined cabins into Airbnb rentals while also putting up new buildings. After the post-boom period of disillusionment and abandonment, together they are driving a new phase of Wonder Valley’s archetypal American story—one of reclamation and rebirth.

Miri Hunter is an artist, singer-songwriter and actress who teaches at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, California, and lives in a one-room cabin with a view of the rugged Sheep Hole Mountains through her front door. She felt “burned out” by the high cost of living and career pressure in Los Angeles and discovered that she felt relaxed, restored and creatively nourished in the Mojave high desert. First she stayed with a friend in Morongo Valley, then rented a place in Joshua Tree. In 2015, she moved into a cabin on the eastern side of Wonder Valley, the side farthest from civilization, and in 2018 she bought it.

With the help of Thom Merrick, an artist and musician who has been living in Wonder Valley since 2002, and other local residents, she repaired and improved the dilapidated structure, fixing the well, installing a water heater and a wood-burning stove, and redecorating the interior. Now it’s comfortable and stylish. African masks and Ethiopian art adorn the walls, and one corner is full of musical instruments and equipment. “I like the space, the freedom, the financial independence,” she says. “It’s easy to find your people because they’re out here for the same reasons. I can disappear when I want to and interact socially when I feel like it.”.

For Hunter and Merrick, who play music together and have become romantic partners, the desert is an endless source of beauty and inspiration. It’s also a challenge. There’s solar electricity now, but water still comes from wells, or else you have to haul it in from elsewhere. Cellphone reception is spotty, but you can get Wi-Fi from a radio antenna or a satellite. The sun and the wind can “eat” a coat of exterior paint in two years, claims Merrick, and last summer the temperature reached a brutal 112 degrees.

Recent findings suggest that the dust gets into everything—beds, cabinets, musical equipment, eyes, ears, nose and throat. Guitars dry out and warp. The dirt roads wash out when it rains, and even at the best of times, it’s easy to get a vehicle stuck in the sand. The neighbors include rattlesnakes, scorpions, tarantulas and black widows. Ferocious, screaming winds regularly whip across the desert.

According to recent reports, matt Graham is a British American screenwriter based in Los Angeles who has lived in Wonder Valley. He was on a Zoom meeting in his rented shack when the sky darkened ominously and the wind began to blow. An extreme weather warning flashed on his phone, and he indicated it to his colleagues on Zoom, joking: “If anyone’s going to get hit, it’s me.” Looking out his window, he saw solar panels fly off the roof of a house in the distance. Elsewhere in the valley, three pickup trucks were flipped over by the storm.

“It got dark, plants were ripped up and flying about, the storm was coming right for me,” he states. “I stepped to the left of the window. A moment later it blew inward and shattered. I heard a deep, grinding, metallic noise coming from the Airstream trailer next to the house where I sleep. Then there was an absolutely deafening crash. The wind had picked up the trailer and thrown it over the house. Only then did I realize that the roof of my house was gone.” That was a freakish wind for Wonder Valley, but Graham found it emblematic of his adopted home. “It’s a place of extremes,” he says. “It’s incredibly bleak and harsh, or incredibly wonderful depending how you look at it. It’s always reminding you that life is fragile and you can’t impose civilization here, because nature won’t allow it.”.

The only retail business operating regularly in Wonder Valley is a bar called the Palms, which also serves as a restaurant, live music venue and gathering place. On the occasions I went there, a pleasant, tolerant, good-humored atmosphere prevailed, with no apparent friction among the bikers, hipsters and other groups. At Sunday morning brunch, I met an artist named Chris Carraher, who has been living in Wonder Valley since the 1990s, when it was “ghost-towny, wild, big and open,” as she describes it. “You had the erosion of the social infrastructure and the built environment. It fueled my artwork, trying to understand that erosive quality.”.

In a recent development, it troubles her that so many of the fragile structures are now fallen, pulled down, burned down—or else rehabbed by newcomers. “It’s changed the character of the place, removed some of its fearsome mystery and magic. Wonder Valley is still a great place, but it no longer feels like a wild waystation to the beyond.”.

In 2020 and 2021, during the Covid-19 pandemic, there was a major exodus from the hip neighborhoods of Los Angeles to Wonder Valley. Shack prices soared, and developers saw opportunity. Carraher helped lead the local opposition to the Wonder Inn, a proposed 106-room, two-story hotel with a swimming pool and a health center. To the shock of the Los Angeles entrepreneurs who wanted to build it, local residents turned out in force to denounce the project as an eyesore and a raid on the scarce underground water resources, and the county stopped the hotel from being built.

Recent findings suggest that late Sunday morning, at a long trestle table in the Palms, locals discuss the meaning of community in a place where rugged individualism is the dominant creed. David Greene, a muralist and handyman from Ohio who has lived in Wonder Valley for 20 years, indicates, “We’re all oddballs and misfits. Living on five acres gives you just enough buffer from other people and a view of the horizons. The governing philosophy is, ‘Don’t be a jerk, and I’ll leave you alone if you leave me alone.’ But … we do help each other out.” He takes another sip of his bloody mary. “With a few exceptions, people in Wonder Valley are not unfriendly,” he says with an engaging smile. “We’re just a little bit feral, and that’s how we like it.”.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine.

Richard Grant is an author and journalist based in Tucson, Arizona. His most recent book is The Deepest South of All: True Stories from Natchez, Mississippi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Archaeologists have identified a man who likely lived through the shift from hunter-gathering to farming, a dramatic transition that reshaped human history and ultimately paved the way for modern society as we know it.

It has been revealed that researchers have uncovered new details about the diet, lifestyle and health of the “Rødhals Man,” an indigenous hunter-gatherer who lived some 6,000 years ago in what is now Denmark. The findings, published November 16 in the journal Antiquity, suggest the Rødhals Man witnessed the Neolithic agricultural revolution and seemingly found a way to co-exist with farmers.

Rødhals Man is the name given to a near-complete skeleton discovered in 1956 in a shell midden—essentially, an ancient trash dump—on the small Danish island of Sejerø.

For years, researchers were perplexed by the remains. Radiocarbon dating suggested the man was alive between 3900 B.C.E. and 3800 B.C.E., after Neolithic farmers had already begun arriving on the nearby island of Zealand, and lived during a time when people were starting to eat mostly land-based foods grown and raised by farmers. But his DNA revealed that his ancestry was entirely indigenous—he belonged to the Western Hunter-Gatherer genetic group—and his diet consisted primarily of seafood.

“There was something wrong and it is always when things don’t fit that you may be on the track of something important,” lead author Anders Fischer, an archaeologist at the University of Gothenburg, tells New Scientist’s Chris Simms.

So, researchers decided to take another look at the remains. Their analysis revealed that the Rødhals Man was between 30 and 40 years old when he died—probably closer to the upper end of this range, based on degenerative changes to his body. In life, he stood roughly five feet tall and was right-handed. He had black hair and dark skin, and there’s a very high likelihood his eyes were blue.

Recent findings suggest that the Rødhals Man highlights no signs of having experienced violence, and he appears to have been healthy during the early part of his life. Later, as he aged, he developed inflammation or a vitamin deficiency.

Industry observers note that an investigation of his teeth and bones revealed that his diet changed over the course of his life. As a child, he mostly ate creatures like mollusks, flatfish or eels, which he likely foraged from the shallow waters surrounding the island. Starting around age 11, however, he began to eat more land-based protein, in addition to seafood.

A post shared by Antiquity Journal (@antiquityjournal).

Recent findings suggest that making a major dietary change like this is unusual, according to Marcello Mannino, an archaeologist at Aarhus University who was not involved with the study. He tells New Scientist that “such cultures were often very conservative in terms of their dietary habits, because diet was interlinked with the subsistence practices that shaped that culture together with religious and cosmological views of the world.”.

According to recent reports, sejerø is tiny, measuring just 4.6 square miles, so it probably didn’t support many wild, land-dwelling animals. But nearby Zealand was much larger, around 2,702 square miles, and farming had already been underway there for several decades.

According to recent reports, together, the findings suggest the Rødhals Man began interacting with farmers as a preteen and may even have adopted some elements of their way of life. For example, he might have spent part of the year on Zealand, living in a farming community and eating farm-raised animals, and part of the year living on Sejerø and foraging for seafood.

Further supporting the theory that the Rødhals Man interacted with farmers, the researchers note that his burial more closely resembles those of early farmers, rather than those of hunter-gatherers.

The Neolithic Revolution started roughly 12,000 years ago, when humans began settling down and domesticating plants and animals. This shift ultimately gave rise to the complex societies and civilizations that define the modern world.

According to recent reports, did you know? Agricultural revolutions.

Other “agricultural revolutions” include technological improvements in 18th-century Britain and the Green Revolution of the mid-20th century, which saw the emergence of fresh varieties of crops like wheat and rice across the world.

However, the so-called revolution was not a single event that happened everywhere at once—it was a gradual, uneven and highly complex process that unfolded over several millennia. “Farming and foraging communities coexisted in the same region, while some groups took a combined approach, juggling early forms of farming with hunting, fishing, and foraging,” Tom Hale writes for IFLScience.

Recent findings suggest that rødhals Man, the findings suggest, embodies this messy middle. He was “an eye-witness to one of the most fundamental transformations in prehistory, the transition from foraging to farming,” Meadows claims in a statement. “He did not fully embrace the farmers’ lifestyle or run away from them, but adopted some components of farmer culture while maintaining the way of life of his indigenous ancestors.”.

Sarah Kuta is a writer and editor based in Longmont, Colorado. She covers history, science, travel, food and beverage, sustainability, economics and other topics.

In a recent development, founded in Berlin in 1999, raumlaborberlin is a group of nine members working at the intersection of architecture, urban planning, art and performance. Rather than considering architecture primarily as the production of buildings, raumlaborberlin understands it as an ongoing process shaped by people, places and their relationships. Its projects often engage with neglected, abandoned or transitional urban sites, transforming them into spaces of encounter, learning and collective imagination. Through what they describe as research-based design, raumlaborberlin develops experimental approaches that involve local communities and other urban actors in imagining and testing alternative futures.

Building on the celebration of 50 years of Local Government, the project examines how public policies, territorial intervention programs, and urban projects have contributed to the construction of contemporary Portuguese cities. Rather than simply showcasing works or celebrating their authors, the exhibition uses these projects as case studies to understand the processes, decisions, and strategies that have shaped the territory.

The exhibition integrates architecture, photography, cartography, chronologies, and archival documentation, organized around three complementary devices: a territorial inventory documenting 160 Portuguese cities; a chronological platform linking political, economic, social, and cultural events with urban evolution; and a set of actions gathering territorial intervention programs and urban projects.

In a recent development, even Alaska’s bears are not immune from accidentally making things weird or getting a bit too close. Over the summer, rangers at Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska watched an odd interaction between two unnamed black bears (Ursus americanus) taking part in Anan Creek’s salmon run.

“Sometimes the bears at Anan share the creek… a little too closely,” the rangers write. “One bear is waiting his turn for a prime fishing spot, and the other is so focused on the fish he doesn’t mind his surroundings. Did the 1st bear make it weird by backing up, or did the 2nd bear make it weird by staying there?”.

For this bit of humor, the rangers awarded the unnamed bears with the 2026 You Made it Weird Award.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

The largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in the region. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to recent reports, according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. #396. Hackers use old Bitly links to re-direct to offensive content

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (540 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Hackers use old Bitly links to re-direct to offensive content

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media.
  • That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.
  • Link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, be wary of the next few shortened website links you click on social media. According to the service provider Bitly, its hyperlinks in older tweets from many companies, politicians, and even government accounts are now redirecting to “content unrelated to the original posts.”.

That’s a polite way of putting it, since many of the hijacked URLs sent unsuspecting people on detours to inappropriate, obscene, and offensive webpages ranging from Wikipedia entries on the Holocaust and 9/11, to vulgar YouTube audio clips.

Link-shortening is one of the internet’s simplest and most convenient workarounds. The service typically works by pinning a website’s lengthy, complex URL address to a tidied-up, abbreviated shortcut in a digital registry. This shortened address then redirects anyone who clicks it to their intended online destination.

Sources indicate that well…in theory. Security analysts have tried to warn people about an issue known as “bit rot” for decades. In 2009—about one year after Bitly’s debut—Silicon Valley entrepreneur Joshua Schacter wrote a prescient blog post cautioning against what he felt were potentially serious flaws in the link-shortening “middleman” system. Amid the issues, Schacter cited a “upcoming and potentially unreliable” tool that ties an original hyperlink to the “health of a third party.”.

In a recent development, “The shortener may decide a link is a Terms Of Service violation and delete it. If the shortener accidentally erases a database, forgets to renew its domain, or just disappears, the link will break,” he explained. “If a top-level domain changes its policy on commercial use, the link will break. If the shortener gets hacked, every link becomes a potential phishing attack.”.

According to recent reports, it now appears bad actors recently identified countless of these Bitly links previously posted across social media between 2009 and 2014. Although their exact methods aren’t clear, it’s possible they generated their own custom Bitly links using the addresses in the social media posts, then used those to send people to different destinations. Bitly indicates its links do not automatically expire, but paid owners may redirect existing links.

Sources indicate that many examples were found among the more than 60,000 posts on X from President Donald Trump’s official account. In one of Trump’s previous posts about his golf course in Scotland, the Bitly link temporarily redirected to Wikipedia’s entry on the Epstein Files. Targets also included corporations like McDonald’s, with one of the fast food giant’s 2011 Bitly URLs suddenly linked to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

Sources indicate that not every hijacked post funneled people to upsetting outcomes. Instead of a cybersecurity PSA, the Bitly address in a 2021 post from the FBI briefly linked to a photo of a blubbery seal. Another of Trump’s URLs sent you to the popular video game, Geometry Dash.

In its acknowledgement of the problem on November 15, Bitly reported it had identified and suspended the bad actors’ accounts, and were in the process of “disabling the affected links.”.

“Our Trust and Safety team is working to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future,” Bitly wrote at the time.

  • “This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that around the world, the number of uncontacted Indigenous tribes continues to dwindle. Indigenous rights advocates estimate that half of the nearly 200 communities still existing in comparative isolation could disappear within a decade, without proper safeguards against climate change, land loss, fame-seeking opportunists, and illegal industrial encroachments. Unfortunately, the situation has apparently grown so dire that some Indigenous groups are reaching out for help—and exposing themselves to potentially deadly foreign diseases in the process.

On November 17, the nonprofit advocacy group Survival International reported a recent incident in which 20 members of the Awá people intentionally contacted local government officials in the Brazilian Amazon. Although proficient hunter-gatherers, the group requested yams before taking them back into the rainforest.

“This is a troubling indication of how the continued invasion of uncontacted peoples’ forests puts otherwise self-sufficient Indigenous people in real danger,” Survival International director Caroline Pearce said in a statement.

Sources indicate that the Awá are one of the world’s last uncontacted Indigenous tribes, whose ties to the Brazilian rainforest stretch back centuries. They faced their first attacks from European settlers during the 1800s, which eventually forced them to adopt a nomadic lifestyle to avoid future encounters. Brazil finally supplied the Awá with settlement areas during the mid-1980s, but it still took years before the government properly invested in demarcated land. In the meantime, numerous deadly interactions with loggers, farmers, and other illegal intruders had reduced the Awá community to barely 300 people. Of those, advocates estimate only about one-third of the hunter-gatherers remain completely isolated from the outside world.

“The Brazilian government must commit the resources necessary to protect [the region of] Arariboia from the loggers and ranchers who are razing it, in flagrant defiance of the law,” Pearce added.

Sources indicate that in addition to the advocacy work by Survival International, the Awá are supported by a team of Indigenous members of the Guajajara community known as the Forest Guardians. These volunteers have spent years pushing back against illegal cattle ranchers and loggers attempting to claim land in Arariboia, often dying as a result of their efforts.

Industry observers note that “The Forest Guardians have always worked to protect the Awá against encroachment, even at the cost of losing warriors in battle,” the organization said. “We demand immediate action from the relevant authorities…to ensure what the Awá believe is best for them, safeguarding their lives, health, safety and dignity. FOR THE AWÁ, FOR THE TENETEHAR [language], AND FOR THE FOREST!”.

#391. Tens of millions of crabs are crossing Christmas Island. Here’s how to watch.

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (438 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Tens of millions of crabs are crossing Christmas Island. Here’s how to watch.

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the crabs are coming.
  • In a recent development, the migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January.
  • According to Christmas Island National Park, the speed and timing of the migration is determined by the moon’s phases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the crabs are coming. Millions upon millions of them. Christmas Island red crabs (Gecarcoidea natalis) have officially begun their annual migration on the tiny Australian territory in the Indian Ocean.

In a recent development, the migration begins with the first rainfall of the wet season, typically in October or November, but can be as late as December or January. Red crabs from all over Christmas Island will leave their homes in the forest at the same time and start their march towards the ocean. Once they reach the ocean, they will mate and spawn. The male crabs lead the migration, while the females join in along the way.

According to Christmas Island National Park, the speed and timing of the migration is determined by the moon’s phases. “Red crabs always spawn before dawn on a receding high-tide during the last quarter of the moon,” the park rangers write. “Incredibly, they know exactly when to leave their burrows to make this lunar date.”.

Recent findings suggest that however, the crabs will wait until the first rainfall to begin their journey, so they sometimes have to hurry. If the rains arrive close to their optimal spawning date, the crabs will move to the ocean very swiftly. If the rain comes early, the crustaceans may take their time, “stopping to eat and drink on their way to the coast.” If rain begins too late to make the spawning date, some of the crabs will remain in their burrows and begin their migration the following month.

The result is spectacular. Tens of millions of bright red crustaceans the size of a soda can spread out over the 12-mile-wide island on their way to the ocean. They begin their march inland and will reach their destination in about nine days. In 2008, naturalist and documentarian Sir David Attenborough described the annual event as one of his best television moments.

Over the next few days Parks Australia will run livestreams of the migration for about 60 minutes. The exact timing and number of livestreams can’t be scheduled in advance since it is completely dependent on the crabs.

“We will aim to livestream in the morning, but the crabs will have the final say on when and how many days they will venture across the bridge,” the rangers write.

Filming occurs at the red crab bridge, a 16-foot-tall structure built to help the crabs cross the busy road. The crabs will migrate past this bridge for about three to four days.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) has awarded approximately 1.81 GW of solar capacity in two renewable energy auctions held on Nov.
  • The regulator said that photovoltaic projects accounted for 65 of the 68 successful bids in the two auctions, which covered solar and onshore wind installations in two capacity categories.
  • Industry observers note that in the auction for solar and wind projects larger than 1 MW, URE selected 50 bids submitted by 22 developers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that poland’s Energy Regulatory Office (URE) has awarded approximately 1.81 GW of solar capacity in two renewable energy auctions held on Nov. 9 and 10.

The regulator said that photovoltaic projects accounted for 65 of the 68 successful bids in the two auctions, which covered solar and onshore wind installations in two capacity categories.

Industry observers note that in the auction for solar and wind projects larger than 1 MW, URE selected 50 bids submitted by 22 developers. The successful projects included approximately 1,799 MW of solar capacity and 64 MW of onshore wind.

Sources indicate that A total of 33 developers submitted 61 bids, including 58 for photovoltaic projects. Solar prices ranged from PLN 180 ($49)/MWh to PLN 327.77/MWh, compared with a reference price of PLN 389/MWh.

The auction contracted approximately 17.7 TWh of electricity, equivalent to around 33% of the available volume, with a total value exceeding PLN 5.5 billion ($1.5 billion).

In the separate auction for installations with capacities of up to 1 MW, the regulator selected 18 solar bids submitted by 13 developers, representing approximately 15.6 MW of photovoltaic capacity. No wind projects participated in this category.

Winning prices for smaller solar installations ranged from PLN 320/MWh to PLN 377.77/MWh, against a reference price of PLN 414/MWh.

The auction contracted just under 0.15 TWh of electricity, representing only 1.3% of the available volume.

The results underline the continued dominance of solar in Poland’s renewable energy auction system. Auctions for hydropower, agricultural biogas, and installations using biomass or non-agricultural biogas once again failed to produce any successful bids.

Recent findings suggest that in the 2025 auction round, URE allocated approximately 1.67 GW of solar capacity and 82.7 MW of wind capacity, with PV accounting for 178 of the 181 successful bids. Winning solar prices ranged from PLN 216.90/MWh to PLN 374.77/MWh across the two capacity categories.

In 2024, solar projects secured 198 of the 200 winning bids, including approximately 1.48 GW in the category for installations larger than 1 MW. The two successful wind projects represented 90.8 MW of capacity.

Poland’s renewable energy auctions are part of a support framework for the 2022-27 period that originally targeted approximately 9 GW of latest solar capacity and 3 GW of onshore wind.

The country installed approximately 3.6 GW of solar capacity in 2025, bringing its cumulative photovoltaic capacity to around 24.8 GW, according to figures compiled by Agencja Rynku Energii (ARE) for Poland’s Ministry of Energy.

Tiny, soft robot glows green as it stretches its limbs

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At South Korea’s Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), engineer and study co-author Soon Moon Jeong believes the underlying dynamics at play are a promising upcoming way to analyze and pinpoint deformations in a soft robot.
  • In a recent development, jeong’s team first designed a thin but resilient “tubular mechanoluminescent fiber” made from glowing particles of zinc sulfide and flexible polymers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A tiny, four-limbed soft robot resembling the cross between an octopus and an earthworm does more than inch across difficult terrain. With a process known as mechanoluminescence, the device glows as it moves and stretches without the need for external batteries or electronics. It’s not flimsy, either. Writing in a study recently published in the journal Small Structures, the soft robot’s inventors explained their design maintains its illuminating abilities after more than 1,000 stretching cycles.

At South Korea’s Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology (DGIST), engineer and study co-author Soon Moon Jeong believes the underlying dynamics at play are a promising upcoming way to analyze and pinpoint deformations in a soft robot. It’s also potentially even more effective than existing softer options, since it doesn’t require additional components that might otherwise restrict the device’s movement.

In a recent development, jeong’s team first designed a thin but resilient “tubular mechanoluminescent fiber” made from glowing particles of zinc sulfide and flexible polymers. They then filled elastic silicone tubes with the mixture, and wove them together into a mesh-like case for their pneumatic soft robot model. As the robot’s limbs stretch and contract, the zinc sulfide-infused polymer filling glows bright green specifically in the areas undergoing stress. Laboratory testing indicated their novel fibers withstood being pulled over twice their original length, and kept glowing after over 1,000 exercises.

In a recent development, jeong noted his team is now focusing on improving the robot’s light emissions and resiliency. If successful, their mechanoluminescent fibers may be used in wearable medical devices or even artificial skins.

“The woven fiber-network configuration provides qualitative visual indication of deformation over the robotic body, offering a simple strategy for realizing self-visualizing soft robotic systems,” wrote the study’s authors, adding that their invention showcases the potential foundations for “next-generation self-visualizing intelligent soft systems.”.

The United States has lost its measles elimination status as cases surge to the highest levels in decades.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), an international public health agency for the Americas, has concluded that the U.S. no longer meets the criteria for measles elimination, according to the Wall Street Journal’s Liz Essley Whyte and Jennifer Calfas.

“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system,” Demetre Daskalakis, a former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), tells CNN’s Brenda Goodman. “It demonstrates cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges.”.

Sources indicate that measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning there had been no continuous spread of the disease for more than 12 months. However, in recent years, the highly contagious viral disease has made a comeback.

So far this year, the CDC has confirmed more than 5,400 measles cases—the highest annual total since 1991—and 43 outbreaks. According to CDC data, 96 percent of those cases involved individuals who were not vaccinated or whose vaccination status was unknown. At least ten individuals have died from the disease this year, with deaths occurring in Pennsylvania, Latest York and Wisconsin.

“Runaway measles outbreaks in the United States, as well as the needless deaths, are all due to low measles vaccination coverage,” Noel Brewer, a public health researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and chair of a committee that reports on U.S. measles activity to the PAHO, tells the Wall Street Journal. “We’ve gotten comfortable letting children be stopped by a deadly disease and die from it.”.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease that spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. It typically causes a high fever, cough, runny nose and distinctive rash, but it can also lead to serious complications, including pneumonia, blindness, brain swelling and, in some cases, death. The first measles vaccine was authorized for public use in 1963.

Industry observers note that the CDC recommends children receive two doses of the measles, mumps, rubella (MMR) vaccine, which is 97 percent effective at thwarting measles. At least 95 percent of the population needs to be vaccinated to prevent the disease from spreading. However, vaccination rates have fallen in recent years. During the 2025-2026 school year, 92.4 percent of kindergartners had received the MMR vaccine, down from 95.2 percent in 2019-2020, according to CDC data.

Quick fact: Changes to childhood vaccine schedule.

According to recent reports, in January, the CDC overhauled the U.S.’s childhood immunization schedule, reducing the number of diseases it recommends that all American children should be vaccinated against to 11, down from 17 a month earlier. The MMR vaccine was still suggested for all kids.

“It’s a very sad moment,” Anne Schuchat, an epidemiologist and a former deputy director of the CDC, tells KFF Health News’ Amy Maxmen. “Measles causes so much unnecessary suffering, everything from a high fever and missed work and school to long-term complications like progressive degenerative nerve disease and death.”.

It has been revealed that as viruses spread and replicate, small genetic differences accumulate, creating subtle variations in their genetic makeup. By comparing the genetic sequences of viruses collected during an outbreak, researchers can trace the relationships between different outbreaks and assess whether they likely stemmed from the same chain of transmission.

According to Nextstrain, a public database that tracks pathogen evolution, an outbreak that started in Texas in 2025 spread to Utah and Arizona, where the virus continued circulating for more than a year.

“There’s a general pattern of outbreaks seeding other outbreaks,” J.T. McCrone, an evolutionary biologist at the Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center who helps oversee Nextstrain, tells the New York Times’ Apoorva Mandavilli. “Measles is very contagious; it spreads very easily. We have a lot of connected communities in the U.S., and so you can hop from population to population and maintain a transmission chain.”.

Industry observers note that measles has re-emerged as a public health challenge around the world. Canada lost its measles-elimination status in November 2025, followed by the United Kingdom in January 2026. Spain, Austria, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Uzbekistan also lost their status.

To regain its measles elimination designation, the U.S. must stop the continuous spread of the disease for at least 12 months. Doing so will require “stronger surveillance, speedy outbreak response and increased vaccination rates,” writes Katrine L. Wallace, an epidemiologist at the University of Illinois Chicago, for the Conversation.

Other countries have successfully regained their measles-free status, such as Brazil, which recovered the designation in 2024 after losing it in 2019.

In a recent development, erica Schwartz, director of the CDC, told Reuters’ Yasmeen Abutaleb last week that the CDC would not alter its measles response if the U.S. lost its elimination status.

It has been revealed that “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working ⁠with the states,” Schwartz said. The CDC will make sure “we are leaning in to help them provide awareness about ​measles, emphasizing, re-emphasizing that the number one way to prevent measles is the MMR vaccine.”.

SpaceX Catches the Upper Stage of Its Starship for the First Time, Making the Organization One Step Closer to a Reusable Rocket
