#322. Latest Update: A French Court Annuls the $1.6-Million Sale of This Camille Pissarro Painting, Allegedly Looted During World War II

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (941 w)
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: A French Court Annuls the $1.6-Million Sale of This Camille Pissarro Painting, Allegedly Looted During World War II

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (941 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in 1941, German forces in occupied Paris looted a Jewish banker’s collection of impressionist artworks.
  • A 1902 landscape by Camille Pissarro titled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing Dock and Duquesne Basin, Dieppe, Sunny Afternoon) was auctioned by Sotheby’s London on June 25, 2024, to an anonymous buyer for roughly $1.6 million.
  • Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in history, seizing more than 650,000 artworks across Europe—some 20 percent of the continent’s art—including from Jewish families, collectors and museums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in 1941, German forces in occupied Paris looted a Jewish banker’s collection of impressionist artworks. Now, more than eight decades later, a French court has stepped in to demand the return of one allegedly looted painting to the descendants of its owner.

A 1902 landscape by Camille Pissarro titled Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée (Fishing Dock and Duquesne Basin, Dieppe, Sunny Afternoon) was auctioned by Sotheby’s London on June 25, 2024, to an anonymous buyer for roughly $1.6 million. On November 5, the Paris Judicial Court annulled that sale and ordered Sotheby’s to “disclose the full identity of the buyer of the work” within two months or pay a $1,115 fine for every additional day it fails to do so, CNN’s Lianne Kolirin reports.

Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in history, seizing more than 650,000 artworks across Europe—some 20 percent of the continent’s art—including from Jewish families, collectors and museums.

Salomon Flavian, a Jewish banker of French and Romanian heritage, purchased Pissarro’s view of the Normandy port town of Dieppe at the Hôtel Drouot auction house in Paris in March 1935, according to the Sotheby’s listing.

When war erupted in September 1939, Flavian placed the canvas and dozens of other works into the care of the Westminster Foreign Bank in Paris. In 1941, German forces seized his collection. Although Flavian survived the war and recovered some pieces, the Pissarro remained missing and was listed in France’s official register of looted property.

Nearly eight decades later, the painting resurfaced at Sotheby’s London with a note stating that it was “offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian.” That settlement had been brokered by the Mondex Corporation, a Toronto-based firm specializing in recovering Nazi-looted art.

Industry observers note that at a hearing in this fall, seven descendants of Flavian told the court that two relatives had signed the deal without consulting the rest of the family. The descendants claimed they had only found out about the sale months later, when Mondex sent a letter explaining that it had accepted in their name a “relatively modest” 8 percent share of the net sale price “in exchange for their cooperation,” while the two heirs who signed the contract received a 16 percent commission, the Art Newspaper’s Vincent Noce reported in September.

Recent findings suggest that at the hearing, Sotheby’s and Mondex presented research claiming that Flavian had parted with the painting before the war, pointing to a 1939 Pissarro catalogue raisonné by Paris dealer Paul Rosenberg that listed British artist and collector Edward Le Bas as the owner. Sotheby’s auction provenance similarly traced the canvas from Flavian to Rosenberg by 1937 and to Le Bas by 1939. It then eventually passed through several American collections, including David Rockefeller’s, and a 1985 sale at Sotheby’s Upcoming York.

According to recent reports, earlier this month, the Paris court rejected that timeline, finding “no direct and convincing evidence” of prewar sales to Rosenberg or Le Bas, according to the Art Newspaper. Instead, the court concluded that the family presented “a set of precise, serious and concurring elements demonstrating that Pissarro’s work was indeed looted during” the war.

The court ordered “the restitution of the work, wherever and in whoever’s possession it may be, to the descendants of Salomon Flavian,” the London Times’ David Chazan reports.

“It is a very important ruling, which opens the way to a restitution that the Flavian family has demanded since the war,” Corinne Hershkovitch, the claimants’ lawyer, tells the Art Newspaper.

Did you know? Looted art on display.

In May, the Musée d’Orsay in Paris opened a new permanent exhibition titled “Who Owns These Works?” It showcases 13 artworks that may have been looted or sold under suspicious circumstances during World War II with the hope that public exposure may help locate the rightful owners.

Mondex, which was ordered to pay $11,000 to the heirs, plans to challenge the verdict. Mondex founder James Palmer tells ARTnews’ Brian Boucher that an appeal will be filed “forthwith.” He adds: “We are confident that when the vast amount of complex provenance research evidence is properly understood and considered that the court of appeal will reach a different conclusion.”.

Because the French judgment applies immediately despite any appeal, the legal battle now shifts toward enforcing the order across the English Channel. Hershkovitch, however, tells the Times that cross-border enforcement between France and England is “a fairly simple procedure.” She adds: “Sotheby’s will have to find a solution very rapidly because their reputation is at stake.”.

Recent findings suggest that in a statement, Sotheby’s London noted its disappointment in the verdict, welcomed the dismissal of charges against the auction house and recognized the “profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era,” per CNN. A spokesperson indicates that Sotheby’s is considering whether to join Mondex’s appeal, while stressing that “client confidentiality is of paramount importance,” according to the Art Newspaper.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

It has been revealed that “These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, noted in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”.

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

Sources indicate that the IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

Industry observers note that one of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting.

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

Recent findings suggest that however, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other looks. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of latest coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

A 16th-Century Castle in England Is Falling Into the Ocean, Sparking a Debate Over Whether It Should Be Saved or Allowed to Disintegrate With Dignity

  • Sources indicate that as the beach gradually eroded away, the castle’s foundations first started to poke through the rocks in 2017, growing weaker each year.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For centuries, Hurst Castle, built on England’s south coast by Henry VIII in 1544 to protect the passage to Portsmouth, was unassailable. Through Tudor spats with France and the Holy Roman Empire, the English Civil War, skirmishes with Napoleon and both world wars, the squat artillery fort was garrisoned and at the ready, but never once attacked. After sitting almost at sea level for four centuries unchallenged, the castle is now under attack from a different sort of enemy, one even more pernicious than the French. Climate change, in the form of rising tides and worsening storms, is washing out the rocky beach from underneath Hurst’s walls.

Sources indicate that as the beach gradually eroded away, the castle’s foundations first started to poke through the rocks in 2017, growing weaker each year. Then, in 2021, its east-facing wall collapsed.

It has been revealed that standing on the eroded shore in front of Hurst on an overcast morning in 2024, castle keeper Jason Crane recalled the calm February day of the breach. He pointed to a gash of rubble where the east wing used to face the waves. “The whole of that wall ejected,” he said. “It puked right out into the sea” and left a 38-ton cannon rolling down onto the beach. Crane has known Hurst since he was a child, playing with crab shells through its halls while his grandfather was castle keeper, so the destruction was wrenching to watch. “The noise was something really low and horrible,” he remembered. “I definitely took it to heart.” Crane means that literally: a month after the collapse he suffered a heart attack from stress.

It has been revealed that in all likelihood, that 2021 collapse was just the opening salvo in a slow siege which could eventually destroy entire sections of the castle. That would mean the end of one of Britain’s most fascinating historical mosaics: 20th-century concrete bunkers built on a Victorian extension of a Tudor venture in castle making.

If you go: Other Tudor castles worth visiting.

Crane, working in concert with English Heritage, the charity that runs England’s historic monuments, has worked on several aims to save the site before the waves come crashing through. After coastal modeling and 3D surveys of the castle’s foundations, engineers estimate they can buy Hurst another few decades. But the work would cost more than £6 million (around $7.5 million), and time is already short. After the first collapse, engineers wired dozens of sensors through the precarious east wing to watch for signs of the next break. “You can’t just leave a pile of rocks,” noted Crane. “It’s definitely going to be a painful process.”.

Hurst therefore presents a fork in the road for English Heritage: fight to preserve a jewel in the country’s historical crown or start curating its transition from a castle into a ruin.

Sources indicate that rob Woodside, who joined Crane in the quest to solve this problem, showed me around the site in October 2024. For the seven years he spent as a director at English Heritage, Woodside worried about Hurst. “It’s a race against time,” he said.

It has been revealed that hurst sits on a small headland. The spit connecting it to the mainland is not as reliable as it used to be, so like most visitors we took a small boat, the Henrietta Rose, steered by a beanie-wearing pilot. As the castle’s outline came into focus, Woodside got nervously animated. “It always feels a little bit like a school trip … really exciting,” he remarked. “And then on the way back I’m more depressed,” he shrugged, “because, oh God, all that we’ve got to do.”.

Industry observers note that from the roof of the Tudor keep—now ringed with World War II anti-aircraft swivels—Woodside’s voice was almost drowned out by an ominously churning patch of water at the foot of the castle walls. Once inside the castle, Woodside walked me up a flight of stairs: “This is the global classroom,” he mentioned, opening the door to Hurst’s old barracks. On the large, wood-paneled floor, we encountered a big, dark puddle. “A leak,” he muttered, craning his neck at the ceiling. “Oh God, please not more.”.

Industry observers note that subsequent monarchs after Henry VIII added to Hurst to protect it against new advances in warfare, not from waves. Each of the Victorian wings is built from heavy Norwegian granite to protect canons and their crews from enemy fire. In the 20th century, the Ministry of Defense added anti-aircraft turrets—all on top of a brick foundation built directly on the beach. Since its first Tudor incarnation, Hurst has become more than a little top-heavy.

As the foundations wore away, in fact, the entire west wing started to rotate under its own weight, spinning slowly and gloomily out toward the sand. From the central keep, I saw a snaking crack along the roof where the structure was beginning to tear away into the water.

Woodside had wanted to be more proactive than previous government stewards of the castle. In 2019, a couple of years into his tenure, English Heritage spent more than $900,000 replenishing the sand and installing wooden barricades to stabilize the castle. But the beach kept disappearing, and those barricades appear to have backfired, casting up particularly aggressive torrents of water during storms. Two years later, of course, the wall collapsed anyway. It became clear, Woodside remarked, that the only way to protect Hurst in the long-term was to try to hold back the sea itself.

First, engineers suggested dropping huge boulders underwater to break up tidal surges. The catch: boulders significant enough to do the job (20 tons each) would have to be shipped from Norway. This strategy, which Woodside called the “gold-plated” approach, would likely have protected the castle for around a century, at a cost of more than $137 million. That would’ve been a landscape-changing feat of engineering that Woodside simply stated was “not for us.”.

Blueprint B still involves substantial boulders—but slightly smaller and strategically placed at the surf line. These rocks would disrupt the flow of water approaching the castle, creating a calmer area where sand doesn’t wash away so swiftly. They would protect the castle for only a few decades, engineers estimate, before the rocks would need maintenance themselves. But an imperfect plan is better than no plan, stated Woodside, and crucially, the smaller rocks cost only the equivalent of roughly $7.5 million.

In a recent development, through most of our interviews, Woodside remained cautiously optimistic about raising that sum. Saving the castle for decades would cost about as much as running the British health service for 15 minutes—his point being that the work might be expensive by heritage standards, but only a drop in the bucket of overall public finances.

In a recent development, then, a month after I visited, the British government’s body for protecting heritage sites rejected Woodside’s pitch. “We had a bit of a crunch, really,” he said when we caught up later. Not long after the news, he left English Heritage.

The decision didn’t just mark the end of Woodside’s hopes of saving Hurst, but the beginning of a strange, liminal time for the castle. Britain has historically notable buildings, and it has historical sites where buildings used to be. As the destruction slowly continues, Hurst is sliding into some uncomfortable middle ground between the two.

According to recent reports, engineers predict that water will finally enter the castle via the first wall that collapsed. “Eventually you’ll have to start to close the western end, then the property entirely, on safety grounds,” Woodside noted. Woodside left emergency instructions behind for when the water starts to break through: which artifacts to remove first; how to shut down the site’s generator. “Basically, you’re in a process of ruination. You’re going from a structure to an archaeological monument.”.

Industry observers note that that means taking stock of the castle “block by block,” said Matt Thompson, a curator at English Heritage who has taken responsibility for Hurst since Woodside left. Archaeologists and curators will give the castle a complete “family history,” after which Thompson wants to bring in locals to build an oral history of the site. “If you think you might lose something, capturing its memory is really key,” he said. “It’s like a grieving process.” Meanwhile engineers will monitor the sensors to gauge when health and safety concerns start to override this memorialization; parts of the castle will gradually grow unsafe and be cordoned off.

According to recent reports, after the first collapse and his heart attack, Crane entered counseling to deal with the stress and, he said, guilty  feelings. Now he is finished with grieving. “I probably took too much to heart,” he said. “You have to detach; I step back from it a lot more emotionally now.” He is even prepared to be merciless about how to save the castle, suggesting tearing down the newer Victorian wing before it falls in a storm and damages the Tudor parts in the process. “The same gun emplacements are replicated a number of times through the castle,” he said. “How do you choose which part of history is vital?”.

Recent findings suggest that thompson was keen to stress that English Heritage has not committed to a single plan nor to letting Hurst simply “fall into the sea.” Still, he offers a different view on the changes shaking the castle. “You can’t stand there and turn the tides,” he said. “[But] there are lots of things you can do to try and preserve the idea of a place, even if its actual fabric is under severe pressures.”.

In a recent development, hurst will not be the first ruins wrought by climate change. From old slave-trading forts in Ghana to Ernest Shackleton’s Antarctic expedition hut on Ross Island, conservationists are working to save waterfront monuments from warming and rising oceans. Droughts brought the Cambodian city of Angkor to its knees in the 15th century, while in modern-day Scotland, some historians think sea level rise, not Vikings, may have displaced Pictish settlements in the sixth century. Nor will Hurst be the last climate ruin: In August, academics from the United Kingdom, Greece and South Africa published a list of nearly 400 coastal World Heritage Sites that are at risk from erosion, storms and rising seas.

Perhaps Hurst will still be a flagship for coastal monuments, just not in the way English Heritage first thought: not a model of preservation, but the herald of a newer, more sweeping era of curated ruination. “We can choose to see that as something we want to arrest … or we can begin to embrace the beauty that comes with the different stages of the life of a place, a thing, a person,” Thompson said. “Impermanence is actually quite a beautiful thing.”.

Eagles will typically defend their nest from intruders so Shadow’s willingness to share his space with an eagle other than Kaydee surprised many viewers.

Shadow returned the nest solo later in the afternoon as the sun set over Significant Bear Lake.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

Sources indicate that joshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to blueprint a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers revealed that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, remarked Frieman, now at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”.

In a recent development, within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

In a recent development, now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” remarked Simone Ferraro, a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”.

Joshua Frieman, a physicist at the University of Chicago, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro stated.

In a recent development, experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

It has been revealed that in previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

Industry observers note that but newly introduced observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

It has been revealed that then came the bombshell 1998 findings that the expansion of the universe was not actually slowing down; it was ever so slightly speeding up. By the end of the year, the unknown stuff driving that acceleration had a name: dark energy. Frieman charged off to measure it.

In 1998, cosmologists were like detectives with a thin dossier. They had a blurry image of light from the early universe known as the cosmic microwave background (CMB). And they had observed several million galaxies, along with dozens of supernovas. Because light takes time to travel, these observations gave cosmologists snapshots of what the universe looked like at different moments over the past few billion years.

The Dark Energy Camera holds an array of charge-coupled devices, or CCDs, similar to the sensors in normal digital cameras but designed specifically for astronomy.

It has been revealed that DOE/FNAL/DECam/R. Hahn/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

In a recent development, that was just enough data to show that the universe was experiencing an unexpected growth spurt. But to figure out exactly when it had started and how fast it was happening, Frieman and his colleagues would need to fatten their file. Their solution was DES.

In a recent development, DES began in 2003, with a handful of physicists at Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory brainstorming what it would take to get a more comprehensive view of the cosmos. They went on to design and build the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera, the most powerful digital camera of its era, and install it on the 4-meter-wide Blanco telescope in the Chilean Andes. They then used it to conduct the Dark Energy Survey, which ran for 758 nights between 2013 and 2019. During this time, DES increased the number of recorded galaxies to hundreds of millions. DES was supposed to end in 2018, but the researchers extended it to make up for lousy observations due to clouds from a strong El Niño season.

According to recent reports, every couple of years the DES collaboration, which grew to include more than 400 scientists across seven countries, would analyze the data they had collected so far to see what it suggested about the history of our universe. Again and again, what they found was consistent with the theory that had coalesced after the 1998 supernova papers: The universe was about 30% matter (mostly an invisible and lethargically drifting “cold dark matter,” or CDM), and the remaining 70% of the universe was dark energy. Physicists noted that this energy acted like an unchanging property of the vacuum of space, referred to as “lambda.” The bigger space gets, the more of this vacuum energy there is, and the faster the cosmos expands. This theory of the universe became known as Lambda-CDM.

In a recent development, then, in 2024, researchers from a next-generation experiment, DESI, combined the DES observations with a sharper image of the CMB and new observations of their own. They found that the Lambda-CDM theory no longer quite fit.

Whereas DES uses one big camera in Chile, DESI at Kitt Peak in Arizona uses thousands of tiny eyes. Each can swivel to focus on a single galaxy. The individualized attention more precisely captures each galaxy’s motion.

According to recent reports, this technology lets DESI see hidden cosmic structures. Due to the way that sound waves rippled through matter in the early universe, spherical shells of slightly dense matter formed. Over time, matter in these shells gathered into galaxies. Each shell is the same size, so by looking at how substantial or small it appears from Earth, scientists can tell how far away its galaxies are.

Combining the distances to the galaxies with other observations, the researchers can calculate how fast the universe has grown over the past 10 billion years or so (out of the 13.8 billion years since the Major Bang).

Young stars emitting stellar winds shaped the dust and gas of the Dragon nebula, captured here by the Dark Energy Camera, into a form that resembles a pair of fighting dragons.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA.

In 2024, the DESI collaboration dropped a bombshell report. When researchers added their shells to the existing dossier, they couldn’t get the Lambda-CDM model to fit all the data. What fit better was an exotic theory that replaced lambda, the constant vacuum energy, with a different form of energy that weakened over time. A year later, an analysis of more data found the same thing.

It has been revealed that in the meantime, the DES collaboration continued to analyze the galaxies they had photographed. Those researchers focused on building a different contribution to the dossier: a detailed record of a cosmic tug-of-war.

It has been revealed that while gravity pulls matter — mostly dark matter — together, dark energy fights back, pushing matter apart. By measuring how much matter has clumped together in different eras, cosmologists can infer the strength of dark energy over time.

DES assesses this clumping using three methods, explained Sujeong Lee, a physicist at Ohio University. First, DES measures how tightly galaxies of visible matter cluster together, which reveals how much dark matter floats around them. Second, it maps out visible matter in the foreground by looking for the ways it distorts light coming from galaxies in the background. And third, it maps out foreground dark matter in a similar way.

Industry observers note that each of these measurements involves comparing pair after pair of DES’s hundreds of millions of galaxies, looking for tiny distortions in their positions and shapes. After seven years of rigorous analysis, the collaboration published their final results in early 2026. “It’s been a real tour de force,” remarked Ferraro, who isn’t part of DES. “It pushed the analysis to a newly introduced level.”.

In a recent development, alongside these measurements, DES also reprocessed a catalog they had compiled of 1,600 recently observed supernovas, establishing the sharpest view yet of the modern universe. “I trust the DES-reanalyzed supernova data much more than I trust any other supernova dataset,” said Seshadri Nadathur, a DESI cosmologist.

Recent findings suggest that cosmologists have now assembled their thickest file on the universe to date. DES merged its map of matter clumping, its supernova catalog, DESI’s galaxy shells, and a CMB image, then checked to see how well Lambda-CDM could still account for the whole cosmic history.

The answer: not very well. In their final report, DES scientists found that their data fit somewhat better with the theory that dark energy is not stable and has slackened in recent eons. In the statistical language of physicists, DES reports a “three-sigma” preference for the new theory. That’s significant enough to make people pay attention, especially since it combines data collected in different ways, but it falls far short of the “five-sigma” confidence physicists need to claim a new discovery.

Industry observers note that the Dark Energy Camera was mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope, famous for its role in the 1998 discovery that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, a process thought to be driven by dark energy.

CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA/R. Hahn (Fermi National Accelerator Laboratory).

Adding to the intrigue, DES found that the mismatch can’t be explained away if, for instance, one of the datasets holds some hidden error. If you assume Lambda-CDM is right, the CMB picture doesn’t quite match the matter maps; the matter maps don’t quite match the supernovas; and the supernovas don’t quite match the CMB picture. There is no single item that you can toss from the file to make everything fit, so no single observation looks fishier than the others.

This suggests that the tension is less likely to be a random artifact — the kind that could easily arise from the merger of millions of observations using different instruments — and is more likely to reflect a clash between the real universe and our understanding of it. “There’s something that doesn’t fit,” Ferraro stated. And “we’re trying to figure out what that something is.”.

Sources indicate that some theorists are deeply skeptical of the idea that dark energy can change. They already face a major challenge in explaining why the vacuum of space has the specific energy that it seems to have — an almost imperceptible amount of oomph filling every cubic kilometer of space. Confirmation that dark energy is also changing would layer on a second major challenge: explaining why that mysteriously tiny amount of energy is evaporating at a mysteriously slow rate.

Some cosmologists wonder if they should tweak other assumptions of Lambda-CDM instead, such as the time at which early stars (and possibly other bright objects) burnt off a hydrogen fog that filled the early universe. Lambda-CDM puts this event at roughly 700 million years after the Significant Bang. But if this happened roughly 200 million years earlier, Ferraro and collaborators found in a 2025 analysis, then Lambda-CDM would fit the cosmological data better. “This number is crucial,” Ferraro said. “However, it’s extremely hard to measure.”.

Sources indicate that the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, seen here, sits on Cerro Pachón, about six miles from Cerro Tololo, the home of the Dark Energy Survey.

RubinObs/NOIRLab/SLAC/NSF/DOE/AURA/A. Pizarro D.

Other theorists are looking into the implications of a changing dark energy, such as the possibility that it could shift in tandem with the mass of dark matter.

For observational cosmologists, the next steps are clear: Keep fattening the dossier on the universe. While DES has ended, DESI will continue collecting data until at least 2028. And on the summit of Cerro Pachón in Chile, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory started its survey operations in 2026.

Rubin is a spiritual successor to DES. It now holds the honor of hosting the world’s largest digital camera, and astronomers expect its powerful eye to spot roughly 10 billion — with a “b” — galaxies. DES veterans are already flocking to the Rubin collaboration to help analyze those galaxies, pair by pair, just as they did for DES.

Recent findings suggest that back in the 1990s, the quickening expansion of the universe became clear from the motions of just a few dozen supernovas. Rubin should find millions more. In a dossier comprised of millions of supernovas and billions of galaxies, an exquisitely detailed cosmic history — and an accounting of the forces that shaped it — will be laid bare for all to see.

#315. Latest Update: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Latest Update: These Adorable Hatchlings Are From the U.S. West Coast's First Known Natural Sea Turtle Nests. Now, They've Returned to the Wild

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast.
  • Recent findings suggest that the two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County.
  • Sources indicate that aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, stated Lance Adams, the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in September, authorities in California were baffled to find two sea turtle nests on their beaches—the first natural ones ever confirmed on the United States’ West Coast. Now, dozens of the eggs have hatched. Experts released the baby olive ridley turtles over the weekend, allowing the tiny creatures to begin their perilous journeys to adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that the two nests were identified on Seal Beach and Huntington Beach in Orange County. Because a tropical storm was coming soon after the nests were found, biologists moved the more than 200 eggs to the Aquarium of the Pacific. The Ping-Pong ball-size spheres stayed in closed incubators under sand in a temperature- and humidity-controlled room, simulating their ideal natural conditions.

Sources indicate that aquarium staff first saw signs of hatching activity on November 12, when they noticed changes in the surface of the sand in the incubation container with the Seal Beach eggs, stated Lance Adams, the aquarium’s veterinarian, during a press conference on November 14. The team spotted a depression and some cracks in the sand, indicating something was happening beneath it. The first turtle emerged the following day at around 7:15 p.m. Pacific time. Around two hours later, more of the baby turtles from the Seal Beach nest started popping out, resulting in 54 squirming critters.

“It kind of went from looking like very smooth beach sand to looking like an eruption of baby sea turtles,” Adams explained. It “was really exciting and very, very cute.” As of the press conference date, 50 eggs from the nest had not hatched. Experts do not know whether they’re viable, but they will continue monitoring the makeshift home.

The Seal Beach hatchlings were released in the same location where their nest had been, very early on Saturday morning, before the sun had risen, according to a social media post. That’s because baby turtles use moonlight to navigate toward the ocean. After reaching the water, hatchlings experience a “frenzy period” in which they swim continuously for 24 to 48 hours, according to the post. The energetic outburst is justified; experts estimate that only one in 1,000 olive ridley turtle hatchlings survive to adulthood, according to a statement.

In a recent development, the Huntington Beach eggs weren’t too far behind, with many hatchlings emerging shortly after the Seal Beach eggs. They were returned to Huntington Beach on Sunday, also under the cover of darkness during the wee morning hours. All the released hatchlings made it to the water, according to the statement.

Industry observers note that did you know? Tiny turtle species.

Olive ridley turtles are among the smallest sea turtles in the world, growing to approximately two feet long and weighing between 70 to 100 pounds.

Sources indicate that olive ridleys are some of the most abundant and widespread sea turtles in the world. Unfortunately, all their populations are considered threatened or endangered. The species is mostly found in the tropical regions of the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, and experts still don’t know why or how these nests ended up in the contiguous United States.

It has been revealed that “There’s never been a recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on a California beach,” Jeff Flocken, president and CEO of the Aquarium of the Pacific, told SFGate’s Olivia Harden in September. “Typically, the most north we know of any olive ridley or any sea turtle that nests are in Mexico, so this is quite a bit farther north for them.”.

According to recent reports, around that time, Justin Viezbicke, California stranding coordinator for the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, told the Guardian’s Lois Beckett that the mother turtles may have lost their way because of a hurricane. The ongoing “super” El Niño in the Pacific Ocean, which is affecting water temperatures, currents and weather, may also have helped push them to California.

However, biologist Jonathan Snyder, of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, has a more hopeful outlook. “I think the warm waters along the coast are certainly part of the story, but I think there’s another really important part of the story,” he said during the press conference.

Decades of sea turtle conservation efforts have “really moved the needle” for olive ridleys, he noted. “Their populations have increased substantially throughout the portions of the range, and it’s the reason that there are these sea turtles along our coast that could take advantage of these unique environmental conditions.”.

It has been revealed that in fact, authorities found a third nest farther north in California’s Ventura County on November 1, but it was destroyed by high tides, Snyder tells the Los Angeles Times’ Corinne Purtill. Regardless, experts still aren’t sure whether the recent nests will continue to represent an unusual event or they are the start of a latest normal.

In a recent development, margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science, Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass.

#314. The Bloomsbury Group's Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Tangled Their Art and Lives Together for Decades. A Final Sketch of Bell on Her Deathbed Just Resurfaced After 60 Years

The Bloomsbury Group's Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant Tangled Their Art and Lives Together for Decades. A Final Sketch of Bell on Her Deathbed Just Resurfaced After 60 Years

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell—collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.
  • The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms.
  • In a recent development, grant and Bell were often the subjects of each other’s work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The lives of artists Duncan Grant and Vanessa Bell—collaborators, companions and sometimes lovers—were deeply intertwined both on canvases and in private quarters.

The pair were central figures in the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of artists and intellectuals active in early 20th-century Britain who radically, and often controversially, challenged contemporary creative and social norms. These included public sentiments on philosophy, sexuality and mental illness. The group featured, among others, the economist John Maynard Keynes, as well as the writers E. M. Forster and Virginia Woolf, Bell’s biological sister.

In a recent development, grant and Bell were often the subjects of each other’s work. Among their most well-known collaborations is one of Grant’s first and most extravagant depictions of Bell, a full-length portrait painted in 1915.

But this summer, while preparing for “Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury,” an exhibition that opened this week at Tate Britain, scholars discovered an intimate, previously unknown work that sheds new light on the end of Grant and Bell’s relationship.

Recent findings suggest that hidden for some 60 years among private family papers, the newly recovered drawing is thought to be Grant’s final depiction of Bell. Created in an uncharacteristically simple style—soft monochrome pencil and biro on paper—the piece highlights an ailing Bell with her eyes closed, head resting on a pillow, from the perspective of an artist who likely was sitting at her bedside. In the bottom right-hand corner, Grant dated the piece April 14, 1961—one week after Bell succumbed to an illness at the age of 81, and two days after her burial.

Sources indicate that “I found this drawing deeply moving when I first saw it. We know Duncan’s drawings of Vanessa so intimately, made over the course of their long friendship, that the discovery of a previously unknown work is remarkable in itself,” Nathaniel Hepburn, director of Charleston, the pair’s former home and studio in East Sussex, indicates in a statement. “But there is something incredibly poignant about imagining Duncan sitting beside Vanessa, drawing her after her death.”.

According to recent reports, the drawing is considered an emotional bookend to the pair’s decades-long relationship. In a 1937 letter to her son, Bell described Grant as “so incredibly full of charm, his genius as an artist seems to overflow so into his life and character & he is so amusing too and odd and unaccountable that lots of people I think don’t see clearly what to me is really his most adorable quality—his honesty…”.

Scholars believe that Grant may have erred slightly, perhaps affected by grief, in his dating of the drawing.

Industry observers note that “What seems very likely here is that Duncan knew this drawing had been made around Vanessa’s death and later added a date from memory,” Darren Clarke, head of collections and research at Charleston, indicates in the statement. “He got remarkably close, but apparently not quite close enough. Everything about the drawing itself—its viewpoint, its intimacy and its extraordinary economy—suggests someone sitting quietly beside Vanessa’s bed and drawing the face he had known for half a century.”.

Though it won’t feature in the newly introduced Tate show, the drawing will enter into a permanent collection at Charleston as part of the institution’s “50 for 50” campaign, which seeks to secure 50 more works by prominent Bloomsbury Group figures by 2030. In May 2027, after the completion of renovations, it will be put on display for the very first time.

Did you know? Bell and Grant’s daughter.

Bell had a daughter, Angelica, with Grant in 1918. Bell raised Angelica as the daughter of Clive Bell, her husband, and did not reveal Angelica’s true father until she turned 18.

At the Tate exhibition, which opened last week and runs through April, some 300 portraits, still lives, landscape paintings and other works guide visitors through the intertwined lives of Grant and Bell, as well as their involvement with the Bloomsbury Group.

“It’s so fascinating to see the ways they differ,” Thomas Kennedy, curator of Modern British art at Tate Britain, tells the Art Newspaper’s Andrew Pulver. “We should recognize their individual accomplishments of course, but also the works they made together and how they influenced each other.”.

“Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury” is on view at Tate Britain in London until April 11, 2027.

Christian Thorsberg is an environmental writer and photographer from Chicago. His work, which often centers on freshwater issues, climate change and subsistence, has appeared in Circle of Blue, Sierra magazine, Discover magazine and Alaska Sporting Journal.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) is advising households with solar installations to check if their current energy contract is still the most suitable ahead of the end of net-metering on Jan.
  • Recent findings suggest that the end of net metering will mean households can no longer offset electricity exported to the grid against electricity imported from it.
  • The regulator adds that the feed-in payment is generally lower than the retail electricity rate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Netherlands Authority for Consumers and Markets (ACM) is advising households with solar installations to check if their current energy contract is still the most suitable ahead of the end of net-metering on Jan. 1, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the end of net metering will mean households can no longer offset electricity exported to the grid against electricity imported from it. ACM’s latest patch explains that from the start of next year, households will pay the full retail electricity rate, including energy taxes, for power drawn from the grid, while receiving a separate feed-in payment for surplus electricity.

The regulator adds that the feed-in payment is generally lower than the retail electricity rate. Under Dutch legislation, suppliers must pay at least 50% of the basic electricity supply rate, excluding taxes, for exported electricity until Dec. 31, 2029.

ACM is expecting feed-in charges to decline after the scheme ends, as suppliers will no longer incur costs associated with net metering, but adds that suppliers will continue to face other costs related to solar customers, including expenses associated with balancing the electricity grid when solar generation fluctuates unexpectedly.

Industry observers note that ACM, which is responsible for supervising the tariffs of energy suppliers, indicates it will now include contracts with feed-in charges for solar panels in its monthly overview, known as Energiemonitor. Its most recent monitor says a number of suppliers are charging significantly higher rates for their standard contracts as opposed to dynamic contracts.

The discontinuation of net metering may make home batteries more attractive for some households, ACM added.

The number of home batteries is growing significantly in the Netherlands. Figures from ACM state approximately 89,000 home batteries belonging to households and small businesses were registered with grid operators by the end of October but add that as small plug-in battery systems are not always registered, the total is likely even higher. Total installed home battery capacity amounted to 1.1 GW by the end of October, compared to 0.3 GW at the end of October 2025.

ACM claims consumers considering a home battery should carefully check what best suits their individual situation.

“Whether a home battery is worthwhile depends, among other things, on the home, energy consumption, and the energy contract,” the regulator noted. “Before purchasing a home battery, it is therefore wise to first determine how much energy you use, where you can save, and what suits your home.”.

It also warned against unreliable sellers taking advantage of the uncertainty surrounding the end of the net metering scheme.

“They are luring consumers into expensive purchases with misleading sales pitches, sometimes home batteries costing more than €20,000 [$22,035],” ACM said.

ACM’s latest patch also reveals that negative electricity prices in the Netherlands at the moment stand at just over 400 in 2026, lower than in the same period of 2025 and 2024. The regulator claims a possible explanation for this is the increase in the number of installed batteries.

Cumulative solar capacity in the Netherlands reached 29.4 GW by the end of last year, according to figures recorded by the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO), 43% of which was located on the rooftops of homes, smaller commercial buildings and public buildings.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The number of corporate solar power purchase agreements (PPAs) signed in Japan is increasing, according to analysis from infrastructure intelligence platform Global Infrastructure Sherpa.

Roberto Krell, founder of Global Infrastructure Sherpa, told pv magazine the tech giant logged around 30% more corporate solar PPAs in Japan from January to October this year than across the first ten months of 2025.

Industry observers note that notable examples of agreements signed this year include two solar PPAs between Microsoft and pan-Asian renewable energy platform Blueleaf Energy, confirmed late last month, with Microsoft acting as the sole offtaker for two solar projects due online mid next year. In May, Spanish developer EDP Renewables commissioned a 44 MW solar project in Fukushima for Amazon under a long-term corporate PPA.

Global Infrastructure Sherpa claims that while large-scale players, such as Microsoft and Amazon continue to attract attention, Japan’s corporate PPA market is moving beyond the hyperscalers with manufacturers, logistics companies and advertising groups also entering into long-term solar agreements.

Examples include a 15-year virtual PPA involving a 54 MW solar plant and approximately 130 MWh of battery storage between Japanese manufacturer NSK and Tokyo-based developer Eneos Renewable Energy and a 20-year solar PPA in Hyogo and Kyoto between Nippon Electric Glass and Japanese utility Kansai Electric that is expected to begin delivery in March next year.

Krell told pv magazine climate targets are driving corporate solar PPAs in Japan, with some companies looking to solar deals to meet carbon-neutrality targets.

He cited virtual PPAs as another factor, noting that many of this year’s corporate solar PPAs are virtual. “The tech giant buys the green certificates from a newly introduced solar plant at a fixed price and keeps its existing electricity supplier,” Krell explained. “That makes a deal much easier to sign, and it’s bringing in buyers that wouldn’t have signed a few years ago, such as railways, retailers and mid-sized manufacturers.”.

It has been revealed that krell looked to data centres as another driver. “Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Equinix and At Tokyo have all signed solar PPAs in Japan, and theirs tend to be the large ones,” he stated. “[Data center company] Equinix’s 121 MW deal in February is the biggest corporate solar PPA we’ve seen in Japan this year, followed by Tokyu Railway’s 98 MW.”.

Krell predicted that the upward trend in corporate solar PPAs in Japan is likely to continue in the coming years.

“The data centre build-out around Tokyo and Osaka hasn’t peaked yet, and every new campus is another potential buyer. More companies also have climate targets to meet, and virtual PPAs make it easy for them to sign,” he told pv magazine. “What could slow things down may be challenges like finding good sites without local opposition, and getting grid connections in time.”.

Analysis published last year by data platform Japanese Energy Hub noted that, since the first corporate PPA in Japan was signed in 2021, the number of disclosed deals has grown to over 500, totaling over 2.5 GW in installed and planned capacity.

Japan’s cumulative solar capacity is estimated at around 100 GW after adding approximately 5.8 GW of solar last year.

South Korea opens storage subsidy call for community solar villages

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Korea Energy Agency (KEA) mentioned last week that it has launched its 2026 Community Solar program.
  • The KEA said the program is intended to help establish “sunlight income villages” in parts of the network that have little spare capacity left for fresh generation.
  • The call for proposals runs from Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Korea Energy Agency (KEA) mentioned last week that it has launched its 2026 Community Solar program. The initiative supports energy storage systems run by VPP operators in grid-saturated areas.

The KEA said the program is intended to help establish “sunlight income villages” in parts of the network that have little spare capacity left for fresh generation. Under the government’s sunlight income village policy, residents take part in local renewable energy projects, and the generation revenue goes to village welfare and community activities.

The call for proposals runs from Nov. 13 to Dec. 11. The KEA mentioned it will accept applications by email from 9 a.m. on Nov. 16 until 6 p.m. on Dec. 11 (KST). The online notice does not state the program’s budget, subsidy rate or project size limits. The agency has attached the program’s operating rules to the notice, along with a document on the status of distribution lines by region in areas linked to the solar villages.

South Korea selected 86 communities for the scheme from 129 applicants in the first round. A second call drew 617 applications from 116 cities and counties. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety is targeting 700 solar villages in 2026 and 2,500 by 2030 under South Korea’s community solar cooperative push, with financial support covering up to 85% of solar installation costs.

The storage subsidies add to South Korea’s grid-scale procurement. In September, the government tendered 6.6 GWh of six-hour storage under 15-year contracts, and it aims to ease storage container rules as part of a battery deregulation push.

The program also follows South Korea’s launch in July of its first distribution-line energy storage program and a grid overhaul aimed at connecting more than 100 GW of renewables in October. The country is forecast to add 3.5 GW of solar in 2026.

Coal plant failure, not solar PV, triggered Sri Lanka’s latest blackout

💡 Key Takeaways

  • This emerges from a preliminary investigation report submitted by the National System Operator (NSO) to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), which explicitly identifies the sudden loss of generation from Lakvijaya Coal Power Plant Unit 1 (LVPP Unit 01) as the initiating event of the blackout.
  • “LVPP Unit 01 rapidly de-loaded from the unit net generation of 187 MW to 5 MW within 450 ms,” the authors of the report state, noting that grid frequency fell from 49.906 Hz to 48.75 Hz within two seconds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the cause of Sri Lanka’s nationwide black occurred on Oct. 17 was the the loss of 187 MW of electricity from a coal power plant and not the high solar PV penetration as initially thought.

This emerges from a preliminary investigation report submitted by the National System Operator (NSO) to the Public Utilities Commission of Sri Lanka (PUCSL), which explicitly identifies the sudden loss of generation from Lakvijaya Coal Power Plant Unit 1 (LVPP Unit 01) as the initiating event of the blackout.

“LVPP Unit 01 rapidly de-loaded from the unit net generation of 187 MW to 5 MW within 450 ms,” the authors of the report state, noting that grid frequency fell from 49.906 Hz to 48.75 Hz within two seconds.

The unit has a capacity of 300 MW and is located at the 900 MW Norochcholai Power Station in Puttalam, in the country’s North Western Province.

The report does not fully explain why the coal unit lost output or whether distributed PV behaviour contributed to the cascading failure.

Industry observers note that following the blackout, the NSO instructed all PV system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid. The decision appeared to have been informed by a previous nationwide blackout on Feb. 9, 2025, when the Ceylon Electricity Board (CEB) identified high solar PV penetration as a major contributing factor.

Industry observers note that according to a CEB investigation published in April 2025, the blackout was triggered at noon by a fault at the Panadura grid substation. At the time, solar PV accounted for more than 50% of electricity demand, leaving the grid with insufficient system inertia to withstand the disturbance. The resulting voltage drop and cascading disconnections led to a nationwide blackout.

At the time, the authorities also instructed rooftop solar system owners to disconnect their installations from the grid during restoration efforts.

Sri Lanka’s rooftop PV capacity reached 1.94 GW by the end of 2025, following rapid growth in installations and generation.

Sri Lanka’s daily electricity demand stood at approximately 58 GWh to 60 GWh in March 2026, equivalent to an average continuous power requirement of around 2,400 MW to 2,500 MW.

#308. Breaking: Why silicon won the solar race and what emerging PV technologies can learn from thin film

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (929 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Breaking: Why silicon won the solar race and what emerging PV technologies can learn from thin film

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Crystalline silicon has dominated the global photovoltaic market for decades, while alternative technologies, including thin-film solar cells, have struggled to secure a comparable market share.
  • The study, “Technology (Non)Emergence: How System Interdependencies Among Activities by Heterogeneous Actors Shaped Alternative Solar Technology Trajectories,” published in Organization Science, examines how manufacturing capabilities, accumulated industrial knowledge, investment patterns and policy support influence competition between PV technologies.
  • In a recent development, “We can think of competition as competition between manufacturing ecosystems, rather than competition in terms of technological characteristics such as efficiency, cost or other design elements,” lead researcher Mara Guerra told pv magazine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Crystalline silicon has dominated the global photovoltaic market for decades, while alternative technologies, including thin-film solar cells, have struggled to secure a comparable market share. This dominance is often attributed to technological performance, cost competitiveness and efficiency improvements. However, research from City St George’s, University of London, challenges this explanation, suggesting that the commercial success of solar technologies depends on more than their technical characteristics.

The study, “Technology (Non)Emergence: How System Interdependencies Among Activities by Heterogeneous Actors Shaped Alternative Solar Technology Trajectories,” published in Organization Science, examines how manufacturing capabilities, accumulated industrial knowledge, investment patterns and policy support influence competition between PV technologies.

In a recent development, “We can think of competition as competition between manufacturing ecosystems, rather than competition in terms of technological characteristics such as efficiency, cost or other design elements,” lead researcher Mara Guerra told pv magazine. “This does not mean that technological characteristics are not notable, but that competition depends on how manufacturing ecosystems evolve with respect to market requirements.”.

According to Guerra, even technologies with promising performance characteristics may struggle commercially without the manufacturing infrastructure, industrial expertise and market support needed to scale production.

“Not even the best-performing tech can succeed if the system of activities around it fails to support its interface with evolving requirements of the market,” she stated.

The researchers found that thin-film PV technologies could have achieved greater commercial success if industrial investments and policy interventions had followed a different path.

“Hindsight is amazing, but thin film could have had greater success with a different pattern of investment across the ecosystem,” Guerra stated.

Industry observers note that she explained that thin-film technologies struggled to compete in mainstream PV markets, which benefited from policy support and increasingly established manufacturing capabilities. At the same time, some of their characteristics made them suitable for emerging applications, such as building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV), which received comparatively limited policy attention.

“Its characteristics made it ideal for niches such as building-integrated PV which did not receive as much support. Bold policy interventions in these more transformative markets may have helped thin film achieve a larger market share,” Guerra remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the study also identified shortcomings in investment strategies across the thin-film industry. Rather than prioritizing shared manufacturing knowledge, compatibility with existing industrial processes or expertise from related sectors, investments often focused on the technological uniqueness of individual approaches.

While this differentiation helped attract investors, it did not necessarily support manufacturing scalability.

“Higher investments that rewarded reusing existing manufacturing knowledge or focusing on manufacturing compatibilities could have contributed to more rapid scaling of the technology and larger market share in the mainstream markets,” Guerra said.

The findings suggest that commercial success depends not only on technological breakthroughs, but also on the ability to develop manufacturing processes and industrial knowledge that can be replicated and deployed at scale.

The researchers noted the historical development of thin-film PV offers important lessons for emerging technologies, including perovskite solar cells and silicon-perovskite tandems, which are attracting significant investment but still face commercialization challenges.

According to Guerra, developers should focus on two priorities: demonstrating reproducible technological performance and balancing innovation with manufacturing standardization.

It has been revealed that “Firstly, entrants must move beyond technological records to achieve credible and replicable performance earlier on,” she mentioned. “Technological breakthroughs are useful to build expectations, but in the end commercialization requires demonstrating that these breakthroughs can be consistently reproduced.”.

Industry observers note that laboratory efficiency records can generate investor interest and strengthen expectations surrounding emerging PV technologies. However, they may also introduce uncertainty if the reported performance cannot be consistently reproduced.

“Performance records attract investment and generate enthusiasm but may also create unrealistic expectations. When performance records cannot be verified or replicated, they can create more uncertainty than they resolve,” Guerra mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that the second lesson concerns the relationship between technological differentiation and industrial standardization. According to the researcher, thin-film manufacturers frequently emphasized proprietary technological approaches and distinct manufacturing ecosystems, limiting opportunities to benefit from established industrial knowledge and common production practices.

Recent findings suggest that “Thin film overemphasized uniqueness across technology and ecosystems. This helped with attracting investment but undermined scalability,” Guerra remarked. “Those who combined innovation and uniqueness in their technology with standardization in manufacturing or leveraging existing knowledge from related industries did better when commercializing their technology.”.

The findings also have implications for governments seeking to develop domestic PV manufacturing capabilities and compete with established production ecosystems.

It has been revealed that according to Guerra, mature industrial ecosystems benefit from accumulated manufacturing expertise, supplier networks and industrial knowledge that reinforce their competitive advantages. Although these advantages become increasingly difficult to challenge over time, they do not necessarily prevent fresh manufacturing ecosystems from emerging.

“While challenging an established advantage is increasingly difficult, especially when it is based on existing manufacturing ecosystems that have accumulated capabilities and knowledge that positively reinforce each other, this does not obstruct the creation of new successful and competitive manufacturing ecosystems,” she said.

Guerra argued that the effectiveness of public support depends on how emerging industrial ecosystems position themselves relative to established competitors.

Rather than attempting to replicate existing manufacturing structures or directly displace dominant producers, policymakers could support complementary technologies, specialized manufacturing activities and upcoming market segments.

“The effectiveness of public support in creating competitive manufacturing ecosystems depends on how fresh ecosystems position themselves relative to others,” Guerra said. “Rather than trying to replicate or dislodge an existing ecosystem, focusing on support or complementary technologies and activities can contribute to the creation of a new and localized industrial advantage.”.

#307. Tech Report: Silver prices find $50 floor as solar industry seeks to accelerate shift toward copper

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Tech Report: Silver prices find $50 floor as solar industry seeks to accelerate shift toward copper

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Silver prices appear to have stabilized around $50 per ounce following an exceptionally volatile year, but the photovoltaic industry should not expect a return to the much lower prices of previous decades, according to Philip Newman, managing director of Metals Focus.
  • “I think the price, the floor seems quite strong, but I think you’re still going to see more volatility,” Newman told pv magazine.
  • His comments follow the publication of fresh silver market estimates by the Silver Institute and Metals Focus on November 13.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silver prices appear to have stabilized around $50 per ounce following an exceptionally volatile year, but the photovoltaic industry should not expect a return to the much lower prices of previous decades, according to Philip Newman, managing director of Metals Focus.

“I think the price, the floor seems quite strong, but I think you’re still going to see more volatility,” Newman told pv magazine. “Could prices dip below 50? Of course they can. But I think the 50 still seems like a decent floor.”.

His comments follow the publication of fresh silver market estimates by the Silver Institute and Metals Focus on November 13. The organizations expect the global silver market to record its sixth consecutive annual deficit in 2026, with demand exceeding supply by 35 million ounces.

Silver reached an all-time high of $121.65 per ounce on January 26, driven by strong investment demand and tight physical liquidity in London. It subsequently retreated to approximately $52 by November 4, as shifting US interest rate expectations, a stronger dollar and rising bond yields weighed on precious metals.

Despite the correction, prices remain exceptionally high. The annual average was approximately $40 in 2025, while Newman suggested the 2026 average could exceed $70 per ounce.

The impact of elevated prices is particularly apparent in photovoltaics, where manufacturers are accelerating efforts to reduce silver consumption.

In a recent development, according to Metals Focus, global industrial silver demand is expected to decline by 3% to 640 million ounces in 2026. Industrial consumption outside photovoltaics is forecast to grow by 4.5% to 492 million ounces, but this will be more than offset by weaker demand from solar cells.

The consultancy attributes the decline to slower-than-expected PV installations, particularly in China, and accelerated silver thrifting and substitution.

In a recent development, newman remarked the industry’s response to higher prices has evolved significantly over the past year. When silver first exceeded $50 in late 2025, manufacturers focused on extending silver-coated copper metallization, already used in heterojunction (HJT) cells, to tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon) technology.

Replacing silver entirely with copper was still regarded as a longer-term objective because of potential performance trade-offs. However, January’s price surge changed the discussion.

“Let’s move to copper and we can think about the trade-off afterwards and improve the efficiency,” Newman remarked, describing the industry’s initial reaction.

Since then, the transition has become more measured, with manufacturers considering not only conversion efficiency but also long-term reliability.

“I think the move to copper has now become more measured,” Newman said, pointing to growing attention to “the shelf life, the longevity of these cells.”.

According to Newman, the transition is also shaped by diverging interests among manufacturers and module buyers.

For manufacturers facing overcapacity and intense price competition, reducing silver consumption represents an opportunity to lower costs. Developers and installers, however, may hesitate to adopt new metallization technologies without sufficient evidence of long-term reliability.

In a recent development, “From the panel manufacturer, to your point about overcapacity and the pressure on costs, they would really like to move to copper quite quickly,” Newman said. “On the other side, the companies that are buying those panels and installing them, I think there’s a lot more hesitancy, more reticence, more cautiousness about doing so.”.

This divergence could encourage manufacturers to offer conventional high-silver modules alongside alternatives with reduced silver content or potentially silver-free metallization.

Although research into copper metallization has intensified, fully copper-based solutions have yet to become mainstream in commercial TOPCon products. Intermediate approaches involving silver-coated copper or lower silver loadings appear more realistic in the near term.

The economic incentive remains substantial even after the recent price correction.

Newman estimated that at $60 per ounce, silver accounts for approximately 17% of TOPCon module costs. At $50, the proportion falls to around 14%, compared with roughly 11% when silver traded at $40.

In a recent development, metals Focus expects global PV installations to decline modestly in 2026 before returning to growth in 2027. Nevertheless, Newman expects silver thrifting to continue, even if prices stabilize.

Despite the sixth consecutive annual market deficit, Newman does not anticipate a physical shortage that would materially disrupt photovoltaic manufacturing.

“No, not really,” he said when asked about potential supply problems.

He pointed to China’s substantial silver imports in 2026, continued availability of silver powder from Japan, and gradually recovering inventories in London.

In a recent development, the Silver Institute expects total silver supply to decline by 3% to approximately 1.045 billion ounces in 2026. Mine production should remain broadly stable at 834 million ounces, while recycling is forecast to increase by 6% to 210 million ounces.

The overall deficit is expected to narrow from 54 million ounces in 2025 to 35 million ounces in 2026, bringing the cumulative shortfall since 2021 to approximately 746 million ounces.

Newman acknowledged that sudden increases in investment demand could generate temporary physical market tightness.

“I don’t think you would ever say never, but I think it’s unlikely,” he mentioned when asked about a repetition of the severe market tightness experienced in October 2025.

He added that metal could be transported from CME inventories to London to relieve pressure, even if renewed investment demand temporarily pushed silver lease rates higher.

Looking beyond photovoltaics, Newman believes monetary policy and investor expectations will remain major influences on silver prices.

Geopolitical tensions can support precious metals through safe-haven demand, but rising energy prices can also reinforce inflation concerns and expectations of higher US interest rates.

“I think you’re going to look at each on a case-by-case basis,” Newman noted, referring to the impact of geopolitical crises such as the war in Iran.

Silver’s outlook also remains closely linked to gold, which Newman expects to face continued pressure until Federal Reserve policy becomes clearer.

“I think gold will remain under pressure until we have clarity from the Fed,” he said, although he believes the $4,000-per-ounce level could hold.

Metals Focus‘ central scenario assumes tensions surrounding Iran will gradually de-escalate sufficiently to ease inflation expectations and limit further US interest rate increases. Under those conditions, investment demand for precious metals could strengthen again in 2027.

“Maybe it doesn’t happen that early next year. But maybe by the summer, prices for gold and silver are considerably higher than we see today,” Newman said.

Sources indicate that for the photovoltaic industry, such a scenario would reinforce the case for reducing silver consumption, even if the recent price correction has eased immediate cost pressures. The central challenge remains balancing the savings offered by copper-based metallization against the efficiency and long-term reliability requirements of commercial solar modules.
